title: Metal: add SSD expert streaming for Qwen3.8 Flash Next
body:
Qwen3.8 Flash Next currently rejects `--ssd-streaming`, so the Q2 pack requires about 41.73 GiB of resident weights even though its n-gram table already stays on disk. This change enables routed-expert SSD streaming through the existing option on single-host Metal. The Q2 model runs on a 32 GiB M1 Max.

Dense/shared/GDN/attention/HC weights remain mapped. Routed experts use the existing explicit-pread cache, extended to 512 IDs and top-10 routing. A function constant switches the existing row/MM/NAX kernels between contiguous weights and expert addresses; their arithmetic and final reductions are preserved. Q2 down projections retain their physical 768-column stride with 640 logical activations.

Cache overflow and differently sized MTP layers use compact owned buffers containing only the distinct selected experts, addressed through private tables with the original expert IDs. This preserves the trunk cache. Selecting every expert, or running without GPU buffer addresses, retains the three contiguous full-layer reads. All staging buffers survive until GPU completion, including unretained command buffers; read failures propagate without falling back to rereading the whole layer.

Cache sizing conservatively reserves static weights, context, GDN/PLE recurrent state, MTP snapshots, prefill workspace, two full staging windows and runtime headroom first. Session creation and direct generation also check their additional memory. Router/list validation, read-error recovery and command-buffer lifetimes are covered by tests.

### Validation

Executed on Apple M1 Max, 32 GiB:

- Full `make -j4 all` build and `test-qwen4-memory`.
- New `test_qwen4_ssd_experts`: bitwise resident/SSD parity for mid, down, reduce and HC with IQ2/Q2, Q4/MXFP4 and Q8; 1–128 tokens, IDs through 511, cold/warm cache, eviction, overflow, invalid input, failed reads and retries. Also passed with `DS4_METAL_UNRETAINED_COMMAND_BUFFERS=1`.
- A test-only Metal backend intercepts actual `pread` calls, rejecting unselected expert ranges and checking byte totals: ten experts for off-size MTP, 24 for overflow, zero reads for cache hits, and the full 512-expert fallback. Production builds continue to call the system `pread` directly.
- Existing Qwen MoE decode specialization and ordered Q4 geometry tests; existing Metal SSD IQ2, Q4 and MXFP4 tests and host cache sizing. After selective staging, reran the resident MoE exact and Metal SSD IQ2 tests.
- Real-model `test_qwen4_ngram_state MODEL.gguf --ssd-streaming`: two sessions with a 1024-expert cache; exact logits after simulated read failures during prefill, decode and MTP.

### MTP performance

Compared selective staging with the initial full-layer streaming implementation (`e37f185`) in three alternating before/after runs. Model: `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf`; prompt: `narrami la storia di roma`; 29 prompt tokens; `--ctx 4096 --prefill-chunk 128 -n 50 --temp 0 --nothink --mtp-timing`.

- Median MTP generation: **4.55 -> 7.86 t/s (+72.7%)**.
- Generated output was identical in all runs, with 27 verifier cycles and 21 accepted drafts per MTP run.
- A separate profiling comparison reduced expert bytes returned by `pread` from **48.40 -> 12.02 GiB (-75.2%)**. These counts include filesystem-cache reads.

The performance result is specific to this short MTP workload.

### Scope and limitations

- Single-host Metal only. CUDA/ROCm execution and M5 NAX execution were not tested.
- Expert reads currently finish before routed computation; I/O overlap and next-layer prefetch remain future work.
- Off-size MTP experts are staged again on each invocation; their temporary buffers do not replace trunk cache entries.
- Qwen demand-fills its cache; popularity preloading and GLM full-resident-layer options are rejected.

Example:

```sh
./ds4 --metal -m /path/to/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf \
  --ssd-streaming --ctx 4096 --prefill-chunk 128 --mtp \
  -n 50 -p "narrami la storia di roma" --temp 0 --nothink
```

title: Remove unsupported Hugging Face download resume promise
body:
`./download_model.sh ds41f-q2` uses `hf download` but tells users that rerunning an interrupted download will resume it. That promise is incorrect with `huggingface_hub 1.31.0`: a new attempt creates a fresh temporary file instead of reusing the previous partial file.

Remove the unconditional resume message from `download_one_hf()`. The curl path retains its message because it explicitly uses `curl -C -`.

Evidence from the Hugging Face v1.31.0 source (links pinned to its commit):

- [`_download_to_tmp_and_move`, lines 1961–1970](https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface_hub/blob/495b17c8529614759ae0f1ccf1ebe9a61c148b7c/src/huggingface_hub/file_download.py#L1961-L1970) creates a UUID-suffixed temporary filename and opens it with `wb`. The preceding comment explains that shared partial files could be corrupted by concurrent writers on filesystems whose locks are not honored.
- [Lines 1978–2009](https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface_hub/blob/495b17c8529614759ae0f1ccf1ebe9a61c148b7c/src/huggingface_hub/file_download.py#L1978-L2009) use that temporary file for the Xet or HTTP transfer, then delete it in `finally` on failure. The cleanup comment explicitly explains why that partial file cannot be reused.

This removes a guarantee the wrapper cannot make across installed Hugging Face client versions. It does not change download behavior.

Validation: `sh -n download_model.sh`; `python3 tests/test_model_download.py` (9 tests passed); `git diff --check`.

title: perf(v41): reuse gathered KV across scalar reuse layers
body:
V4.1 scalar decode gathers the same compressed KV rows again in every Reuse layer. These layers retain their source layer's KV owner and selected indices, and the gathered buffer stays live until the next index source. Gather once at each source and reuse those rows for subsequent layers.

The change is restricted to resident, single-box Metal scalar decode. Projected prefill/batch rows keep their own gathers. Rollback: `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_V41_REUSE_GATHER=1`. No new allocation or arithmetic changes; this PR is independent of the queue and fusion PRs.

Measured on an M3 Ultra 512 GB (60 GPU cores), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Q4_K, context 32768, 668 prompt tokens, 256 greedy output tokens, ABBA:

| Branch | Rollback t/s | Reuse t/s | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| This PR, `c3f5621` | 16.62 / 16.63 | 16.64 / 16.62 | flat |
| Integration stack, `8a486d9` | 30.96 / 31.13 | 31.45 / 31.42 | +1.26% |

The integration stack includes queued decode (#1041), parallel Engram reads (#1035), fusion (#1042) and group6 experts (#1043). The gain is visible with those scheduling improvements; standalone performance is flat.

All eight generated outputs are byte-identical, MD5 `40e4c6fa5651b8ca8be4a2cb5eb1166e`. On this PR's exact commit, `make -j8 ds4 ds4-bench tests/test_deepseek41_metal`, the full V4.1 Metal suite (including sparse gather), `--hc-scaled` and `--bf16-linear` passed. On integration, all three fusion tests passed, as did the M4 Pro CPU build.

Reproduce A/B with `./ds4 -m /path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-Q4.gguf -p "$(head -c 2000 speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt) Continua la storia:" -n 256 --temp 0`; set the rollback env for A. Each measurement fetched the committed SHA into an isolated Studio clone.

title: Qwen tool-call error: say where the tool name belongs
body:
### The slip

Qwen3.8 sometimes opens a tool call with `<parameter=NAME>` where `<function=NAME>` belongs, while still closing with `</function>` — so it knows the wrapper, it just mis-spells the opener:

```
<tool_call>
<parameter=bash>
<parameter=command>
ls
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
```

In one long session here that was 5 of 98 stanzas — `bash` parsed fine 38 times and failed 4. Not a parser bug: `agent_qwen_tool_parse` is right to reject it.

### Why the message matters

The old text stated only the expected shape. To the model that reads as a description of the call it believes it already wrote, so it hunts for the fault somewhere else. Verbatim from the transcript, after the first failure:

> The error was about tool call syntax... odd. Possibly the `$R` with `---` confused parsing? Let me just re-run with simpler command.

It blamed a string in its own shell command and simplified that command to route around a problem that did not exist. It recovered, but for the wrong reason, and lost the turn.

The worst instance cost 2604 tokens and 1m6s: a complete file body generated into `<parameter=write>` / `<parameter=path>`, discarded whole, then regenerated.

### The change

One message, plus a regression test:

```
expected <function=...> in Qwen tool call: the tool name goes in
<function=NAME>, not <parameter=NAME>
```

No behavioural change — same condition, same point, same state.

### Why not quote the offending tag

That was my first attempt and I backed it out. `agent_dsml_feed` parses per streamed byte, so this branch decides after as few as two (`<p`) — the full tag is not in the buffer yet. Waiting for it means waiting for bytes whose verdict is already known, and since `agent_dsml_finish` does not re-parse, a stream ending inside that wait would leave the stanza in neither DONE nor ERROR and swallow it silently. That trade seemed clearly wrong for a diagnostic.

### Testing

`make ds4_agent_test` builds clean, no new warnings. Test suite shows the same 2 pre-existing failures before and after this commit (`tests/ds4_agent_test.c:249`, cwd-related, also failing on untouched `main` here); no new ones.

title: Fix GLM-5.3 Metal decode masking for padded selections
body:
GLM-5.3’s pooled selection pads unused tail slots with 0xffffffff. The serial decode call currently passes selected_rows_valid = true, causing Metal’s split-group8 kernel to skip bounds checks and read those slots as cache rows, diluting the attention output.

This addresses the decode counterpart of the prefill masking fix in 0e9cc2d.

title: Link the HIP runtime explicitly on ROCm builds
body:
`make strix-halo` fails to link on hosts that use Fedora's distro ROCm packages
(ROCm 7.1, `ROCM_PATH=/usr`, libraries in `/usr/lib64`):

```
ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: hipSetDevice
ld.lld: error: undefined symbol: hipMalloc
... (all HIP runtime symbols)
```

Every translation unit compiles; only the final link fails.

## Root cause

`hipcc` hands the linker an empty `-L` immediately before `-lamdhip64`:

```
... ds4_rocm.o ... -lm -pthread -lhipblas -lhipblaslt -lrocblas -L -lamdhip64
```

The bare `-L` consumes `-lamdhip64` as its directory argument, so the HIP
runtime is never linked. `hipcc -v` shows why: clang's HIP installation
detection comes up empty on this layout (`Found HIP installation: , version
3.5.0`), because the distro package does not use the single-prefix `/opt/rocm`
tree that the detector expects.

## Fix

Name the runtime in `ROCM_LDLIBS`. On a normal AMD `/opt/rocm` install clang
already links it, so this is a harmless duplicate; the link records a single
`DT_NEEDED` entry for `libamdhip64`.

## Testing

- Fedora 44, Ryzen AI Max+ 395 / Radeon 8060S (`gfx1151`), distro ROCm 7.1:
  `make strix-halo` fails before and succeeds after; `ldd ds4` shows
  `libamdhip64.so.7`.
- Fedora 44 container with the same distro ROCm packages: the unpatched tree
  fails at link, the patched tree builds all five binaries and
  `tests/test_mxfp4_rocm`.

Compiling and linking need no GPU, so this is reproducible in CI. The
maintained container uses AMD's official ROCm 10.0 under `/opt/rocm`, which
does not hit the bug.

title: Shutdown checkpoint is never found on restart when the conversation began after another live conversation in the same process
body:
**Build:** main `9139e2a`, Metal, M4 Max 64 GB, `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf` (self-contained), `--mtp -c 163840 --prefill-chunk 1024 --kv-disk-dir DIR --kv-disk-space-mb 16384`. Same result on ivanfioravanti/ds4-metal `6c1e836` (identical `ds4_kvstore.c`), so it predates the Qwen merge and is not specific to this model's checkpoint payload.

## Repro (10 minutes, two small OpenAI-compatible clients)

1. Conversation **A**: 4 chat turns, ~35–40K tokens.
2. Conversation **B**: 8 turns with tools, ~80K tokens. B's first request logs
   `live kv cache miss live=38403 prompt=11129 common=3 vision=match reason=token-mismatch`
   then `kv cache stored tokens=38403 ... reason=evict` (A goes to disk), and B is prefilled.
3. `SIGTERM` the server. Log: `persisting resident KV cache before shutdown slot=0 tokens=79188` → `kv cache stored tokens=79188 ... reason=shutdown key=token-text`. The file is on disk; its header SHA matches its text; the text starts with B's system prompt.
4. Restart with the same flags and `--trace`; resend B's exact history plus one user turn (~90K tokens).

**Result: full re-prefill.** Trace for that request:

```
memory_miss_reason: no-live-checkpoint
cache_source: none
cached_tokens: 0
disk_cached_tokens: 0
```

No `kv cache hit` and no `kv cache skipped` line; the lookup found nothing, not even B's smaller continued checkpoints.

## What does and does not matter (all tested)

| Variant | Restores after restart? |
|---|---|
| B alone in the process (no A), empty cache dir | **yes** (`cache_source: disk-text`, 80,091 tokens, ~0.3 s) |
| B alone, cache dir at budget (`--kv-disk-space-mb 3072`) | yes |
| A (with tools) then B (with tools) | **no** |
| A **without** tools, then B with tools | no |
| A with tools, then B **without** tools | no |

So tool calls, cache pressure and the eviction order of #444 are ruled out. The one condition that flips the result is whether B started **cold** (fresh process, live position 0) or **warm** (another conversation was live; B's first request matched a few common tokens of it and the rest was re-prefilled). In every warm case B's first continued checkpoint lands at 8,192 tokens instead of the cold case's 10,240, so B's session bookkeeping differs from the first turn on.

## Where I got to in the code (pointers, not a diagnosis)

- `ds4_kvstore_find_text_prefix` hashes the prompt prefix against every index entry (longest SHA1 match), so a miss means no stored text is a byte prefix of the replayed prompt.
- The stored text comes from `slot->thinking_live.visible_text` / `responses_live.visible_text` when that record is valid and `live_tokens == tokens->len` (`kv_cache_store_current`, ds4_server.c ~11275), otherwise from `ds4_kvstore_render_tokens_text` (detokenised). `token_text_disk_key` is set from `prompt_preserves_reasoning && !visible_continuation`.
- My guess is that after a warm start the stored text for B is produced on a different path than after a cold start (detokenised vs the client's rendered text, or with/without the thinking-visible handling), so its SHA1 can never equal the hash of the client's bytes. I did not verify which branch was taken; a log line naming the text source at store time would settle it in one run.

## Why it matters

A daily server always has other conversations behind it (cron jobs, side requests), so in practice the live conversation is never restored after a graceful restart; at 160K that is an ~8-minute first turn every time the service restarts.

Clients used: two ~150-line Python scripts (streaming, tools); happy to attach them or run a variant with extra logging.

title: Progressive JPEG: AC refinement scan desynchronises mid-stream, ds4_image_decode_memory fails on files libjpeg decodes cleanly
body:
**Environment**

- ds4 commit `9139e2ae58a41503968a500f36f75895c1ba63fc` (main, 2026-09-14)
- macOS 26.5.2, Apple M4 Pro, 64 GB, Apple clang 21.0.0
- No model involved: `ds4_image.c` compiled standalone, exactly as `tests/test_jpeg_decode.py` does.

**Summary**

A share of ordinary progressive JPEGs are rejected with `invalid or unsupported JPEG image`.
libjpeg-turbo (`djpeg`) and Pillow decode the same bytes without a warning. The failure is inside
the progressive AC **refinement** path (`Ah != 0`), mid-scan, with plenty of entropy data left.

On a set of 50 photographs from our own pipeline, 15 fail. Re-encoding the pixels at a different
quality does not simply fix them: 10 of the 15 start decoding and **7 files that decoded before
start failing**. So the trigger is a property of the coefficient data, not of a particular camera
or file.

**Steps to reproduce**

```sh
cc -shared -fPIC -O2 ds4_image.c -lm -o image.so
python3 - <<'PY'
import ctypes
class Img(ctypes.Structure):
    _fields_ = [("width", ctypes.c_uint32), ("height", ctypes.c_uint32),
                ("rgb", ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_uint8)), ("fingerprint", ctypes.c_uint8 * 32)]
lib = ctypes.CDLL("./image.so")
lib.ds4_image_decode_memory.argtypes = [ctypes.POINTER(Img), ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_size_t,
                                        ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_size_t]
enc = open("ds4-progressive-refine-320x240-q85.jpg", "rb").read()
img, err = Img(), ctypes.create_string_buffer(256)
rc = lib.ds4_image_decode_memory(ctypes.byref(img), ctypes.create_string_buffer(enc, len(enc)),
                                 len(enc), err, len(err))
print("rc", rc, "err", err.value)
PY
```

The attached file is generated (drawn text over pseudo-random noise); it contains no photograph
and no personal data. It was produced with nothing but:

```sh
cjpeg -quality 85 -progressive -outfile out.jpg in.ppm     # libjpeg-turbo, default scan script
```

Roughly one in five images generated this way is refused, so the attachment is one instance of a
class, not a hand-crafted edge case.


**Generator for the reproducer class** (no attachment needed; about one in five outputs is refused — try seeds 1..6):

```python
# needs: pip install pillow numpy ; and libjpeg-turbo's cjpeg on PATH
import subprocess, numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
def make(w, h, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    img = Image.new("RGB", (w, h), (247, 245, 240)); d = ImageDraw.Draw(img); y = 4
    while y < h - 10:
        d.text((3, y), "SYNTHETIC 0123456789 ABCDEFG", fill=(12, 12, 16)); y += 12
    arr = np.array(img).astype(np.int16) + rng.integers(-18, 19, size=(h, w, 3))
    return Image.fromarray(np.clip(arr, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8))
for seed in range(1, 7):
    make(320, 240, seed).save(f"in{seed}.ppm")
    subprocess.run(["cjpeg", "-quality", "85", "-progressive", "-outfile", f"repro{seed}.jpg", f"in{seed}.ppm"], check=True)
```
Then run the `ds4_image_decode_memory` probe above on each `repro{seed}.jpg`; `djpeg` decodes all of them.

**Expected**

`rc == 1`, matching libjpeg:

```sh
$ djpeg -pnm ds4-progressive-refine-320x240-q85.jpg | head -c 15
P6
320 240
255
```

**Actual**

```
rc 0 err b'invalid or unsupported JPEG image'
```

**Where it goes wrong**

Instrumenting a copy of `third_party/iris/jpeg.h` to log the scan header and the failing block:

```
SCAN 1  ss=0 se=0  ah=0 al=1  ncomp=3
SCAN 2  ss=1 se=5  ah=0 al=2  ncomp=1
SCAN 3  ss=1 se=63 ah=0 al=1  ncomp=1
SCAN 4  ss=1 se=63 ah=0 al=1  ncomp=1
SCAN 5  ss=6 se=63 ah=0 al=2  ncomp=1
SCAN 6  ss=1 se=63 ah=2 al=1  ncomp=1
SCAN 7  ss=0 se=0  ah=1 al=0  ncomp=3
SCAN 8  ss=1 se=63 ah=1 al=0  ncomp=1
SCAN 9  ss=1 se=63 ah=1 al=0  ncomp=1
SCAN 10 ss=1 se=63 ah=1 al=0  ncomp=1
FAIL ac_refine scan=10 by=9 bx=33 of 40x30 pos=3244/10514 eof=0 eobrun=0
```

Every scan before the last luma AC refinement decodes. In scan 10,
`jpeg_prog_decode_ac_refine()` returns -1 after `jpeg_decode_huffman()` runs out of valid codes
(`third_party/iris/jpeg.h:391`), with the bitstream only 31% consumed and `eof` clear — i.e. the
reader has drifted out of alignment somewhere earlier in that scan rather than hitting the end of
the data.

The same signature appears on real photographs (a 1200x1600 file fails at scan 8 of 8,
`Ss=1 Se=63 Ah=1 Al=0`, block (116, 95) of 150x200, `pos 73742/139400`, `eof=0`).

**What we ruled out**

Rejected and accepted files are structurally identical: SOF2, 8-bit, 3 components, 4:2:0, no
restart interval, 2 quantisation tables, 7 Huffman tables (max code length 16 bits in both
groups), the same 8-scan script, the same 5 DHT segments after the first SOS, JFIF only, no fill
bytes, no trailing bytes. `jpegtran` keeping the coefficients and re-emitting them **baseline**
makes all 15 decode; re-emitting them **progressive** with libjpeg's default script leaves all 15
failing. So it is neither the container nor the scan script.

Two candidate areas in `jpeg_prog_decode_ac_refine()`, offered only as pointers:

1. `size != 1` is treated as fatal (`return -1`). libjpeg warns (`JWRN_HUFF_BAD_CODE`) and
   proceeds as if `s == 1`. That difference alone turns a recoverable stream into a hard failure.
2. The correction-bit loop and the `if (size == 1 && k <= dec->se)` commit after it advance `k`
   in a slightly different order from libjpeg's `do { … } while (k <= Se)` plus the outer `k++`,
   which is where a one-coefficient drift would come from.

Happy to test a patch against the 50-file set and report back.

title: server: advertise the loaded GLM model id in /v1/models
body:
## Summary

- derive the advertised GLM model ids from the loaded engine instead of
  hardcoding `glm-5.2*`
- GLM 5.3 now reports `glm-5.3-flash`, `glm-5.3-flash-chat`,
  `glm-5.3-flash-reasoner`
- GLM 5.2 keeps `glm-5.2`, `glm-5.2-chat`, `glm-5.2-reasoner`

## Why

`send_models()` hardcodes the `glm-5.2*` ids for every GLM DSA engine, so a
server loaded with GLM 5.3 advertises `glm-5.2` while its `name` field already
says "GLM 5.3 Flash". `server_model_id_from_engine()` already distinguishes the
two, and the `-chat`/`-reasoner` aliases are already recognized by
`model_alias_disables_thinking()`, `model_alias_enables_thinking()` and
`server_model_alias_known()`. Only the list endpoint was wrong.

## Tests

Built and run on Strix Halo ROCm (`gfx1151`) with
`gguf/GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2.gguf`:

    glm-5.3-flash           | GLM 5.3 Flash | ctx 1000000
    glm-5.3-flash-chat      | GLM 5.3 Flash | ctx 1000000
    glm-5.3-flash-reasoner  | GLM 5.3 Flash | ctx 1000000

    GET /v1/models/glm-5.3-flash          -> 200
    GET /v1/models/glm-5.3-flash-chat     -> 200
    GET /v1/models/glm-5.3-flash-reasoner -> 200

No inference or caching changes; only the model-list payload.

title: Metal: add Qwen3.8 SSD expert streaming and optimize inference
body:
## Summary This PR adds bounded SSD expert streaming for **Qwen3.8 Flash Next on Metal**, together with improvements to kernel execution, prefill scheduling, memory budgeting and MTP state handling. It supports the existing Q2 and Q4 GGUF packs directly. It includes the streaming foundation originally submitted in #1047, which is now closed, and the subsequent optimization and correctness work. Validated head: `8d543ecc`, including upstream `main` at `fc80bd69`. ## Main changes - **Bounded expert streaming.** Keep dense weights and shared experts resident while loading missing routed experts into an owned, bounded cache. Prefill, ordinary decode and built-in MTP are supported. Cache overflow and different predictor expert sizes use temporary staging, restricted to distinct selected experts when GPU buffer addresses are available, with a full-layer fallback where required. - **Overlap reads with GPU work.** Run cached and shared expert computation while missing experts are read. Extend overlap through down projections, MTP verification and the prefill gate/up-to-down pipeline. Prefill overlap applies across Metal devices, while specialized kernels retain their device and shape guards. - **Reduce repeated kernel work.** Reuse inputs across Q8 projections, IQ2_XXS gate/up, Q2_K down and hyper-connection operations. Add compact dispatches for active experts, sparse prefill tiles, and guarded Q4/MXFP4 staging and row-reuse paths. - **Improve cache and memory planning.** Plan eviction victims once per batch, bound transient MTP staging, and make execution and admission use the same prefill-chunk resolution. Qwen’s complete memory admission accounts for static weights, context, staging and runtime reservations without discounting Metal’s working-set recommendation twice. - **Prepare and preserve MTP history.** Populate historical predictor K/V and indexer state while skipping unused projections and expert computation. Retain the pending final trunk row until its successor is known, and preserve predictor state across append, verification, rollback and checkpoint restore. - **Extend guarded device tuning.** Apply the established M1 Max choices to M2–M4 under the existing format, shape, batch and math-mode constraints. Preserve M3 Ultra’s dedicated policies and extend the relevant M5 selection to M6. ## Numerical correctness The series fixes inconsistent prefill-chunk handling, late Q8 decode drift and attention dispatch across internal prefill partitions. The resident correction in `37f66ba` restores **main’s resident prefill arithmetic**: FP32 small-batch F16/Q8 projections, F32 split-K reductions and per-range attention dispatch. SSD streaming retains its established prefill policy. An independent **M4 Max 64 GB / Q2 resident** retest confirmed identical first-token logits and 64-step logprobs against main `0aaea5a` on 29-, 575- and 5,942-token prompts. Greedy text also matched with MTP enabled and disabled. The decode tuning remained active. See the [correctness confirmation](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/pull/1056#issuecomment-5968477399). These checks establish parity for the tested references and configurations. Different GPU architectures and batching schedules can still produce different floating-point results. ## Performance evidence Measurements below have different baselines and workloads. Their gains should be read separately. | Hardware and workload | Comparison | Reported result | | --- | --- | --- | | M4 Max 64 GB, Q2 resident | Main `0aaea5a` → corrected branch `37f66ba` | Across 32 context frontiers from 2K to 64K: median **+7.5% generation** and **+1.3% prefill**. Three runs per arm; output parity retained. [Results](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/pull/1056#issuecomment-5975493326). | | M1 Max 32 GiB, Q2 SSD, 575-token prompt with MTP | Streaming foundation `d6cbc77` → early optimization series `5cbdb6e` | Prefill **34.650 → 51.245 t/s (+47.89%)**; decode **7.480 → 10.670 t/s (+42.65%)**. This historical comparison includes cache and predictor-state changes. [32-run comparison](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/pull/1056#issuecomment-5678216257). | | M1 Max 32 GiB, Q4 SSD, 8,631-token prompt, MTP off | Controlled comparison of the `b96a12b` prefill defaults | Prefill **154.31 → 161.49 t/s (+4.65%)**; decode changed by **−0.21%**, within observed variation. Eight runs with identical output. [Benchmark report](https://github.com/GiorgioOppo/ds4/blob/b96a12be7bb3001e5ac3f5d43004c69ab865e48c/speed-bench/qwen38-m1-q4-k32.md). | | M6 32 GB, Q2 SSD | Earlier branch → all-device overlap and M6 tuning | Independent testing reported **+16% to +25% prefill**, primarily from enabling read/compute overlap. All arms used the same external SSD. [Results](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/pull/1056#issuecomment-5830097606). | These results do not constitute a benchmark of merge head `8d543ecc`. SSD measurements include filesystem-cache effects, and device eligibility does not imply a measured improvement on every supported chip. ## MTP preparation tradeoff Preparing predictor history can improve subsequent speculation, but its prefill cost does not pay back on every resident workload. The M4 Max report for `37f66ba` measures approximately **6–7% slower prefill with MTP enabled**. Its 35K-token request took **5.7% longer overall**, while shorter requests were 2–6% faster. This tradeoff remains after the numerical correction. See the [MTP performance measurements](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/pull/1056#issuecomment-5975493326). `DS4_QWEN4_MTP_PREFILL` makes the policy configurable: | Value | Behavior | | --- | --- | | `on` — default | Prepare predictor history for resident and streaming runs. | | `auto` | Prepare history only with SSD streaming. | | `off` | Skip historical projections and initialize those cache rows to zero. | Draft generation and target verification remain enabled. Skipping history can change drafts and reduce acceptance, so compare total request time on the intended workload. The setting affects newly prefilled rows; reused and restored checkpoints retain their existing predictor history. ## Validation At `8d543ecc`, validation on an M1 Max 32 GiB includes: - Complete Metal and CPU application builds. - Qwen memory, MTP policy, device selection, kernel, exact Q2, prefill-reuse, Q8 and HC tests. - Resident/SSD arithmetic regression tests across fast/safe math and retained/unretained command buffers. - SSD selected-read, cache, fallback and failure/retry tests. - DSpark host confidence, window, EOS and rewind contracts. - `git diff --check`. Development validation additionally covers full-vocabulary model comparisons, MTP cache/reference comparisons, checkpoint restore, rewind and continuation. CUDA/ROCm hardware, distributed transport and full-model performance were not retested after the merge. ## Compatibility and research material **Checkpoint compatibility:** Qwen checkpoints use payload version 3; older Qwen disk checkpoints must be rebuilt. All arms used the same external SSD. Results.

title: GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K Metal SSD-streaming (M4 Max, 128 GiB): host-side per-layer bookkeeping dominates token time (15 % GPU), and the async selected-id load is a no-op
body:
Hi antirez, thanks for ds4 — it runs a 178 GiB GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K on a 128 GiB M4 Max, which is remarkable.

I spent a day measuring the GLM SSD-streaming decode path before touching it, and I think the findings below are worth an issue rather than a patch: I could not turn any of them into a net win. All numbers are from real runs on this machine; raw stderr is available on request.

## Environment
- current fork build on top of `origin/main` @ `9139e2a`, no local changes for these numbers
- Mac Studio M4 Max, 128 GiB, macOS 27; Metal 4 tensor API unavailable on this device (log: "Metal 4 tensor API disabled for pre-M5/pre-A19 devices")
- Model: `GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K.gguf`, 177.77 GiB, 1412 tensors, types f32/q8_0/**q4_k**/bf16 (129 q4_k = 42 routed layers x 3 expert tensors) — a *uniform* Q4_K expert layout, no Q5_K, no IQ2_XXS
- Protocol: `--ssd-streaming --ctx 4096 --tokens 128 --temp 0`, a prompt that actually generates 128 tokens, cold + warm run, values parsed from stderr with `DS4_METAL_STREAMING_EXPERT_TIMING_SUMMARY=1 DS4_METAL_MEMORY_REPORT=1`

## Finding 1 — the timing summary is easy to misread, and 1-token runs measure the wrong thing
A prompt like "answer with exactly one word" yields a single-token answer: `selected_calls=42` and `read_avg=11.7 ms`. That is **42 layers x 1 token**, not a decode rate — the reported `generation: 1.8 t/s` is the *first* token, which carries the whole page-fault / cache-fill warmup. With a prompt that fills the token budget the same build reports:

| run | prefill t/s | decode t/s | selected_calls | read_total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q4 streaming, cold | 2.60 | **6.21** | 5334 | 7813 ms |
| Q4 streaming, warm | 2.64 | **6.22** | 5334 | 7793 ms |

`selected_calls = 42 x 127` confirms the counter is per layer x token. A sanity line printing the generated token count next to `generation: t/s` (or a doc note that the timing summary needs a prompt that exhausts `--tokens`) would prevent this class of misreading.

## Finding 2 — the host readback is not the bottleneck; removing it entirely changes nothing
`uniform_streaming_selected_cache` and `stream_addr_q4` are both true for this GGUF, so the decode already runs the address-table path (stage profile: `pair=q4_stream_addr_swiglu`, `down_path=q4_stream_addr_down_simd`), not a legacy path. I then removed the synchronous selected-id readback completely. It was gated twice: `glm_graph_layer_uses_generic_routed_moe()` (IQ2 only, from the initial GLM 5.2 commit 005afed) and, on Metal, an opt-in env var (`ds4.c`: `return getenv("DS4_METAL_ENABLE_GLM_STREAMING_SELECTED_ASYNC_LOAD") != NULL;`). With the gate opened for `streaming_selected_cache` and the flag set:

| | baseline | async path |
|---|---|---|
| decode t/s | 6.21 / 6.22 | 6.22 / 6.24 |
| `selected_calls` / `read_total` | 5334 / 7793 ms | **0 / 0 ms** |
| output (temp 0) | 584 B | **byte-identical** |

`DS4_METAL_GLM_STREAMING_ASYNC_PROFILE=1` shows why: `async_calls=5334 total=20007 ms avg=3.751 ms signal_start=17 ms flush_router=18 ms shared=42 ms flush_shared=7 ms finish=10945 ms routed=8974 ms`. The work moves from the decode thread into the service thread, and the decode thread then waits in `finish` — no overlap is gained, because there is almost nothing left to overlap with (`shared` = 42 ms total).

## Where the token time actually goes
Stage profile per layer x token in steady state: `pair=0.31 ms down=0.25 ms` -> GPU ~0.58 ms x 42 layers = **~24 ms of ~161 ms per token (15 %)**. The rest is host-side expert-cache bookkeeping per layer x token: `read_total` 61 ms (only without the async path), `bind_total` 25 ms, `missing_bind` (split path) 20 ms, `readahead` 22 ms (14769 calls in 127 tokens), buffer preparation ~11 ms. Cache pressure is real but not the lever either: 48 GB / 56 GB / 85 GB budgets give 5.3 / 5.3 / 4.6 t/s with hit_rate 0.74 / 0.77 / 0.84 — the automatic budget (70.1 GiB, hit_rate 0.83, 4575 evictions) is already the best, and 85 GB starts swapping.

## Flags I tested (all neutral)
I also swept the knob surface around this path with the same 128-token protocol, two runs each, output byte-identical in every case: `DS4_METAL_ENABLE_Q4_GROUPED_EXPERTS=1` (enable-only gate, default off), `DS4_METAL_ENABLE_Q4_BATCH_EXPERT_TABLE=1`, `DS4_METAL_ENABLE_Q4_EXPERT_ADDRESS_TABLE=1` (already default on), `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_STREAMING_EXPERT_READAHEAD=1` (slightly *worse*: 6.04 vs 6.22 t/s), `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_STREAMING_EXPERT_SPLIT=1`, `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_STREAMING_EXPERT_HIT_VALIDATOR=1`, `--ssd-streaming-full-layers 2` and `4`, `--ssd-streaming-preload-experts 2000`. All stay within noise of 6.2 t/s, and whatever is removed reappears elsewhere (readahead disabled -> `bind_total` +0.8 s). The per-layer chain looks serial rather than dominated by any single removable cost — which is why I am not sending a patch.

For completeness: `--mtp` on this path measures 5.28 / 5.22 t/s (i.e. ~15 % *slower* than without it) with byte-identical output, and I have switched my launcher default to MTP off for GLM streaming.

## Related work in this tracker
- #437 (M4 Max 128 GiB SSD-streaming benchmark and alternative supply strategies) — same machine class, DeepSeek graph; my numbers are for the GLM path, which does per-layer host-side address resolution in `ds4_gpu_glm_routed_moe_one_tensor`.
- #840 (byte-identical streaming speedups on V4 Flash) — I could not reproduce a gain of that class on GLM Q4_K: see the sweep above.
- #636 (L+2 router lookahead from an offload prototype) — the per-layer chain described there matches what I measure here; a lookahead across layers is what I would try next.
- #810 (smaller expert cache faster on M5 Pro) — on M4 Max 128 GiB with GLM Q4_K the automatic budget was the best of the four budgets I tested.
- #495 (`--mtp` together with `--ssd-streaming`) — 15 % slower here, byte-identical output.

## Question
For the DeepSeek/MXFP4 streaming path the same counters show `read_avg=0.000 ms, bind_avg=0.444 ms` at 15.6 t/s, i.e. per-layer address resolution looks much cheaper there. Is the intended direction for GLM to move this per-layer/per-token bookkeeping to the GPU (compact/validate style) instead of the host loop over routed experts? And is the Metal async selected-id load meant to stay opt-in for uniform Q2_K/Q4_K layouts, or is enabling it by default just untested?

I can provide raw stderr for all runs, the exact flag matrix, and the (correctness-neutral) patch if that helps. Thanks!

title: Key tool-conversation KV checkpoints by the client-visible transcript
body:
Fixes #1053.

## Problem

After a graceful shutdown, the disk KV checkpoint of a tool-using Chat
Completions conversation was never found on restart (`kv cache stored ...
reason=shutdown key=token-text`, then a full re-prefill). The report was on
Qwen, but the bug is generic: it reproduces on DeepSeek Flash and the same
code path serves GLM.

Root cause, in `ds4_server.c`:

1. `should_remember_thinking_checkpoint` refused to remember a client-visible
   key for any request with tools (or a prompt that preserves reasoning)
   unless the model syntax was Qwen. On DeepSeek/GLM no thinking-visible key
   ever existed for a tool conversation, so evict, shutdown and continued
   stores fell back to the detokenized session as key. That text embeds the
   sampled hidden reasoning, which OpenAI-compatible clients never send back
   as `reasoning_content`, so it can never byte-prefix-match a replayed
   prompt. The same mismatch made every later request in the conversation
   miss live KV at the previous assistant turn's `<think>` and re-prefill from
   the last disk checkpoint (up to 10K tokens behind).
2. Even with the gate opened, `build_thinking_visible_text` produced
   `<｜Assistant｜></think>content` for DeepSeek, while in tool context the
   renderer echoes earlier assistant turns as `<think>{reasoning}</think>content`,
   i.e. `<think></think>content` when the client omits reasoning. Qwen renders
   the same shape in both contexts, which is why the Qwen-only exception
   worked and the bug looked model-specific.
3. Tool-call turns had a visible checkpoint only for Qwen; DeepSeek/GLM
   tool-call turns cleared it, so the request carrying the tool result missed
   as well.
4. `continued` checkpoints written while prefilling turn N+1 of a
   live-continued session were keyed by tokens that include turn N's hidden
   reasoning, so they were dead after a restart too (the reporter's "not even
   B's smaller continued checkpoints").

## Fix

- Remember the visible key for tool / preserved-reasoning prompts on every
  syntax on Chat Completions (Responses and Anthropic keep their own live
  records). The existing `token_text_disk_key` behaviour is unchanged: the
  first disk key stays exact and switches to the visible key once a request
  actually continues without reasoning.
- DeepSeek and DeepSeek 4.1 build the visible key as `<think></think>content`
  when the prompt is in tool context (same predicate the renderer uses).
- Add a DSML tool-call turn visible checkpoint (DeepSeek, DeepSeek 4.1, GLM)
  next to the Qwen one. The key ends at the raw tool block, like Qwen, and a
  live-tail check refuses the shortcut if the sampled frontier carries extra
  bytes past the end marker.
- Key continued stores that cover a visible frontier by the visible text plus
  the detokenized prefill suffix, and re-arm the frontier after a
  thinking-visible disk restore so later continued stores stay matchable.

Behaviour note: tool conversations on DeepSeek/GLM now keep their own hidden
reasoning in KV across turns, as tool-less chats (and Qwen with tools) already
did. Outputs of tool conversations can therefore differ slightly from before,
where the model was silently re-conditioned each turn on `<think></think>`.

## Impact

Measured on DeepSeek Flash (Metal, M5 Max), a 12K-token tool conversation:

| Request | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| short follow-up / tool-result request | 815-877 tokens re-prefilled, 2.1-2.2 s | 12-17 tokens, 0.18-0.23 s |
| restart replay | 1905 tokens re-prefilled, 3.8 s (partial checkpoint hit) | 14 tokens, 0.22 s |
| disk files for the conversation | 9 files / 1270 MB, 5 unmatchable | 6 files / 827 MB, all matchable |

In-session, the fix removes an average of ~5K tokens of re-prefill per request
(half the 10240-token continued spacing); at 80-160K contexts that is tens of
seconds per request in an agent loop. On restart with no matchable checkpoint
(the issue's case) it replaces a full re-prefill, ~8 min at 160K per the
report, with the new turn only.

## Tests

- Unit (`./ds4_test --server`): `test_thinking_checkpoint_remember_gate`
  updated (fails on main); new `test_thinking_visible_text_deepseek_tool_context`
  checks the DeepSeek/DS41 key against the renderer in tool context (fails on
  main); new `test_dsml_tool_visible_checkpoint_boundary` covers the tool-turn
  key for DeepSeek, DeepSeek 4.1 and GLM.
- End-to-end (second commit): `make test-kv-restart-restore DS4_TEST_MODEL=...`
  runs `tests/kv_restart_restore_smoke.sh`: warm-up conversation, tool
  conversation with a client that omits `reasoning_content`, SIGTERM, restart,
  replay. Model-gated like the DSpark/GLM smoke scripts, skips without a model,
  ~6 min. On `9139e2a` it fails with the issue signature
  (`reason=shutdown key=token-text`); with this PR it restores 12235 of 12249
  tokens.

Not verified at runtime: Qwen (no local model; the continued-key change is
the part expected to matter there) and GLM (covered by the unit tests only).

title: server: find token-text disk stores by the request's rendered tokens
body:
## What

A token-text KV disk store (`key=token-text`) is keyed by the *rendered* text of the
session's tokens, and rendering is not the prompt text: a literal `<|system|>` inside a
source file tokenizes to the special token and renders back as `<｜System｜>`. So the cold
store of a 570k-token prompt never matched the same prompt again, and every server
restart re-prefilled the whole prompt.

When the text lookup misses, look the request's own tokens up rendered the same way; on
a hit, continue with the request's tokens (the stored prefix must be exactly theirs)
instead of re-tokenizing rendered text.

`tests/tok_roundtrip.c` (make tests/tok_roundtrip) checks token-prefix rendering against
a prompt file.

## Measured

M5 Max 128 GiB, macOS 26.5, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Q2, `--ssd-streaming -c 1048576
--kv-disk-dir ... --kv-cache-cold-max-tokens 2000000`. The second 869k-token prefill of
the day resumed from the 570401-token cold store and prefilled 570401 -> 868904 in 13.7
min, where before the change every restart re-prefilled the whole prompt (25-38 min).
`./ds4_test --server`: OK on upstream main + this change (branch pr/server-disk-store-rendered-lookup). No kernel or backend code touched.

title: metal: radix-select top-k for the V4.1 indexer
body:
## What

The indexer's top-k (`kernel_argsort_f32_i32_desc` + merge) keeps every 1024-row block's
top 512 and merges them in log2(blocks) dependent passes: at 435k rows that is 9 passes
over 217k survivors, 2-3 ms per call, and the 32-row causal batches of prefill took ~5 ms.

`kernel_topk_select_{init,hist,scan,tiecount,compact,finish}` (metal/argsort.metal) find
the k-th key exactly with four 8-bit histogram levels over the sortable-int form of the
scores, count the ties at it per chunk, compact the winners in one pass (the rows above
the k-th key, then the first ties by index), and let one threadgroup order them (score
desc, index asc). Taken when a row has at least 4096 visible entries and top_k <= 2048;
the sort stays for everything else. The choice is made per visible width, the same for a
token alone and inside a causal batch — a batch straddling 4096 is cut in two — so a
position's top-k does not depend on how it was submitted; `make test-deepseek41-metal`
checks exact IDs across frontiers 1024..65535, including rows of all-equal scores.
`DS4_METAL_DISABLE_TOPK_SELECT=1` restores the sort.

Where the two differ: scores exactly tied at the k-th boundary. The sort keeps the
members of the tie its comparison network happens to leave in place; the select keeps
the lowest indices, deterministically. The set and its order are identical whenever the
k-th score is not tied.

## Measured

M5 Max 128 GiB, macOS 26.5, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Q2, Metal SSD streaming.
- Standalone (tests/test_metal_topk_select, best of the loops, two runs each; sort =
  DS4_METAL_DISABLE_TOPK_SELECT=1):

  | rows x tokens, k            | sort         | select      |
  |-----------------------------|--------------|-------------|
  | 435000 x 1, k=512           | 1.7-2.4 ms   | 0.4-1.0 ms  |
  | 435000 x 3, k=512           | 2.0-3.8 ms   | 1.0-1.4 ms  |
  | 869000 x 1, k=512           | 2.5-3.8 ms   | 1.2 ms      |
  | 54000 x 1, k=2048           | 1.0-1.3 ms   | 0.8 ms      |
  | 435000 x 32 causal (prefill)| 4.8-4.9 ms   | 2.7-5.2 ms  |
- Encoder timeline of a 869k-context decode: kernel_topk_select_hist 58 us x 7348 calls =
  428 ms over the prefill tail where the causal argsort was 3.4 ms per batch.
- Decode: 435k rows / 3 tokens 3.0 -> 0.35 ms per call, 869k 2.7 -> 0.43 ms (earlier
  build, quiet GPU).
- On upstream main + this change (branch pr/indexer-topk-select), V4.1 Flash Q2 under SSD
  streaming at 16k with a 23 GiB bank: greedy output byte-identical with and without the
  select; prefill of the 10k prompt 169 -> 178 t/s (single runs). `./ds4_test
  --metal-kernels`: OK. `make test-metal-topk-select`: PASS. `make test-deepseek41-metal`:
  PASS.

Revision: the first push failed `make test-deepseek41-metal` at the 4096-row frontier
(the batch and the single-token call chose different algorithms for the same row) and
ordered ties by arrival past a 2048-tie cap; both fixed as described above — one more
pass, no tie buffer.

title: metal: decode-shaped V4.1 indexer kernels for long contexts
body:
## What

Decode at long context ran the prefill-shaped indexer (`kernel_glm_indexer_scores_tiled`
/ `_batch`) for 1-3 tokens over hundreds of thousands of compressed rows: one threadgroup
per key tile, with the q side redone per tile. Two kernels for the decode shape:

- `kernel_dsv41_indexer_scores_decode_rows`: one dispatch per token, 8 simdgroups per
  threadgroup, each streaming a run of rows; q for the token lives in threadgroup memory.
- `kernel_dsv41_indexer_scores_decode` (default): C(8 rows x 32 heads) = K(8x128) .
  Q^T(128x32) from simdgroup_float8x8 tiles -- 16 key tiles read once from the cache and
  64 q tiles from threadgroup memory per 8 rows, then the per-row relu/weight reduction.
  ~25 instructions per row and lane against ~280 for the row-streaming kernel.

Taken for n_tokens < 8 at n_comp >= 4096 (the tiled kernel stays for prefill batches).
`DS4_METAL_V41_INDEX_DECODE_ROWS=1` selects the rows kernel; `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_V41_INDEX_DECODE=1`
the old path.

## Measured

M5 Max 128 GiB, macOS 26.5, quiet GPU, standalone harness (K f32, 32 heads x 128):

| rows x tokens | rows kernel      | MMA kernel       |
|---------------|------------------|------------------|
| 435000 x 3    | 0.72 ms / token  | 0.50 ms / token  |
| 869000 x 3    | 1.45 ms / token  | 1.09 ms / token  |

The MMA kernel reads 222 MB of keys per token at 435k in 0.50 ms (445 GB/s): it is at
the cache-read floor; the remaining cost of the indexer at 1M is that every token reads
K again. Worst |diff| against a double reference 8e-10 (both). On the 869k-context
DSpark decode timeline the indexer went from the largest single kernel to 23 ms of a
~160 ms GPU cycle (8 calls of ~2.9 ms for 2-3 tokens, GPU shared with a backup at the
time). Greedy 16k output byte-identical to the tiled path with DS4_METAL_V41_INDEX_SCALAR=1.

title: Qwen3.8 Flash Next: batched decode and MTP across sessions on Metal (16 streams: 203 tok/s aggregate), single stream +8%
body:
Qwen3.8 Flash Next on Metal: native batched decode across sessions (1–16 streams), batched multi-token prediction, single-stream gains, and a session-concurrency benchmark. Measured on an M5 Max (128 GB) with `ds4flash.gguf` (Q4).

## Headline numbers (context 4096, `speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt`)

| | upstream main (9139e2a) | this branch |
|---|---:|---:|
| 16 streams, plain, aggregate | 3.1 tok/s (sessions decode one at a time, each with private transients: 16 of them at 4k do not fit) | **203 tok/s** |
| 8 streams, plain, aggregate | — | 133 tok/s |
| 1 stream, plain | 50.2 tok/s | **54.3 tok/s**, same tokens as main (32/32 checked), same prefill (1408 vs 1414 tok/s) |
| 1 stream, MTP, prose / code | 50.5 / not measured | **59–66 / 78–84** |
| 8 streams, batched MTP, prose | — | 149 tok/s (+12% over plain) |
| 16 streams, batched MTP, code | — | 214 tok/s |

Batched MTP is lossless against plain greedy decoding (`session_concurrency_bench --spec --verify`). Where drafts do not pay (prose at 16 streams: every verify row reads its own expert bytes), a per-cycle policy measured on the engine falls back to plain decoding, so it does not lose against plain.

## Throughput and memory by context (4k → 256k) and concurrency

![decode t/s by context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/polymorf/ds4/qwen3.8-flash-next-batched/speed-bench/m5_max_ctx_sweep_throughput.png)

![session memory by context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/polymorf/ds4/qwen3.8-flash-next-batched/speed-bench/m5_max_ctx_sweep_memory.png)

Tables, protocol and caveats (one run per cell, thermal drift of 5–15% over the three-hour sweep) are in [`speed-bench/m5_max_ctx_sweep.md`](https://github.com/polymorf/ds4/blob/qwen3.8-flash-next-batched/speed-bench/m5_max_ctx_sweep.md); CSVs and the plotter sit next to it. The 16-stream cells stop at 32k because 16 sessions × 64k need 45 GiB on top of the 69.7 GiB model.

## What is in the branch (30 commits, each self-contained)

**Harness.** `speed-bench/session_concurrency_bench`: cells over concurrency × context, cumulative tok/s, memory pricing from the engine's own accounting (cells that would not fit are skipped), `--verify` (batched tokens against sequential decoding, with the logit distance on a mismatch), `--spec --verify` (speculative against plain greedy), paired A/B mode (`--candidate-env`), CSV output.

**Batched decode.** One forward over the sessions' rows on a shared transients arena: the GDN convolution/scan and the block-sparse attention run as rows through GPU address tables (one dispatch per stage, byte-exact against the per-row kernels), the routed experts are grouped per expert across the batch with the shared expert as dense GEMMs, the Q8_0 projections multiply on fp32 simdgroup matrices (16 rows, weights read once), the F32/F16 narrow projections take a fp32 tile with a k-split for decode batches.

**Batched MTP.** A ragged batch of token + draft rows with per-token attention entries and snapshot/restore of the recurrent state, the predictor layer batched across sessions with one head product, and a per-cycle decision to draft or not from the measured acceptance and cycle costs. Single-stream MTP gains from priming the predictor's cache with the prompt during prefill (acceptance on code 1.60 → 1.94 tokens per cycle), a measured depth policy, the chained second draft in the predictor's own submission, and next-token embeddings gathered on the GPU.

**Single stream.** A decode token's sixteen n-gram rows are read from disk concurrently instead of in sequence (1.3 ms of SSD latency off the critical path, +6% decode, bit-identical logits).

**Fixes found by the sweep.** The shared arena is replaced when a session at a larger context finds it idle (sessions used to fall back to private transients and run out of memory at the next context size); the dense k-split no longer splits prefill chunks (their partial planes outgrew the scratch and every call fell back to the per-token kernel, −8% prefill from 8k); the F16 fp32 tile stays on decode batches (on prefill chunks it was slower and moved single-stream tokens off main's).

## Numerics

The single-stream path is unchanged in arithmetic: tokens identical to main on the checked prompt, bit-identical logits across the single-stream commits. Batched rows use tiled GEMMs whose reduction order differs from the matvec; `--verify` checks token agreement against sequential decoding (passes over the 24–48-step runs, per-step logit deviation ~1e-3 amplified by the discrete expert and block selections, so a near-tie can flip on longer runs — documented in the note). Tensor-op tiles were left out of the decode paths because they compute at half precision.

## Tests

`tests/test_qwen4_kernels` gained cases for the attention and GDN row kernels, the Q8 batch tile, the grouped MoE passes, the multi-row MTP stage/combine and the argmax; the harness's verify modes cover the batched paths end to end.

title: CUDA: experimental upstream-native Qwen3.8 Flash Next text support
body:
# CUDA: experimental upstream-native Qwen3.8 Flash Next text support

## Summary

This adds an experimental CUDA text path for the `qwen4exp` architecture on
top of the current `antirez/ds4` graph and CUDA backend.

The patch covers Hyper-Connections, Gated DeltaNet, PLE projection/convolution,
QSA dense and block-sparse attention, routed/shared MoE, output projection, and
state snapshot/restore required by ordinary text inference. CUDA vision and
end-to-end speculative MTP are not claimed by this PR.

## Prior art and relationship to other work

This work was developed independently, but overlaps in scope with Baekpica's
earlier CUDA port:

https://github.com/Baekpica/ds4/tree/feature/qwen38-ssd-ple-handoff

Baekpica's fork has since evolved into a broader and substantially divergent
serving runtime with bounded SSD-PLE caching, vision, embedded MTP, and
multi-bank execution. This PR does not import source from that fork. Its goal
is narrower: a reviewable single-session text implementation that fits the
current upstream graph, tensor APIs, session lifecycle, and regression suite.

Thank you to Baekpica for publishing the earlier CUDA work and validation.

## CUDA implementation

- Hyper-Connection normalization, mixing, injection, and residual update.
- Gated DeltaNet causal convolution, controls, recurrent scan, snapshots, and
  gated RMS normalization.
- PLE gate, normalization, dilated convolution, and persistent history.
- QSA projection preparation, RoPE, KV storage, dense/sparse attention, and
  exact parallel block selection.
- Q4_K routed MoE, shared expert, stable router top-k, route-list construction,
  reduction, and eight-token prefill tiles.
- Float-activation Q8 dense projections for Qwen, including an eight-token
  prefill tile.
- Embedded MTP staging primitives are covered by unit tests, but end-to-end
  speculative generation remains outside the claimed scope.

Diagnostic rollback variables are documented in
`docs/QWEN38_FLASH_NEXT.md`.

## Correctness validation

Machine:

- NVIDIA GB10, `sm_121`
- CUDA 13.0
- driver 580.173.02
- Qwen3.8 Flash Next Q4 GGUF
- model SHA-256:
  `680944460a8cbe93ba8b6d7b6107213ffb7e22320bd913000e563ca0a0f25a8a`

Commands include:

```sh
make cpu
make cuda-spark
make cuda-regression CUDA_ARCH=sm_121
make test-qwen4-cuda CUDA_ARCH=sm_121
python3 tests/test_qwen4_cuda_numerics.py \
  --model gguf/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4.gguf
```

Additional CUDA regression targets exercised DeepSeek V4.1, GLM 5.3 KDA,
GLM attention, MXFP4, DSpark MoE, SSD cache, Q8 scratch/rows, shared helpers,
and CUDA reductions. The complete `ds4_test` model runner passed on the
default DeepSeek V4.0 model, including the 30,474-token long-context test,
official logprob vectors, tool calling, and five tensor-equivalence cases.

Repeated 248,320-value Qwen logit dumps with the scalar and token-tiled routed
MoE paths were byte-identical:

```text
236a799b751dec4ccf6c20341c4b034662de1fbd4f855e65f535093f7e81db6a
```

## Performance

Same GB10, Q4 model, CUDA build, and prompt/chunk conditions:

| Workload | Previous path | This patch | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1K prefill | 39.19 tok/s | 54.21 tok/s | +38.3% |
| 4K prefill | 38.69 tok/s | 54.95 tok/s | +42.0% |

The 4K result includes the parallel sparse selector and routed-MoE token tile.
Older 8K/16K measurements predate the final MoE optimization and should not be
used as final performance claims.

## Known limitations

- Validated locally only on GB10 / `sm_121`; other NVIDIA architectures need
  CI or maintainer testing.
- Text only: CUDA vision is rejected explicitly.
- End-to-end Qwen MTP is not validated or enabled as a claimed feature.
- PLE BF16 n-gram rows remain disk-backed through the upstream model path;
  this PR does not import Baekpica's bounded CUDA SSD-PLE cache.
- The CUDA port remains substantially slower than the Metal implementation.

## Local test-suite note

`tests/test_tp_tcp` can remain blocked on this GB10 host. Neither that test nor
`ds4_tp.c` differs from `origin/main`; all other `make test` commands were run
separately and passed. This should be reproduced on a clean upstream checkout
before changing the PR status from Draft.

Addresses #867; it does not close the issue because CUDA vision and complete
MTP coverage remain outstanding.

title: GLM: render the tool call block inline, as the chat template does
body:
GLM's `append_glm_tool_calls_text()` wraps the reconstructed tool block in a newline on each side (`"\n" + "<tool_call>..." + "\n"`). `tokenizer.chat_template` does not.

Rendering the template straight from the GGUF (Jinja, `trim_blocks` + `lstrip_blocks`, as HF does) gives the inline form in every variant — empty content, non-empty content, reasoning present, followed by an observation or by a user turn:

```
<|assistant|><think></think><tool_call>get_weather<arg_key>city</arg_key><arg_value>Paris</arg_value></tool_call><|observation|>
```

The model samples that same inline form, so the reconstructed turn disagrees with the bytes it is supposed to reproduce.

## Why it stays hidden inside one process

When the raw sampled bytes are available, `calls->raw_tool_text` is emitted verbatim and both paths agree. Only a history replayed by a client goes through reconstruction, so the two forms only meet across a restart — or on a cold prefill, which renders the replayed history before anything is cached.

## Symptom

With visible-transcript KV checkpoints (the approach #1058 takes), a GLM conversation writes its shutdown checkpoint under `key=thinking-visible`, and the replayed prompt then misses it by exactly three bytes:

```
visiblekey: ...<|assistant|><think></think><tool_call>get_weather<arg_key>city...
reqprompt : ...<|assistant|><think></think>\n<tool_call>get_weather<arg_key>city...
                                    ^^
```

Everything after that point shifts, so the checkpoint can never be a byte prefix of a replay.

## Reproduction

`tests/kv_restart_restore_smoke.sh` with GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2, on top of #1058 + #1059:

```
before: FAIL, restored 8192 of 11992 tokens (3800 re-prefilled)
after:  OK,   restored 11998 of 12012 tokens (14 re-prefilled)
```

The shutdown store becomes the one actually hit:

```
kv cache stored tokens=11998 reason=shutdown key=thinking-visible
kv cache hit text tokens=11998 text=64224 key=thinking-visible
```

## Scope beyond caching

Cold prefill renders through the same path, so GLM tool conversations have been rendered in a shape the model was never trained on since this landed in `005afed`.

## Tests

* `test_glm_tool_calls_render_matches_template` (new): asserts the template-true block, and that the raw and reconstructed renders are byte-identical.
* `test_render_glm_preserves_reasoning_with_tools` had pinned the old bytes; corrected.

`ds4_test --server` passes on current main with this applied.

## Two caveats about the smoke test itself

Unrelated to this change, but they block anyone trying to run it against GLM: `start_server` hardcodes `--prefill-chunk 1024`, which GLM rejects (`--prefill-chunk is not supported for GLM 5.2`), and it does not set a cwd, so the server logs `ds4: Metal source metal/flash_attn.metal not found` with the Metal backend unavailable. Working around both locally is what made the numbers above reproducible.

title: Show and tell: DS Menu Bar - lightweight macOS control for ds4-server
body:
I built **DS Menu Bar**, a small, lightweight native macOS menu bar app for running and configuring a local `ds4-server`.

Repo: https://github.com/jiiim/ds-menu-bar

The main goal is to keep `ds4-server` **available without becoming another application you have to work inside**.

There are now several apps that can run or wrap ds4, but many provide their own chat UI, workspace, model-management experience, or other substantial interface. DS Menu Bar deliberately does much less.

It sits in the menu bar, stays out of the way, and handles the local server while you keep using whatever tools you already prefer — Zed, OpenCode, Pi Coding Agent, or any other client that can talk to the server.

It provides:

* start / stop / restart and server status from the menu bar
* optional live prefill and generation throughput in the menu bar
* model-aware settings for server, performance, KV cache, MTP, and diagnostics
* detection and validation of supported DwarfStar model files before launch
* access to the generated `ds4-server` command and rotating server logs
* optional request tracing for diagnostics
* launch-at-login support

The app does **not** bundle `ds4-server`, models, a chat client, or an editor. It uses an existing local build and DwarfStar-compatible GGUFs, and its job is simply to keep the server close at hand without competing with the tools that actually use it.

I mainly built it because I wanted `ds4-server` to feel like a background system service rather than another destination app: unobtrusive when everything is working, but always one click away when I want to change a model, inspect settings, check throughput, restart the server, or look at logs.

Current requirements are macOS 26+, Apple silicon, and a compatible `ds4-server` build.

Sharing here in case this kind of lightweight setup is useful to other macOS users of ds4. Feedback is especially welcome on ds4-specific settings, model detection, and assumptions that may need to change as the server evolves.

title: Metal V4.1 decode: one command-buffer wait per token, Engram reads on threads
body:
+45% speedup (26.07 vs 17.94 tok/s) with identical output, V4.1 on M3 Ultra 512

The changes:
  1. Flush every `DS4_METAL_V41_DECODE_FLUSH_LAYERS` layers, wait once at the logits; one Engram upload buffer per table. 17.7 → 22.8 tok/s
  2. Both Engram tables read on reader threads, joined before the first commit. 23.0 → 25.8
  3. Allocation-free pipeline lookup for the plain getter - neutral, cheaper encode (4.0 → 0.7 ms/token)
  4. Small word aligned copies as a compute kernel instead of a blit. neutral, zero blit passes per token.
  5. Same treatment for ds41_graph_step_batch - 239 → 187 ms/step at 8 sessions.

Gated on `ds4_gpu_device_is_pre_m5_apple_silicon()`

title: speed-bench: Qwen3.8 Flash Next Q2 numbers for M1 Max 64 GB
body:
Adds the first M1 Max entry in `speed-bench/`, and the first Qwen3.8 Flash Next
numbers for a 64 GB machine.

**Machine:** MacBook Pro (MacBookPro18,2), Apple M1 Max, 64 GB, macOS 25.5.0.
Metal backend, built with plain `make` at `8db1d1d`.
**Model:** `./download_model.sh qwen38-q2` — 137.10 GiB on disk, 41.72 GiB
resident, n-grams disk-only.

| ctx | prefill t/s | generation t/s (steady) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2048 | 288.41 | 24.15 |
| 4096 | 274.97 | 24.41 |
| 8192 | 274.78 | 24.45 |
| 12288 | 275.57 | 24.46 |
| 16384 | 273.95 | 24.26 |

Prefill is flat at ~275 t/s and generation holds ~24.4 t/s across the sweep.
Decode lands at roughly 49% of the M3 Ultra Qwen3.8 figures in
`speed-bench/qwen38-checkpoints/results.csv` (50.4 t/s at ctx 8192), which is
close to the memory-bandwidth ratio between the two machines.

### Why a separate filename

Every existing CSV here reports `kvcache_bytes` of 52184460 at ctx 2048 —
they are all DeepSeek V4 Flash Q2. Qwen3.8 Q2 reports 183560284. Naming this
`m1_max.csv` would put a different model into a set that is otherwise directly
comparable, so it is `m1_max_qwen38.csv` instead, with a README section
explaining the distinction. Happy to rename or relocate it if you'd prefer a
different convention for non-Flash results.

### Two deviations from the documented sweep

Both were necessary on 64 GB and are recorded in the README:

- **`--prefill-chunk 2048`.** The default chunk for this model is 8192, which
  plans 49.74 GiB (`buffers 7.49 GiB + resident model 41.72 GiB`) and pushes a
  64 GB Mac into swap. It is visible in the data: `gen_first_ms` rises from
  ~48 ms to 280–460 ms and `gen_tps` scatters between 20.70 and 24.72 rather
  than holding flat. At 2048 the run plans 44.36 GiB and stays resident.
  This may be worth a note in `docs/QWEN38_FLASH_NEXT.md`, which currently
  suggests `--prefill-chunk 1024` for 64 GB machines — that works, but costs
  about 10% prefill (250 t/s) versus 2048.
- **`--ctx-max 16384`.** `ds4-bench` keeps a restorable memory snapshot per
  frontier on top of the 41.72 GiB resident model, and the 32768 frontier
  exhausts memory on this machine. Ordinary inference is unaffected:
  `./ds4 --ctx 32768 --prefill-chunk 2048` reaches 271.94 t/s prefill and
  22.76 t/s generation on a real 32,113-token prompt, and `--ctx 131072` still
  loads at 48.44 GiB planned.

### Reproducibility

The committed CSV is one unmodified `ds4-bench` run. A second identical run
agreed within ~1% at every frontier (prefill 271.79–289.97, steady generation
24.05–24.78). Ordinary desktop background load, no other GPU workloads.

For reference, `--mtp` raises generation to 33.19 t/s on highly predictable
output and 28.91 t/s on prose, at a ~3% prefill cost.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_018G5GN444P7mX5v21BibtjB

title: `--batched-session N`: a request that shares only the system prompt with a live slot evicts it instead of taking an empty slot
body:
**Build:** antirez/ds4 main `8db1d1d`, Metal, M4 Max 64 GB, macOS 26.6.2
**Model:** `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf` (self-contained), `--metal -c 131072 --prefill-chunk 1024 --mtp --batched-session 2 --kv-disk-dir ... --kv-disk-space-mb 65536`
(also reproduced at `-c 163840`)

## Symptom

With two resident slots and two independent chat conversations that share the same system prompt
(11K tokens) but nothing else, sending them one after the other never uses the second slot.
Each request lands in the slot holding the *other* conversation, evicts it to disk, and restores its
own state from disk. `--batched-session 2` then behaves exactly like one slot:

```
14:54:02 live kv cache miss live=80268 prompt=90076 common=11154 vision=match reason=token-mismatch
14:54:02 kv cache stored tokens=80268 ... reason=evict
14:57:05 live kv cache miss live=90166 prompt=90178 common=11154 vision=match reason=token-mismatch
14:57:05 kv cache stored tokens=90166 ... reason=evict
14:57:05 kv cache hit text tokens=80268 ... load=... ms
```

Slot 2 was empty throughout. It only gets populated when two requests are in flight at the same
time (slot 1 busy), after which both conversations stay resident and alternate with no misses, so the
steady state is fine; only the cold start is wrong.

Over 8 alternating turns (A at 70K→120K, B at 80K→130K, 10K new tokens each):
one slot = 23–26 s/turn; two slots from cold = 24–28 s/turn (8 misses, 8 restores);
two slots after one concurrent round = 21–22 s/turn (0 misses).

## Cause

`job_slot_score()` (`ds4_server.c:14642`) scores an idle slot by
`ds4_session_common_prefix(slot->session, &j->req.prompt)` (line 14676). An empty slot has no tokens,
so it scores 0. A slot holding an unrelated conversation scores the length of the shared system
prompt (here 11,154). `dispatch_jobs_locked()` picks the highest score with a strict `>`, so the
occupied slot always wins over the empty one whenever the conversations share any prefix, which with
a fixed system prompt is always.

## Repro

Two OpenAI-compatible chat conversations with the same system prompt and different histories
(≥ 20K tokens each so the miss is visible in timing). Send A, then B, then A, then B, sequentially.
Expect: no `live kv cache miss` after the first turn of each. Observe: one on every turn, and
`--batched-session 2` never logs work in the second slot until two requests overlap.

Harness used: a Hermes-shaped tool-call session bench; happy to share.

title: server: decode an open tool call past a stop token
body:
A model that samples a stop token inside an open `<tool_call>` fails the request.

Seen with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B-A6B Q2: after 351 generated tokens the model emitted `<|im_end|>` while the block was still open.

    ds4-server: incomplete DeepSeek tool call: stop=stop token token=248046 generated=351 limit=32768 room=220010
    ds4-server: chat ... DSML_START finish=error error="unterminated tool call (stop token; token=248046, generated=351, limit=32768)"

`try_repair_dsml()` only restores a missing outer wrapper, and the tool-error continuation is skipped for streaming clients, so a streaming client loses the turn and has to retry the whole request.

A tool block carries no executable call until it closes, so a stop token there is invalid output rather than the end of the turn. Decoding already constrains that region (greedy outside payload sampling); this keeps decoding with the best non-stop token instead of accepting the stop, using the existing `ds4_session_argmax_ignoring_eos()`. Drafted stop tokens drop through the existing rewind path so the next sample sees fresh logits.

The override is bounded by `DS4_TOOL_CALL_STOP_SUPPRESS_LIMIT` (24) so a model that insists on ending inside the block still terminates into the existing error path instead of spending the whole output budget. When a block never closes, the warning now carries the tail of the generation, which is what was missing while diagnosing this.

Testing: macOS 26.5.2 on an M5 Max (128 GB), Metal backend, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125B-A6B Q2.

    make ds4_test && ./ds4_test --server   # ok
    make ds4-server                        # clean, no new warnings

Live checks against the running server: a Responses tool call, a Responses tool-output continuation, an OpenAI chat stream and an Anthropic stream all behave as before, and a Codex session completes a full reasoning -> tool call -> answer turn.

This is independent of the two neighbouring server issues already open: #899 (classify generated text by the prompt thinking state) and #774 (return calls to custom tools as custom_tool_call). I hit all three on the same run; only this one looked unreported.

Happy to add a unit-level regression if you want one: the branch is decode-loop only, so covering it needs an engine-level harness rather than a `--server` case.

title: Let V4.1 single-token decode use the concurrent Engram reader
body:
`ds4_engram_read_batch()` already fans row reads across `ENGRAM_READERS` workers — its comment says *"Fixed concurrency hides random-read latency without caching the table"* — but only above a 256-row threshold.

`ds41_graph_step()` reads `DS4_ENGRAM_COLS` rows per table (48 for the two tables) through the serial `ds4_engram_read()`, so **ordinary decode never reaches that path**. Those 48 preads run in series, and they run before `ds4_gpu_begin_commands()`, so the GPU is idle for all of them. Only bulk prefill ever clears 256.

This routes the decode read through the batched entry point and lowers the threshold to 8. Same rows, same order, same values — only the fetch is concurrent.

### Measured

Mac Studio M3 Ultra (80 GPU cores, 256 GB, macOS 26.6.2), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-Q2, resident (no `--ssd-streaming`), `--ctx 131072`, temperature 0, 200 generated tokens, this branch vs its merge-base:

| build | runs | median |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| `main` | 19.18, 19.14 | **19.16 tok/s** |
| `main` + patch | 20.42, 21.00, 21.11, 21.18 | **21.06 tok/s** |

**+9.9%**, about 4.7 ms/token. Generated text was **byte-identical** between the two builds. (The 20.42 was a cold first run after rebuild.)

The cost is storage *latency*, not bandwidth — a standalone pread benchmark against the same GGUF, 48 random 264-byte rows, `F_NOCACHE`, readahead disabled, 150 batches:

```
serial    5.177 ms/batch  (107.9 us/row)
parallel  0.614 ms/batch  ( 12.8 us/row)
```

The saving is roughly constant per token, so it is worth more on a faster tree: on @ivanfioravanti's `ds41f-optimizations` branch, where I originally profiled this, the same change measured **26.8 → 30.5 tok/s** (Engram wall 5.55 → 1.12 ms/token) across three alternating pairs, also byte-identical.

### Credit

- @ivanfioravanti — his V4.1 optimization work is where this was profiled. His `ds41f-dspark` branch already carries a better version of this fix, `ds41_engram_parallel()`, reading both tables in one dispatch — but gated to speculative sessions, so ordinary decode falls through to the serial loop there too. Ungating that is probably the better long-term shape of this change, and I'd defer to it.
- The oMLX / drowzeys V4.1-on-Mac work, which is what pointed me at Engram as a decode bottleneck at all. Their approach was a RAM cache of hot rows; measured row reuse here was only 22.5% over a 600-token coding generation, worth roughly +1 tok/s — so the win turned out to be concurrency rather than caching. Wrong idea, right place to look.

I've only tested Metal on M3 Ultra. The change is platform-neutral, but the non-Apple path in `read_batch_part` deserves a look from someone with that hardware.

title: Speed up DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Metal
body:
# Summary

This PR speeds up the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash engine on Metal and improves two-Mac tensor parallelism. Plain decoding is byte-identical to `main`: generated texts, `score_official` results and first-case logits match exactly. On one M3 Ultra, plain decode is about 2.2x `main`; two Macs over Thunderbolt RDMA add about 14%.

# Test setup

- Machines: 2x Mac Studio M3 Ultra, 32-core CPU, 80-core GPU, 512 GB
- Base: `main` 5379c1c
- Models: [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-MXFP4](https://huggingface.co/kernelpool/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-MXFP4-GGUF) (revision `dba1be0a`), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 MXFP4 (revision `1bae0e10`) with the support file from `gguf-tools/deepseek41_dspark.py`
- Speed measured at 72ccf36. Its output is byte-identical to 3650da3 (64-step logprob dumps on five prompts, 26 prefill shapes up to 131K, two-Mac decode hashes), and 3650da3's to e2d09d1 (the same dumps, 41 prefill shapes, two-Mac decode hashes).
- Conversion:

```sh
make -C gguf-tools libds4quants.dylib
python3 gguf-tools/deepseek41_quantize.py \
  --hf models/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash \
  --source-revision dba1be0a40aa45a94ad051997016db3960a90277 \
```
