title: [RFC] Evaluate PrismML Bonsai 2 support in ds4
body:
## Summary

I would like to discuss whether ds4 should support PrismML's
Bonsai 2 27B ternary GGUF model.

This is a design and scope discussion, not a claim that I already
have an implementation or a ready-to-submit PR.

Bonsai 2 is based on Qwen3.8-27B, but it uses a rotated ternary
weight representation with custom PTQ1_0/PQ2_0 packing and an
activation-side Hadamard/FWHT transform. It is distinct from the
Qwen3.8 Flash Next support discussed in #867.

References:

- https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo
- https://huggingface.co/prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf
- https://github.com/antirez/ds4/issues/867

## Questions

- Is Bonsai 2 in scope for ds4?
- Would a Metal-first investigation on Apple Silicon be useful?
- Should PTQ1_0 and PQ2_0 be supported natively, or should the work
  first target a canonical model format?
- Should this be tracked separately from #867?
- What minimum validation would maintainers expect before opening a
  draft PR?

## Possible investigation scope

1. Validate the GGUF metadata and tensor layouts.
2. Compare the PrismML llama.cpp fork against a reference implementation.
3. Determine whether the existing ds4 model/session abstractions can
   support the Qwen3.8-27B hybrid-attention graph.
4. Estimate the required Metal kernels, vision integration, and
   speculative-decoding support.

I am opening this issue to get direction before attempting any
implementation.

title: Tool-enabled chat completions buffer content until generation ends
body:
## Summary

Tool-enabled chat completions buffer normal answer text until generation finishes. Reasoning streams incrementally, but the complete answer arrives in one final content delta.

This affects Qwen, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and GLM 5.3 Flash through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint used by pi-web.

## Reproduction

Send a thinking-enabled request with tools and `stream: true` to `/v1/chat/completions`.

Observed before the fix:

| Model | Thinking deltas | Text deltas | Text delivery |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Qwen | not recorded | 1 | complete answer at finish |
| DeepSeek V4 Flash | 163 | 1 | 1,994 characters at finish |
| GLM 5.3 Flash | 132 | 1 | 3,341 characters at finish |

## Cause

`openai_stream_start()` and `anthropic_sse_start_live()` enable `guard_second_reasoning` for every tool-enabled thinking request. The safeguard was added for the escaped second reasoning pass reported in #678, which was measured on Anthropic streaming with legacy DeepSeek formatting.

After the first `</think>`, the guard cannot distinguish a real answer from an unmarked second reasoning pass. It therefore holds all text until another close marker, a tool marker, or the final update appears. For normal generations, that turns a live stream into one final chunk.

## Proposed fix

Limit the guard to the combination it protects: Anthropic streaming with legacy DeepSeek syntax. OpenAI-compatible streams can then emit answer text immediately for every current model family. Anthropic retains the #678 protection for legacy DeepSeek while modern DeepSeek 4.1, GLM, and Qwen stream normally.

Regression coverage should verify incremental answer delivery before finish for:

- OpenAI-compatible DeepSeek, DeepSeek 4.1, GLM, and Qwen streams
- Anthropic DeepSeek 4.1, GLM, and Qwen streams
- Anthropic legacy DeepSeek second-pass rerouting

Live pi-web verification after the fix:

| Model | Thinking deltas | Text deltas | Text stream duration |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen | 143 | 1,082 | 18.5s |
| DeepSeek V4 Flash | 248 | 506 | 13.4s |
| GLM 5.3 Flash | 656 | 762 | 26.6s |

title: Avoid buffering tool-enabled response streams
body:
Review validation: this draft does not yet meet the goal of streaming Qwen, GLM, and DeepSeek V4 Flash while retaining the existing repeated-reasoning protection. A 24-case socket test compared upstream `8db1d1d` and this PR using identical prefixes followed by either normal answer text or a second reasoning close. Upstream buffered and protected all six model/API combinations. This PR streamed and leaked the synthetic draft for OpenAI DeepSeek and both APIs on GLM and Qwen; Anthropic DeepSeek retained buffering and protection. This is a parser test, not a measurement of how often live models produce malformed output. Narrowing by model name does not preserve the same safeguard.

Fixes #1076.

Tool-enabled thinking requests previously held answer text until a tool marker or the final update. A normal answer without a tool call therefore arrived as one final chunk in pi-web. This change streams answer text immediately through OpenAI Chat Completions for all model syntaxes and through Anthropic for DeepSeek 4.1, GLM, and Qwen.

The buffering workaround remains in the Anthropic handler for `SERVER_MODEL_SYNTAX_DEEPSEEK`. This is the original DeepSeek prompt/tool format, also used by the tested V4 Flash checkpoint. It does not mean the model itself is obsolete. The OpenAI handler no longer carries an unused guard field or unreachable rerouting code.

Known behavior change: OpenAI streams lose the repeated-reasoning protection added for #678. That report measured Anthropic traffic but also identified the same mechanism in OpenAI. Restoring the old OpenAI regression test during review reproduces the regression: an unmarked second reasoning pass and its `</think>` tag can reach answer content. Immediate output cannot later be reclassified when a closing tag arrives. This PR chooses incremental output on that path; it does not solve both problems. Anthropic with the original DeepSeek format retains the protection and still buffers ordinary tool-enabled thinking answers.

Regression tests read the socket while it remains open and verify the first answer chunk, a subsequent chunk without replaying prior text, and trailing whitespace plus completion at finish. They cover all four syntaxes on OpenAI and DeepSeek 4.1, GLM, and Qwen on Anthropic. The original Anthropic repeated-reasoning test remains.

Validation after review:

```text
make -j8 ds4-server ds4_test
./ds4_test --server
server: OK
ds4 tests: ok
git diff --check
```

Earlier live pi-web measurements from the implementation task are shown below. Model inference was not rerun for the cleanup commit.

| Model | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Qwen | 1 final text delta | 1,082 text deltas over 18.5s |
| DeepSeek V4 Flash | 1 final text delta | 506 text deltas over 13.4s |
| GLM 5.3 Flash | 1 final text delta | 762 text deltas over 26.6s |

title: cuda: give ldmatrix the .shared state space in token-tile attention
body:
## Summary The three `ldmatrix` helpers in `ds4_cuda.cu` omit the state-space qualifier while being handed an address produced by `__cvta_generic_to_shared()`. PTX then uses generic addressing, and the instruction faults on the **first** `ldmatrix` executed by `attention_tokentile_hmma_kernel`, in every warp of every block, at a provably in-range offset. The first *visible* symptom is a later, unrelated CUDA call failing — a cuBLAS call, a `cudaMalloc`, a model range copy — which may be why this has surfaced as several different-looking reports. ## Why this is not a niche path The comment above the block says the kernel is opt-in. That comment is stale: the launch guard has no enabling flag, only the `DS4_CUDA_NO_WINDOW_ATTENTION` kill switch (`ds4_cuda.cu:17990` on `8db1d1d`): ```c if (g_n_gpus == 1 && !use_comp_mask && n_tokens >= 128u && head_dim == kTTHeadDim && n_head == 64u && window == kTTRawWindow && ratio != 0u && n_comp <= 32768u && n_raw >= n_tokens && (uint64_t)n_raw <= (uint64_t)pos0 + n_tokens && !g_cuda_no_window_attention && ds4_cuda_attn_tokentile_arch_ok()) { ``` `ds4_cuda_attn_tokentile_arch_ok()` is `prop.major >= 8`. So: a single GPU, sm_80 or newer, no comp mask, and a prefill batch of 128 tokens or more at the stock V4 Flash attention shape. That is the default configuration for the flagship model on any single Ampere-or-newer card. This PR corrects the comment too. ## The defect `ds4_cuda.cu:10617` hands over a shared-space address: ```c __device__ __forceinline__ unsigned tt_smem_addr(const void *p) { return static_cast(__cvta_generic_to_shared(p)); } ``` The PTX ISA spells the instruction `ldmatrix.sync.aligned.shape.num{.trans}{.ss}.type`, with `.ss = .shared{::cta}`. `.ss` is optional, and **when it is omitted the instruction uses generic addressing**: the address must then fall inside the shared-memory window of the generic address space, and the behaviour is undefined if it does not. `__cvta_generic_to_shared()` returns the opposite kind of address — a shared-space offset, which as a generic address points outside that window. ## Standalone reproducer, no ds4 One address, three spellings, ~30 lines. One spelling per process, so a sticky error cannot carry over.
probe.cu ```cuda #include #include #include #define BODY \ extern __shared__ unsigned char smem[]; \ for (unsigned i = threadIdx.x; i < 32768u; i += blockDim.x) smem[i] = (unsigned char)i; \ __syncthreads(); \ const unsigned row = threadIdx.x & 7u; \ const unsigned chunk = (threadIdx.x >> 3u) & 1u; \ const unsigned off = (row * 64u + chunk) * 16u; \ unsigned a = (unsigned)__cvta_generic_to_shared(smem + off); __global__ void __launch_bounds__(512,1) k_none(unsigned *o){ BODY uint32_t r[2]; asm volatile("ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x2.b16 {%0, %1}, [%2];" : "=r"(r[0]),"=r"(r[1]) : "r"(a)); if(!threadIdx.x) o[0]=r[0]^r[1]; } __global__ void __launch_bounds__(512,1) k_shared(unsigned *o){ BODY uint32_t r[2]; asm volatile("ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x2.shared.b16 {%0, %1}, [%2];" : "=r"(r[0]),"=r"(r[1]) : "r"(a)); if(!threadIdx.x) o[0]=r[0]^r[1]; } __global__ void __launch_bounds__(512,1) k_cta(unsigned *o){ BODY uint32_t r[2]; asm volatile("ldmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x2.shared::cta.b16 {%0, %1}, [%2];" : "=r"(r[0]),"=r"(r[1]) : "r"(a)); if(!threadIdx.x) o[0]=r[0]^r[1]; } static void go(const char *l, void(*k)(unsigned*)){ unsigned *d=nullptr; cudaMalloc(&d,4); cudaFuncSetAttribute(k, cudaFuncAttributeMaxDynamicSharedMemorySize, 32768); k<<<1,512,32768>>>(d); cudaError_t a=cudaGetLastError(), b=cudaDeviceSynchronize(); unsigned h=0; cudaMemcpy(&h,d,4,cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost); printf("%-14s launch=%-34s sync=%-34s val=0x%08x\n", l, cudaGetErrorString(a), cudaGetErrorString(b), h); cudaFree(d); } int main(int argc,char**argv){ int n=argc>1?atoi(argv[1]):0; if(n==0) go("no state space", k_none); if(n==1) go(".shared", k_shared); if(n==2) go(".shared::cta", k_cta); return 0; } ```
```sh nvcc -arch=sm_86 -o probe probe.cu ./probe 0 ; ./probe 1 ; ./probe 2 ``` ``` no state space launch=no error sync=an illegal memory access was encountered val=0x00000000 .shared launch=no error sync=no error val=0x10101010 .shared::cta launch=no error sync=no error val=0x10101010 ``` Identical under nvcc 13.2 and nvcc 13.0 on the same driver: the result does not depend on the toolkit. ## In-tree A/B RTX 3090 (sm_86), driver 580.178.04, `make cuda CUDA_ARCH=sm_86`, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Q2, `ds4-bench --ssd-streaming`, 256-token prefill at `--ctx-alloc 4096` — about 40 s per cell. | cell | change | result | |---|---|---| | control | none | `cuBLAS f32 matmul failed: status 14`, then `layer-major prefill failed at layer 0`, exit 1 | | workaround | `DS4_CUDA_NO_WINDOW_ATTENTION=1` | passes — the faulting path is simply not taken | | fix | this patch, **no** env var | passes, coherent output text | Under `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck --print-limit 0` the control cell reports **9472 errors, all "Invalid `__shared__` read of size 16 bytes" at the same site** — `tt_ldmatrix_x2_addr`, inside `attention_tokentile_hmma_kernel`. The offsets rule out an index escaping the buffer: only 64 distinct addresses, minimum offset 0 and maximum `0x1f70` = 8048 bytes, all inside the first 32768-byte plane of the ring; the 128 threads involved are exactly the 16 lanes × 8 warps that supply an address to `ldmatrix.x2`. It is the first `ldmatrix` of the kernel, at a valid offset, in every warp. ## Possibly the same cause, not confirmed #881 (`illegal memory access at first 2048-token prefill in ds4-bench (RTX 3090, layer-major FFN encode)`) matches every trigger condition: single RTX 3090, sm_86, first prefill, `n_tokens` 2048 ≥ 128, stock V4 Flash shape. Its reported failing stage is the layer-2 FFN encode and ours was the layer-0 prefill, but in both cases that is the *call after* the real fault, so the difference does not separate the two. The discriminating test needs no patch: re-run that exact command with `DS4_CUDA_NO_WINDOW_ATTENTION=1`. If it passes, it is this bug. #759 and #847 may belong to the same class; we have not checked them, and #847 is a different kernel on sm_120. ## What we have not tested - CUDA 12.4, the toolkit in #881. Our runs are 13.0 and 13.2. - Any architecture other than sm_86. The probe result is toolkit-independent across 13.0/13.2; we do not extend that to other GPUs. Found while building a hybrid CUDA/ROCm split of V4.1 out of tree; the defect itself is untouched by anything we changed, and reproduces on unmodified `main`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01Ds7x2AayRsydxdDiyT6vhR

title: Make the 16-image conversation limit configurable and batching-aware
body:
`ds4-server` rejects requests containing more than 16 images:

```c
size_t count = 0;
for (int i = 0; msgs && i < msgs->len; i++)
    count += msgs->v[i].images.len;

if (count > 16) {
    snprintf(err, errlen, "too many images; at most 16 are allowed");
    return false;
}
```

This counts images across the submitted history, not only the newest turn.

DS4 requires Chat Completions and Anthropic clients to replay conversation history. Its Responses endpoint likewise rejects durable `previous_response_id`/`conversation` references and instructs clients to replay the full input.

The request limit therefore becomes a cumulative conversation limit. Once history contains 17 images, every subsequent request fails before inference, including text-only turns. Retrying cannot recover because it submits the same history. The client must rewrite or discard history, and the model cannot handle the condition because it never receives another turn.

This is easy to reach in agent workflows that retain screenshots or other image tool results.

## Reproducer

Submit a request containing N small images:

| Images | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 16 | 200 |
| 17 | 400: `too many images; at most 16 are allowed` |

Append a text-only message and replay the same history. The request returns the same 400 before prefill.

## Current implementation

The limit was introduced with server-side vision in `4771329` (2026-08-28). It is also embedded in replay bookkeeping:

- Request validation rejects `count > 16`.
- `visible_image_key` contains `offsets[16]`.
- `visible_prompt_key` rejects `req->image_count > 16`.
- `build_live_prompt_suffix` rejects `req->image_count > 16` and uses `ds4_vision_span spans[16]`.

Later image-embedding caching avoids encoder execution on cache hits, although request-owned embedding memory still scales with image count.

## Relation to `--batched-session`

Cold image encoding holds the global `inference_mu`. With `--batched-session N>1`, an image-heavy request can therefore delay other resident sessions, making a conservative default useful for fairness.

With one resident session, there is no cross-slot inference contention. Request memory and abuse protection still justify a limit, but the case for a low ceiling of 16 is weaker: the operator may prefer accepting higher latency or memory use over making the conversation unusable.

## Requested change

Add:

```text
--max-images N
```

Suggested defaults:

- `--batched-session N>1`: default to 16.
- One resident session: use a higher or resource-derived default.
- An explicit `--max-images` value overrides either default.

Implementation would need to replace the fixed `[16]` replay structures and validation literals with the configured limit.

Also:

- Document that replayed history counts toward the limit.
- Include the actual and configured counts in the error:

  ```text
  request contains 17 images; server limit is 16 (--max-images)
  ```

This preserves a conservative fairness bound for batched serving while allowing single-session and replay-heavy deployments to choose an appropriate limit.

Happy to make a PR if the solution direction is ok.

title: tests: fix test_agent_compaction.py
body:
test_agent_compaction.py fails for me locally with DeepSeek 4 Flash (vision), the PR fixes it.

---

The compaction test asks the model to write 80 C functions and compiles them with an oracle that declares `extern int value_N(void)`. The prompt did not require a return type, so a model can emit

    value_0(void) { return 0; }

which clang rejects because implicit `int` is an error since C99. The test then fails for a reason unrelated to compaction.

Fix: state the signature explicitly (`int value_N(void)`).

Verified locally: the generated file now starts `int value_0(void) { return 0; }` and the test passes.

title: CUDA SSD streaming: run the cached experts while the miss reads are in flight (+6 to +12 % decode)
body:
**The limitation.** With `--ssd-streaming`, a decode token's six routed experts split into hits
(already in the GPU expert cache) and misses (read from the SSD, about 9.5 MB each at Q2). Today
the layer waits for every miss read to land before it runs any expert, so each token pays for
its slowest read while the GPU sits idle.

**The change.**
- Run the hits' gate/up/down as soon as the routing is known, while the miss reads are in flight.
- Run the misses when they land, then sum the six down partials.
- A threaded pread pool ships with it, because the miss reads must leave the calling thread for
  the GPU to run anything: 8 workers, pinned staging and a CUDA stream each, gate and up of every
  miss read before the downs, no worker ever touches the O_DIRECT globals.

**Output is byte-identical.**
- The partials are summed in slot order from +0.0f, the float sequence the fused kernel executes.
- Greedy `--temp 0 --dump-logprobs` on a 45-token and a 4,392-token prompt gives the same sha256
  as the unpatched tree.

**Switches.**
- `DS4_CUDA_HITS_FIRST=0` keeps the pool and restores the read-then-launch order.
- `DS4_CUDA_STREAMING_EXPERT_PREAD_POOL=0` as well restores the serial staged reads the tree has today.

**Measured.** DGX Spark GB10, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Q2, `ds4-bench --cuda --ssd-streaming
--ssd-streaming-cache-experts 90GB`, ctx 4096 and 6144, 128 generated tokens, decode tokens/s at
the slower context, each patched run interleaved between two unpatched runs, 4 repeats:

    round   patched t/s   unpatched t/s   delta    repeats above the tip
    A         10.37          9.65         +6.5 %   4 of 4
    B         10.34          8.96        +12.3 %   4 of 4
    C         10.29          9.54         +9.1 %   4 of 4

- Prefill is unchanged within noise.
- Identical binaries swing about 8 % run to run on this box (the model is streamed, not
  page-cached), which is why every number is a median of interleaved repeats.

**Where it does not help.**
- A fully resident model (no misses) does nothing different.
- An io_uring read pool on its own was faster on a quiet box and less stable under CPU load, so
  this PR carries the launch-order change and the plain pthread pool it needs, not the ring.

**Files.** `ds4_cuda.cu` (the pread pool, the split down kernels, the hits-first launch in
`routed_moe_launch`, the task build in the expert cache begin-load path) and a README card with
the numbers and the branches tried alongside. No new dependencies.

title: CUDA SSD streaming: hits-first expert launch, the Metal split's counterpart (+5 to +8 % decode)
body:
**The problem.** With `--ssd-streaming`, a decode token's six routed experts split into hits
(already in the GPU expert cache) and misses (read from the SSD, about 9.5 MB each at Q2). Today
the layer waits for every miss read to land before it runs any expert, so each token pays for its
slowest read while the GPU sits idle.

**This is your own idea, brought to CUDA.** `ds4_metal.m` already does it:
`ds4_gpu_stream_expert_split_worthwhile()` splits the resident experts from the missing ones so
that, in its comment's words, *"their SSD reads can be hidden by resident expert work"*. The CUDA
path had no equivalent. This adds one, and keeps the name hits-first.

**The change.**
- Run the hits' gate/up/down as soon as the routing is known, while the miss reads are in flight.
- Run the misses when they land, then sum the six down partials.
- A threaded pread pool ships with it, because the miss reads must leave the calling thread for
  the GPU to run anything: 8 workers, pinned staging and a CUDA stream each, no worker ever
  touches the O_DIRECT globals.

**Two mechanisms here are not in the Metal path**, and they are what make the CUDA split pay:
- **The reads are ordered, not just started.** Gate and up of every miss are queued before any
  down, so the miss gate/up launch waits on the first stage only rather than on all of an
  expert's bytes.
- **The down is split per slot and summed in slot order.** Six partials accumulated from `+0.0f`
  in slot order, which is the float sequence the fused kernel already executes, so the down can be
  split at all without changing the result.

## Measured

DGX Spark GB10, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Q2, `ds4-bench --cuda --ssd-streaming
--ssd-streaming-cache-experts 90GB`, ctx 4096 and 6144, 128 generated tokens, decode tokens/s at
the slower context, each patched run interleaved between two unpatched runs.

| round | patched t/s | unpatched t/s | delta | repeats above baseline | against |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| A | 10.37 | 9.65 | +6.5 % | 4 of 4 | an older tip of mine |
| B | 10.34 | 8.96 | +12.3 % | 4 of 4 | an older tip of mine |
| C | 10.29 | 9.54 | +9.1 % | 4 of 4 | an older tip of mine |
| D | 10.70 | 9.83 | +8.0 % | 3 of 3 | **main @8db1d1d1** |
| E | 10.57 | 9.62 | +6.9 % | 3 of 3 | **main @8db1d1d1** |

**Only the rounds against your main are a reading of this PR.** Three of those exist, all at the
same cache request and the same delivered expert population, which is the condition for reading
them as three readings of one thing:

| round | binary | cache requested / delivered | delta | sign | that round's floor |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| R22 | 312c37a5, earlier PR state | 90GB / 8,941 | **+7.97 %** | 3/3 | 2.44 |
| R23 | 6803d6db, this PR's head | 90GB / 8,941 | **+6.89 %** | 3/3 | 2.17 |
| DECOMP | 6803d6db, this PR's head | 90GB / 8,941 | **+4.98 %** | 3/3 | 3.96 |

The two binaries are behaviourally the same at default env: `ds4_cuda.cu` is byte-identical
between 312c37a5 and 4c827924d, and 6803d6dba adds only the miss threshold, whose default of 1 is
the earlier behaviour.

⇒ **+5 to +8 % is what those three rounds support, and the title has been corrected to say so.**
The +12.3 % is against an older tip of mine, not against your main, and a title carries no fence.

## The commit has two parts, and neither one ships alone

The pread pool and the hits-first ordering are two env switches over one binary, so this is a
decomposition rather than a build difference. Same round, same file, same cache on every row,
against main @8db1d1d1, min-across-frontiers, floor 3.96:

| arm | cache req / del | delta | sign | verdict |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| what ships, pool and ordering | 90GB / 8,941 | **+4.98 %** | 3/3 | **beats the floor** |
| the pool alone, `HITS_FIRST=0` | 90GB / 8,941 | +1.12 % | 3/3 | inside the floor |
| the ordering alone, `PREAD_POOL=0` | 90GB / 8,941 | +0.15 % | 2/3 | inside the floor |
| both off | 90GB / 8,941 | -0.92 % | 1/3 | inside the floor |

**Both switches off reproduces your tip**, which is the round's calibration control and ran before
anything else was read.

⇒ **Whichever half you credit, the other is load-bearing.** Remove either and the arm drops into
the noise. That is why the two parts are one commit rather than two.

**Which half does the work, here.** Taking the marginals inside one cycle against one shared tip
bracket: the whole commit **+6.46 %**, the ordering's marginal on the pool **+3.80 %**, the pool
alone **+2.56 %**. The ratios compose exactly, `1.0256 x 1.0380 - 1 = 6.46 %`. The ordering's
marginal exceeds the pool's in 3 of 3 cycles, which is what makes naming the commit after the
ordering defensible on measurement rather than on inference.

⚠ **I am not publishing a percentage split.** The round's own preregistered rule releases a share
only when the whole-commit ratio is at least three times the widest noise estimate, and 6.46 %
against a 3.96 % floor does not clear it. So the rough 40/60 is a point estimate, not a
measurement, and it wants 5 cycles rather than 3 if the share itself matters.

⚠ **And the split is regime-dependent, so do not carry it.** On GLM 5.3 Flash Q2 at a 24GB cache,
3,064 slots, the same two switches give the pool about four fifths of the lever: **+20.42 % for
the pool against +4.88 % for the ordering's marginal**, the opposite apportionment. 90GB on this
file leaves a typical per-layer miss batch of 0 or 1 experts, where the pool buys asynchrony but
no parallelism while the ordering still fires; 24GB on GLM is the many-miss regime. That is an
explanation consistent with the numbers, not something the round measured.

## The two switches are not two levers

Read at this branch's head in `ds4_cuda.cu`: the ordering is applied inside
`cuda_stream_selected_cache_begin_load`, guarded by
`if (!tasks.empty() && pool_ok && slot_count <= 8u)`, and the reordered task list is handed to
`cuda_pread_pool_dispatch_start`. With `DS4_CUDA_STREAMING_EXPERT_PREAD_POOL=0`,
`cuda_pread_pool_init` returns 0, that dispatch returns 0 before a byte is read, and the function
falls through to the serial staged copies. **The reorder is computed and thrown away.**

⇒ `DS4_CUDA_STREAMING_EXPERT_PREAD_POOL=0` alone is the whole revert, and `DS4_CUDA_HITS_FIRST=0`
on top of it changes no code path. The two arms the source says execute the same path read
medians 1.07 points apart with no consistent sign, so the source reading survives its own test.

**Switches.**
- `DS4_CUDA_HITS_FIRST=0` keeps the pool and restores the read-then-launch order.
- `DS4_CUDA_STREAMING_EXPERT_PREAD_POOL=0` as well restores the serial staged reads main has
  today, and is on its own the complete revert.

## Output is byte-identical, on all four switch settings

- The partials are summed in slot order from `+0.0f`, the same sequence the fused kernel runs.
- Under the round's lock, before its first timed run: the reference was minted **twice** from the
  tip @8db1d1d1 and agreed on both shas and both byte counts. The same argv then ran on this
  branch's head with no switches, with `HITS_FIRST=0`, with `PREAD_POOL=0`, and with both.
- **12 of 12 runs rc=0, and every sha equals the twice-minted reference on both prompts**: short
  `5ed3e6dfe2177eca` at 73,515 bytes, long `c5cb82566c628bed` at 36,655 bytes, greedy at
  `--temp 0 --dump-logprobs`. `PREAD_POOL=0` had never been output-verified before this round.
- One number in the gate differs from the bench by design: every gate log reads 8,649 slots rather
  than 8,941, because the gate's `--ctx 32768` takes a larger KV reserve out of the same 90GB.

⚠ **The gate does not witness the switch and I would not claim that it does.** Identical shas are
expected whether a switch was honoured or ignored. The switch witnesses are the wall clock and the
calibration control above.

## Two things I am reporting rather than claiming

- **Prefill.** Its reading is not stable across rounds: round E read **-7.05 % and -8.06 %
  min-across at sign 0/3 on both of its arms**, and the later decomposition round read **+0.48 %**
  on the shipped arm against the same tip, same file, same cache. Both arms of round E carry it, so
  it does not separate them. **I am not claiming a prefill result in either direction.**
- **Run-to-run noise.** Every number is a median of interleaved repeats and every round computes
  its own floor from adjacent unpatched pairs: **2.44** (R22), **2.17** (R23), **3.96** (DECOMP).
  R29 read 12.62 once, blown by a single degraded tip run its seal forbade dropping. The larger
  swing is the warm-up: R22's discarded warm-up ran 11.5 % below its first live tip run.

**I tried your Metal threshold and it loses here, so it is not in this PR.** The Metal split
declines below three missing experts, and the measured expert-cache hit rate is 0.957 at top-6, so
the expected misses per layer are 0.26 and most split layers sit at one or two, exactly the regime
your comment names. Ported to CUDA it measured **+3.98 % against this branch's +6.89 %** in the
same round, a 2.91-point cost against that round's 2.17 floor. The reason looks like the cost
model: the Metal comment prices a command stage, whereas the CUDA path pays a kernel launch, which
is single-digit microseconds against the 321 to 411 microseconds one 9.5 MB expert read takes on
this box. Right number for that backend, wrong number for this one.

**Where it does not help.**
- A fully resident model (no misses) does nothing different.
- An io_uring read pool on its own was faster on a quiet box and less stable under CPU load, so
  this carries the launch-order change and the plain pthread pool it needs, not the ring.

**Files.** `ds4_cuda.cu` (the pread pool, the split down kernels, the hits-first launch in
`routed_moe_launch`, the task build in the expert cache begin-load path) and a README card with
the numbers. No new dependencies.

title: Stream assistant content incrementally when tools are enabled
body:
## Problem

With `stream: true` and `tools` present (`tool_choice` other than `"none"`),
the assistant `content` is emitted as a **single** SSE chunk at the end of
generation. `reasoning_content` is unaffected and still streams token by token.
Live-rendering clients therefore show reasoning streaming and then the whole
answer appearing at once.

Reproduction (`deepseek-v4.1-flash`, `max_tokens: 150`, one short prompt):

| request | reasoning chunks | content chunks (before) |
|---|---|---|
| no `tools` | 84 | 20 (streams) |
| `tools` only (default auto) | 21 | **1** |
| `tools` + `tool_choice: "none"` | 85 | 26 (streams) |
| `tools` + `tool_choice: "auto"` | 27 | **1** |

## Root cause

`fe2d3b0` ("Keep repeated reasoning out of streamed answers") added
`guard_second_reasoning`. After the first `</think>` the streamer enters
`TEXT` mode but keeps the guard armed, and:

```c
} else if (!tool && !final) {
    return true;   /* hold everything until generation ends */
}
```

holds *all* content until a tool call or a second `</think>` appears. In the
common case neither appears, so nothing is flushed until `final`.
`tool_choice: "none"` sets `has_tools = false` and bypasses the guard, which
is why it streams.

## Fix

Keep the reroute intent but bound the hold to a short lookahead window
(`SECOND_REASONING_GUARD_BYTES = 32`): a short stray draft, or a `</think>`
split across generated tokens, is still rerouted to `reasoning_content`; past
the window the text is treated as the answer and streamed. Applied to both
`openai_sse_stream_update` and `anthropic_sse_stream_update`.

Note this matches the non-streaming behaviour, where `split_reasoning_content`
splits on the **first** `</think>`; previously the streaming guard made the two
paths disagree.

## Verification

Machine: Apple M3 Ultra, 512 GB, Metal. Model: V4.1 Flash Q4.

```sh
make clean && make
./ds4_test --server
```

Both pass. A focused regression test,
`test_openai_tools_stream_content_is_incremental`, was added. It fails on the
previous code:

```
ds4_server.c:16801: assertion failed: content_deltas >= 2
```

Live end-to-end, same request as above (content chunks after the fix):

| request | content chunks (after) |
|---|---|
| no tools | 29 |
| tools + `none` | 27 |
| tools + `auto` | 10 |

## Tradeoff

A repeated reasoning pass longer than the window would now leak into
`content`. That is already the case on the non-streaming path, so this makes
the two consistent. If a larger window is preferred, the constant is in one
place.

title: Ternary PTQ for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Bonsai-2-style, ~1.72 bpw): could make main weights resident on 256 GB Macs and ~2.5x SSD-streaming decode on 128 GB
body:
**Body:**

## Proposal
Explore a ternary post-training quantization (Bonsai-2-style: Hadamard-rotated {−1,0,+1} weights, ~1.72 bpw, imatrix-calibrated) for the **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash main weights**, produced from the FP16 safetensors (not from an existing quant).

## Why this could matter a lot for ds4 users

**The math (V4.1 Flash, Q4 today = 518.6 GB file):**
- Main weights: 294 GB at ~4.5 bpw → ternary ~1.72 bpw ≈ **112 GB**
- Engram tables: 189 GB (untouched, they are lookup content)
- Ternary file: ~300 GB total (**−217 GB vs Q4**)

**Two user classes liberated:**

1. **256 GB Macs — full residency.** 112 GB of main weights fits in 256 GB unified memory with room for KV and buffers. Today V4.1 Flash Q4 on a 256 GB machine is SSD-streaming-bound at ~8–9 tok/s decode (measured, M3 Ultra; matches the ROCm port's numbers on similar hardware). Resident decode would put the flagship model in a completely different speed class.

2. **128 GB Macs (and all streaming users) — SSD-streaming decode is byte-bound.** Streaming decode speed scales with expert bytes fetched per token. Ternary cuts routed-weight bytes by ~60% (1.72 vs 4.5 bpw), so streaming decode should scale to roughly **2–2.5× today's 4.5–5.5 tok/s** on equivalent SSDs, making 128 GB machines genuinely usable for V4.1.

## Evidence the technique works on this model family

- PrismML's **Bonsai 2 27B** (Apache-2.0, whitepaper linked) applies exactly this method — Hadamard-rotated ternary at a true 1.72 bpw, no high-precision escape hatches — to **Qwen3.8-27B, a hybrid-attention model (~75% linear attention)**, and reports 98.2% of FP16 benchmark retention (84.78 avg across 14 thinking benchmarks, math within 0.5 pt), beating IQ2_XXS by >12 points at 2/3 of its footprint and matching UD-Q4_K_XL at 1/3 the size. They ship custom ternary llama.cpp kernels for CUDA and **Metal**, and PQ2_0 (2-bit-slot packing) now runs on mainline llama.cpp CPU/Metal/Vulkan/CUDA.
- So ternary kernels for a Qwen3.8-family **hybrid-attention** backbone already exist; the missing pieces for V4.1 are (a) the MoE routed-expert path and (b) the Engram/attention specifics of ds4's graph — which is exactly the kernel engineering this project is best at.
- ds4 already has the calibration side: the IQ2_XXS/Q2_K imatrix pipeline for V4.1.

## Fair caveats
- 98.2% retention is a 27B **dense** result; 755B **MoE** expert ternarization is unproven and router sensitivity is a real risk. A first step could be small-scale: ternarize a few expert layers, measure NLL/top-token on the existing quality harness before committing to full kernels.
- Engram tables (189 GB) cannot be ternarized (lookup content), so total-file savings are bounded (~217 GB); the headline win is **residency on 256 GB** and **streaming speed on everything smaller**.
- Vision tower would ship separately as today.

## Suggested incremental path
1. Imatrix ternary PTQ of a subset of routed experts (offline, no kernels needed) → run the existing score harness → decide.
2. If retention looks Bonsai-like: prototype ternary Metal kernels for the routed path, ssd-streaming first (helps 128 GB + all streamers), residency second.
3. Optional: coordinate with PrismML — their kernels are Apache-2.0 and already handle Qwen3.8-family hybrid attention.

A 256 GB M3 Ultra user measurably stuck at the SSD-streaming ceiling would love to help test.

title: server: in-process Prometheus metrics via GET /metrics
body:
Adds a `/metrics` endpoint to ds4-server with the same series the journald-parsing exporter historically exposed, so existing dashboards keep working when the scrape target moves in-process.

This is the focused successor to #861's metrics portion, rebuilt to minimize merge-conflict surface:

- **All metrics state and exposition rendering live in new files** (`ds4_metrics.c` / `ds4_metrics.h`) that upstream never needs to modify.
- `ds4_server.c` carries only one-line hooks at existing log/lifecycle sites: decode progress (tokens by phase + rate gauges), the prefill progress callback (per-chunk token accounting, so long prompts never render as `rate()` spikes), prompt-done (remainder + cache-hit source), live-KV miss reason, request finish (+duration histograms), job begin/end for `ds4_active_requests`, and the route itself.
- Server-state gauges (`ds4_context_limit_tokens`, `ds4_context_tokens{slot}`) are passed into the renderer by value — the module never includes server types.
- `ds4_kvstore` gains only a five-line optional completion-hook typedef + setter, registered at startup for the stored/trimmed/bytes counters.
- Series kept identical: token counters, prefill/decode tps, requests by finish, request/prompt duration histograms, reused tokens (plus by-source), KV hit/miss by source/reason, KV stored/trimmed/bytes, active requests, context gauges. 861-specific machinery series (rewind refusals, capture skips, dispatch holds) are intentionally not carried.
- Observation only: no engine, scheduler, or KV behavior changes.

Tests: `tests/test_metrics` (wired into `make test`) is model-free and asserts exact exposition lines, histogram bucket placement, and the never-negative active gauge. Verified on macOS (Metal): `make`, `make cpu`, `ds4_test --server`, `tests/test_metrics` all pass. A live ROCm scrape from the production deployment follows as a comment.

title: server: content is emptied when a thinking model ends a turn without closing </think> (finish=stop, no tools involved)
body:
## Summary

With thinking mode enabled, when the sampled turn ends with `finish_reason: "stop"`
**without ever emitting `</think>`** and **no tool call is involved**, `ds4-server`
routes the whole buffer to `reasoning_content` and returns `content: ""`.

Two related behaviours are deliberate and stay as they are:

- **#509 (truncation, `finish_reason: "length"`)** — a cut-off reasoning chain must
  not reach clients looking like a finished reply. That is exactly what the
  comment above `ds4_local_unterminated_reasoning()` describes, and it should
  remain.
- **#318 (tool call inside unclosed thinking)** — recovery landed as a forced
  `</think>` so the tool call is delivered ("display whatever the model sampled").

Neither covers the plain case: no `tools` in the request, generation completed
normally, and the model's output is dropped.

## Measured impact

Two thinking models on the same server, same request shape, 50 scored reps each
(long-form analytical prompts, no tools, `reasoning_effort: high`):

| model | reps returning `content: ""` | `reasoning_content` in those reps |
|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2 (GGUF, resident) | 4 / 50 | 3.060 – 18.827 characters |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4 (GGUF) | 5 / 50 | 20.015 – 45.734 characters |

All nine have `finish_reason: "stop"`. The buffer is not a cut-off chain — it is
whatever the model chose to end with, **and it contains the finished answer**.
From the four GLM reps, the first 400 characters of the dumped
`reasoning_content` (the benchmark task asks for a stage-1 base-rate
calculation with a fixed expected solution):

```
rep1: Base rate 2% fraudulent, 200 per 10000. Stage 1: sens 90% → 180 true alarms;
      FPR 5% → 0.05 × 9800 = 490 false alarms. Total alarms = 670.
      PPV = 180/670 = 0.26865... = 26.9%. Alarme per 10000 = 670. Echte Alarme = 180.
rep2: - True alarms: 0.9 × 200 = 180. - False alarms: 0.05 × 9800 = 490.
      - Total alarms: 670. - PPV = 180/670 = 0.26865... = 26.9%. alarme_je_10000 = 670.
rep6: PPV Stufe 1: Sens 0.9 → TP = 0.9*200 = 180. FP = 0.05*9800 = 490.
      PPV = 180/670 = 0.26865... = 26.9% (1 decimal).
rep8: Stufe 1: sensitivity 90% → detects 180 fraud. FPR 5% → alarms 490 legit.
      Total alarms = 670. PPV = 180/670 = 0.26866... = 26.9%.
```

Those are the correct expected values (670 / 26.9% / 180), computed correctly,
in all four reps that the server returned as empty. The work is not missing; it
is discarded.

Reproduced again in a controlled rerun (same prompt, same server, thinking
mode, `reasoning_effort: high`) — 1 hit in 23 reps, and that rep's dumped buffer
is 13,412 characters long. Its first 300 characters already carry the enumerated
solution:

```
Let me compute carefully. Base: 2% fraudulent, 98% legitimate per 10,000
transactions: 200 fraud, 9800 legit. Stage 1: sensitivity 90%, FPR 5%.
- True alarms: 0.9 × 200 = 180
- False alarms: 0.05 × 9800 = 490
- Total alarms: 670 → alarme_je_10000 = 670
- PPV = 180/670 = 0.26865... = 26.9% (1 decimal: 26.9)
- echte_alarme = 180
1. ppv_prozent = 26.9
2. alarme_je_10000 = 670
3. echte_alarme_je_10000 = 180
4. max_fpr: PPV ≥ 90%: 180/(180 + fpr×9800) ≥ 0.9 → ...
```

All five expected values of that task (26.9 / 670 / 29 / 15,025.00 / 78.6) are
present in the buffer. In this rep the model was still weighing two readings of
the last field when it emitted EOS, so the buffer is not always a finished
answer — but it never is nothing, and "show what the model sampled" is the
behaviour the rest of the server follows.

Note on reproducibility: intermittent. Over the original 50-rep runs it hit 9
reps (~10%); a first 12-rep rerun produced no hit, a 23-rep rerun produced one.
Every hit is accompanied by exactly one `thinking not closed` log line.

The only diagnostic on the server side is:

```
ds4-server: thinking not closed, ignoring incomplete GLM tool calls in reasoning
```

The server log line matches the affected reps 1:1 — same timestamps, same `gen=`
token counts, and the next line shows the buffer being emptied:

```
0918 19:42:58 ds4-server: chat ctx=6993..7043:50 gen=5600 THINKING decoding chunk=24.18 t/s avg=22.82 t/s 245.448s
0918 19:43:00 ds4-server: chat ctx=7043..7082:39 gen=5639 THINKING decoding chunk=19.50 t/s avg=22.79 t/s 247.449s
ds4-server: thinking not closed, ignoring incomplete GLM tool calls in reasoning
0918 19:43:00 ds4-server: chat ctx=1443..1443:0 gen=5639 THINKING finish=stop 247.449s
```

For a benchmarking or batch client these reps are indistinguishable from "the
model produced nothing" — they count as total failures, which is a ~10% silent
loss on long prompts with no way for the client to tell it apart from a genuine
empty answer.

## A/B confirmation (same server, same prompt, both binaries)

30 reps each, KV cache cleared before each run, identical request parameters:

| | original binary | with the change below |
|---|---|---|
| `thinking not closed` log lines | 1 | 1 |
| reps with `content: ""` | **1** (`unterminated_reasoning`, scored 0 %) | **0** |
| scored reps | 29 / 30 | 30 / 30 |
| reliability | 96.7 % | **100 %** |
| what the client received | `content: ""` | 3,411 characters of model text |

The rep rescued by the change carries the model's own buffer (identical to
`reasoning_content`) instead of an empty string. It holds the correct
intermediate values of this task — 180 true alarms, 670 total alarms,
PPV 26.9%, max FPR 0.204% — but as prose, not as the JSON the task asks for, so
a strict-schema client still scores it 0.

The same server path fired in both runs — once as a total loss, once delivering
the text. Making the model close `</think>`, and thus produce a properly
formatted answer, is a separate (model/template-side) problem.

*Correction:* an earlier version of this post claimed the rescued rep came back
as the expected JSON with every value correct. That was a mis-attribution on my
side — the JSON belonged to a normal rep from the same run (its `reasoning`
was 6,510 characters ending in a proper `</think>`), not to the rep the server
emptied. The log correlation is unambiguous: the affected rep is the one whose
`gen=` count and duration match the `thinking not closed` line (here
`gen=1504`, 57.5 s).

## Code path

`parse_glm_generated_message_ex()` (`ds4_server.c:6341-6350`, same shape in the
Qwen and DeepSeek variants at `:6545` and `:6131`): no `</think>` and no complete
`<tool_call>...</tool_call>` → `ds4_local_unterminated_reasoning()` (`:6092`),
which sets `content_out = ""` and moves everything into `reasoning_out`. The
decision there cannot see `finish_reason`; the truncation argument in its comment
is the `length` case.

## Suggested fix

`parse_generated_message_for_response_for_syntax()` already has `finish_io` in
scope. After a successful parse, if `content` is empty, `reasoning_content` is
non-empty and `finish != "length"`, re-emit the text as `content`:

```c
const char *finish_final = (finish_io && *finish_io) ? *finish_io : "stop";
if (strcmp(finish_final, "length") != 0
        && content_out && *content_out && !**content_out
        && reasoning_out && *reasoning_out && **reasoning_out) {
    free(*content_out);
    *content_out = xstrdup(*reasoning_out);
}
```

This keeps #509 semantics untouched (finite: `length` still returns empty
content), leaves the #318 forced-`</think>` path alone (it never produces an empty
content), keeps `reasoning_content` populated for diagnostics, and sits in the
shared wrapper so all three syntax parsers benefit from one change.

Branch with the change and four server unit tests (recovery on `stop`, unchanged
behaviour on `length`, Qwen syntax, closed-`<think>` regression guard — `ds4
tests: ok`):
https://github.com/cropduster/ds4/tree/fix/unterminated-reasoning-stop

Happy to send it as a PR if the semantics look right to you — or to adjust: if
an unterminated buffer should stay out of `content` even on `stop`, the
alternative would be an explicit marker the client can detect instead of a
silent empty string.

title: server: recover unterminated reasoning as content when the turn completed
body:
## What this fixes

With thinking mode on, a turn that ends normally (`finish_reason: "stop"`) without
ever emitting `</think>` had its entire buffer routed to `reasoning_content` with
`content` set to `""`. For a truncated turn that behaviour is intended (#509) and
for a tool call inside unclosed thinking #318 added the forced-`</think>` recovery
— but a plain completed turn with no tools in the request lost its answer
entirely.

## Evidence

Same server, two thinking models, 50 scored reps each, long-form analytical
prompts, `reasoning_effort: high`, no tools:

| model | reps with `content: ""` | `reasoning_content` in those reps |
|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2 | 4 / 50 | 3.060 – 18.827 characters |
| Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4 | 5 / 50 | 20.015 – 45.734 characters |

All nine report `finish_reason: "stop"`. The log line matches the affected reps
1:1 (timestamps and `gen=` counts), and the following line shows the buffer being
emptied by `ds4_local_unterminated_reasoning()`:

```
0918 19:42:58 ds4-server: chat ctx=6993..7043:50 gen=5600 THINKING decoding chunk=24.18 t/s avg=22.82 t/s 245.448s
0918 19:43:00 ds4-server: chat ctx=7043..7082:39 gen=5639 THINKING decoding chunk=19.50 t/s avg=22.79 t/s 247.449s
ds4-server: thinking not closed, ignoring incomplete GLM tool calls in reasoning
0918 19:43:00 ds4-server: chat ctx=1443..1443:0 gen=5639 THINKING finish=stop 247.449s
```

The discarded text contains the correct answer. Those four GLM reps were given a
base-rate task with a fixed expected solution, and the first 400 characters of
each discarded buffer already hold it:

```
rep6: PPV Stufe 1: Sens 0.9 → TP = 0.9*200 = 180. FP = 0.05*9800 = 490.
      PPV = 180/670 = 0.26865... = 26.9% (1 decimal).
```

`670` alarms, `PPV 26.9%`, `180` true alarms — correct in all four reps the
client received as empty. The effect is intermittent (~10% over the measured
runs; a 12-rep rerun of the same task produced no hit, so it is not a
deterministic repro).

(An earlier version of this description claimed the affected rep came back as
the expected JSON. That was a mis-attribution on my side: the JSON belonged to a
normal rep from the same run. See the A/B section below for what the rescued
buffer actually contains.)


## A/B confirmation

Same server, same prompt, KV cache cleared before each run, 30 reps each:

| | original binary | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `thinking not closed` log lines | 1 | 1 |
| reps returned as `content: ""` | **1** (scored 0 %) | **0** |
| scored reps | 29 / 30 | 30 / 30 |
| reliability | 96.7 % | **100 %** |

What the rescued rep actually contains: 3,411 characters of the model's own
buffer (the reasoning text), instead of the empty string the original binary
returned. Those characters hold the correct intermediate values of this task —
`180` true alarms, `670` total alarms, `PPV 26.9%`, `max FPR 0.204%` — but as
prose, not as the JSON the task asks for:

```
Compute. Per 10,000 transactions: 200 fraudulent, 9800 legitimate.
Stufe 1: sensitivity 90% → 180 true alarms. FPR 5% → 490 false alarms.
Total alarms = 670. PPV = 180/670 = 0.26866 → 26.9%.
alarme_je_10000 = 670. echte_alarme = 180.
max_fpr: PPV ≥ 90%: ... f ≤ 0.002040816 → 0.2040816% → rounds to 0.204.
```

So a client with a strict response schema still scores that rep 0 — what the
change guarantees is that the buffer is no longer discarded, which is the
difference between "the model produced this" and "the model produced nothing".
Whether the buffer is a finished answer depends on where the model stopped;
making the model close `</think>` is the model/template side of the problem and
is not what this change does.

Fixes #1087.

## The change

Recovery happens in `parse_generated_message_for_response_for_syntax()`, which
already has `finish_io` in scope, so no parser signature changes and all three
syntax parsers benefit:

```c
const char *finish_final = (finish_io && *finish_io) ? *finish_io : "stop";
if (strcmp(finish_final, "length") != 0
        && content_out && *content_out && !**content_out
        && reasoning_out && *reasoning_out && **reasoning_out) {
    free(*content_out);
    *content_out = xstrdup(*reasoning_out);
}
```

- `finish_reason: "length"` keeps the #509 behaviour untouched (content stays
  empty, so a cut-off chain never looks like a finished reply).
- The #318 forced-`</think>` path never produces an empty content, so it is
  unaffected.
- `reasoning_content` stays populated, so the diagnostic information is not lost.
- One change site instead of three parser branches.

## Tests

Four new server unit tests in `ds4_server.c`:

- `test_unterminated_reasoning_content_recovered_on_stop` — the recovery case
  (content filled, `<think>` stripped, `finish_reason` untouched)
- `test_unterminated_reasoning_stays_empty_on_length` — regression guard for the
  #509 semantics
- `test_unterminated_reasoning_recovered_on_qwen_syntax` — same rule for the Qwen
  parser branch
- `test_closed_thinking_split_is_unchanged` — a properly closed block still
  splits, with no duplication into `reasoning_content`

```
$ make ds4_test ds4-server -j8
$ ./ds4_test --server
server: OK
ds4 tests: ok
```

Happy to restructure this if you would rather see the recovery localised in
`ds4_local_unterminated_reasoning()` (it would need `finish_reason` threaded
through the parser signatures), or if the semantics should be gated behind a flag.

title: v4.1: rewind live sessions instead of rebuilding them
body:
**Refreshed 2026-10-25** onto main ee7e840, on top of your fc80bd6 DSpark-boundary rewind.
The first version conflicted with fc80bd6 and with the reuse-probe rework. Image-bearing
rewind is a separate follow-up PR.

## What

A V4.1 session can only move forward except at the DSpark verification boundary.
fc80bd6 restores a verified prefix from the verifier snapshot; any other rewind still
invalidates the checkpoint, so the server re-reads the whole prefix for every prompt
that is not a pure extension of the live tokens. In an agent loop that is every turn:
the sampled tail (reasoning, exact DSML bytes) never matches the client's re-rendered
history.

The compressed and index caches are addressed by valid length, so dropping back to an
even position just stops reading past it, and the pending odd-row pair state is
rewritten by the next even token. What could not be recovered is the 128-row raw
decode window. Every raw row now also goes to a per-layer ring of the last 8192
positions (`DS4_V41_RAW_LOG_ROWS`, 640 MiB by default and counted in the memory plan;
`0` disables it). `ds41_graph_rewind` rebuilds the windows from that ring and
re-derives the Engram history from the kept tokens.

- **With fc80bd6**: `ds4_session_rewind` tries `ds4_session_rewind_speculative` first,
  so targets inside the last verified block still use the verifier snapshot. When it
  declines, the ring rewind runs and truncates the drafter (`ds41_dspark_truncate`:
  captured features and drafter KV of the abandoned tail are forgotten, the verifier
  snapshot is dropped), so the existing readiness check re-warms drafting.
- **Odd targets**: rewind to `pos-1` and replay the one kept token.
- **Ring validity**: rows can exist past the current position (DSpark verification
  writes ahead; an earlier rewind leaves an abandoned tail). `raw_log_hi` plus a slack
  of at least `DS41_VERIFY_ROWS` guards against reading an overwritten slot.
- **Decoder-suffix sweeps** (>= 8192 rows) don't produce raw rows for layers 20-39
  before their tail, so a rewind inside such a sweep invalidates as before.
- **Text-only**: checkpoints holding images are not rewound by this PR.
- **Server**:
  - In `slot_probe_reuse_locked`, V4.1 joins GLM in the memory-rewind tier (strict
    truncation, pair-aligned).
  - A last tier rewinds below a diverged prompt, tried after every tier that needs no
    recompute.
  - Batched `server_session_sync` rewinds to the shared prefix instead of restarting
    from token 0.
  - Execution keeps upstream's re-validation after the rewind.

## Tested

M5 Max 128 GiB, macOS 26.5, Metal, V4.1 1017 Q2, SSD streaming.

- `DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING=1 ./tests/test_metal_rewind`:
  - rewind of n=1800 tokens, deep=1500: rewound-vs-staged logits 0, same greedy tokens;
  - long-sweep rewind: PASS.
- **Server, DSpark on**, one slot, a 5k-token conversation with thinking on, where each
  follow-up re-renders history without the reasoning. Turn 0 took 48.5 s (cold); turns
  1-4 took 9.3 / 10.8 / 10.7 / 6.7 s, logging
  `rewound live prefix from 5174 to 5052; 17 prompt tokens will be reevaluated`, and so
  on. Without the rewind, each of those turns re-prefills the full ~5k tokens.
- `./ds4_test --server` and `./ds4_test --metal-kernels`: OK.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_01E5XGGgxjdnLGWQgfm3NNbm

title: metal: accelerate bit-exact DeepSeek V4.1 and GLM 5.3 Flash on M3 Ultra
body:
Six scoped commits, changes:

- **GLM:** HC/KDA, projection and router/shared-expert fusions; tiled sparse attention and coherent HC publication.
- **DeepSeek:** queued decode, overlapping Engram reads, exact attention/projection fusions, gathered-input reuse and unused Q4 tile culling.
- **Supporting work:** faster checkpoint writes and prefix lookup, memory admission, exact batched verification, native MXFP4 conversion, guarded BF16 requantization and typed GGUF audits.

**Fresh benchmarks vs upstream main `0aaea5a`:** M3 Ultra (80 GPU cores, 512 GiB), macOS 27, the two official Q4 GGUFs, serial ABBA runs within 32K. At the 8K frontier (4K new prefill tokens):

| Model | Decode tokens/s | Incremental prefill tokens/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Q4 | 18.47 → 29.86 (**+61.7%**) | 342.58 → 367.60 (**+7.3%**) |
| GLM 5.3 Flash Q4_K | 20.80 → 26.60 (**+27.9%**) | 380.36 → 437.92 (**+15.1%**) |

Reduces measured 10K-checkpoint continuation HTTP TTFT by **13.9 ms / 60.7 ms** (DeepSeek / GLM) versus `849e039`.

**Bit-identical against current main:** all **216,637,440 FP32 logit values** and **12 complete session snapshots** match through position **32,767**, with no tolerance. GPU exactness oracles, an independent GLM HC soak, SSD/recovery checks and 32 matching HTTP responses versus `849e039` provide additional coverage. Cache images differ only in timestamps.

[Current-main results and protocol](https://github.com/trueimage/ds4/blob/0dec87836b9971c4594ba51096a8523bfcf853b3/speed-bench/ds41f-m3ultra-perf/main-comparison/README.md) · [Exactness and validation](https://github.com/trueimage/ds4/blob/0dec87836b9971c4594ba51096a8523bfcf853b3/speed-bench/ds41f-m3ultra-perf/splash/README.md) · [Incremental comparison / TTFT](https://github.com/trueimage/ds4/blob/0dec87836b9971c4594ba51096a8523bfcf853b3/speed-bench/ds41f-m3ultra-perf/splash/vs-849e039/README.md)

title: GLM tool turns clear the live checkpoint, so every follow-up turn rebuilds its prefix
body:
Hi Salvatore,

while running a long agent session against `glm5_next` (GLM-5.3-Flash, Q2 resident, ctx 393216, MTP on)
I noticed that every follow-up turn after a tool call rebuilds its prompt prefix from an older disk
block instead of continuing the live KV. On this machine that is ~30k tokens of prefill (~100 s) per
follow-up turn.

## What the log shows (one server, one client session)

```
12:32:48 chat ctx=50681..50747:66  gen=92  TOOLS DSML_START DSML_END finish=tool_calls 7.054s
12:57:50 GLM live prefix rewind from 50839 to 50746 requires rebuild
12:57:50 kv cache skipped tokens=50746 reason=evict because KV payload staging failed: session has no valid checkpoint to stage
12:57:51 kv cache hit text tokens=20536 ... load=563.0 ms
12:57:51 chat ctx=20536..50747:30211 TOOLS prompt start          <- 30211 tokens re-prefilled
```

Three observations:

1. The follow-up request is 92 tokens *shorter* than the live frontier (50839 -> 50747): the client
   (Hermes desktop) does not send the generated tool-call text back as reasoning. That is normal for
   an OpenAI-style chat client — it is exactly the case the Qwen path was built for
   (`build_qwen_tool_turn_visible_text`, "Match clients that omit reasoning").
2. The rewind cannot rescue it: `ds4_session_glm_mtp_rewind()` only covers the two-token MTP cycle, so
   `ds4_session_rewind()` finishes with `state_ok == false`, clears `checkpoint_valid` and the caller
   rebuilds. That looks correct for the compressed DSA KV — truncation is not a valid rollback.
3. Therefore the only thing that can keep the live prefix usable is a *visible* checkpoint — and for
   GLM it is never set.

## Root cause

`should_remember_thinking_checkpoint()`:

```c
const bool qwen_chat = r->model_syntax == SERVER_MODEL_SYNTAX_QWEN &&
                       r->api != API_RESPONSES && r->api != API_ANTHROPIC;
if ((r->has_tools || r->prompt_preserves_reasoning) && !qwen_chat) return false;
```

Qwen is exempted here, GLM is not. At the call site in the tool-call branch:

```c
} else if (parsed_calls.len) {
    if (!remember_qwen_tool_turn_visible_checkpoint(...))  /* hard Qwen-only check -> false */
    {
        thinking_live_clear(s, slot);                      /* live checkpoint is dropped */
    }
}
```

For a GLM chat request with tools **and** known raw DSML, `should_canonicalize_tool_checkpoint()`
also returns false (`raw_tool_text` is known -> exact DSML replay is preferred), so no checkpoint is
written on any path. The live checkpoint is cleared instead, the disk staging then fails with
"session has no valid checkpoint to stage", no block at ~50k tokens is stored, and the next request
falls back to the newest older block that still matches.

## Proposed fix

Mirror the Qwen behaviour for GLM: remember the visible key (prompt + closed think block + the
tool-call text) using the existing `build_thinking_visible_text()`, which already has a GLM branch.
The next request renders that same visible surface, `thinking_live_visible_prefix_prompt()` matches it
and the live KV is reused.

My branch adds `glm_tool_turn_checkpoint_eligible()` — eligibility mirrors what
`build_thinking_visible_text()` requires: chat completions, `SERVER_MODEL_SYNTAX_GLM`, not
Responses/Anthropic, `finish == "tool_calls"` (decode finish, not the promoted parser status), not
inside thinking, non-empty tool text, and a prompt that still ends with the open `<think>` marker —
and calls `remember_thinking_checkpoint()` in the tool-call branch when the Qwen helper declines.

Unit test `test_glm_tool_turn_checkpoint_eligible()` covers the positive case plus the rejections
(finish != tool_calls, inside thinking, empty content, no finish, Qwen syntax, Responses API, prompt
without the open marker, NULL request). `./ds4_test --server` passes on the branch.

Status: unit-tested, live before/after not measured yet — the production server was busy with a live
agent run while I prepared this, so I did not restart it. I can report the measured numbers
(visible checkpoint remembered + follow-up prefill tokens) once it has run, if that helps before
review.

## Related, smaller observation

On a client cancel during prefill, `kv_cache_discard_failed_disk_entry()` unlinks the disk entry and
calls `ds4_session_invalidate()`. The entry itself was intact, so the next attempt starts from an
older block than necessary. I left that alone — the defensive delete looks deliberate.

title: server: keep the GLM live checkpoint across tool turns
body:
Keeps the GLM live checkpoint across tool turns — addresses #1092.

## Problem

`should_remember_thinking_checkpoint()` rejects `has_tools` for every non-Qwen syntax, and the
tool-call branch then calls `thinking_live_clear()`. For a GLM chat request with tools and known raw
DSML, `should_canonicalize_tool_checkpoint()` also returns false (exact DSML replay preferred), so no
checkpoint is written on any path — the live checkpoint is cleared instead. The next request then logs

```
live kv cache miss live=8471 prompt=6662 common=6041 vision=match reason=token-mismatch
kv cache hit text tokens=5897 ...              <- falls back to an older disk block
chat ctx=5897..6662:765 TOOLS prompt start     <- 765 tokens re-prefilled
```

`common` stops at the prompt end (6041): the generated reasoning block lives in the live KV but not in
the follow-up prompt, so there is no plain token match, and the compressed DSA KV cannot be rolled
back by truncation (`ds4_session_glm_mtp_rewind()` only covers the two-token MTP cycle).

## Change

Mirror the Qwen path for GLM: remember the visible key (prompt + closed think block + tool-call text)
through the existing `build_thinking_visible_text()` GLM branch, gated like the Qwen helper (chat
completions, GLM syntax, not Responses/Anthropic, decode `finish == "tool_calls"`, not inside
thinking, non-empty tool text, prompt still ending with the open `<think>` marker). The next request
renders the same visible surface, `thinking_live_visible_prefix_prompt()` matches it and the live KV
is reused instead of falling back to an older block.

The tool-call text comes from `parsed_calls.raw_tool_text`: GLM consumes the DSML call out of the
generated content, so `parsed_content` is **empty** on a tool turn (verified with a temporary
diagnostic: `finish=tool_calls inside_thinking=0 content_len=0` before the correction,
`content_len=721` after).

## Measurement

Same probe, same host (M4 Max, GLM-5.3-Flash Q2, ctx 393216, MTP on), server restarted with the KV
cache cleared before each arm. Request 1 is a tool-schema turn that generates a reasoning block;
request 2 replays the turn without the reasoning plus a tool result.

| | without the patch | with the patch |
|---|---|---|
| after the tool turn | `live kv cache miss … common=6041` | `thinking live checkpoint remembered … live=6997` |
| follow-up prefill | **765 tokens** (4.2 s), from disk block 5897 | **84 tokens** (1.2 s) |
| cache source | older disk block | live KV (visible prefix) |

The saving scales with the reasoning the client omits: here 681 tokens of prefill. In a production
agent run on this host the same mechanism showed up as a fallback from a 50 747-token frontier to a
20 536-token block — i.e. ~30k tokens of re-prefill (~100 s) — when no block near the frontier
existed. Caveat: the two arms generated different amounts of reasoning (7497 vs 1537 characters), so
this is one sample per arm rather than a controlled n; the mechanism, not the exact factor, is what
the numbers show.

## Tests

Adds `test_glm_tool_turn_checkpoint_eligible()` (positive case + 8 rejections).
`./ds4_test --server` passes.

title: Add VitePress documentation website
body:
## What

Adds a documentation website under `site/`, built with [VitePress](https://vitepress.dev), and a GitHub Actions workflow that publishes it to GitHub Pages.

The material currently spread across `README.md` and `docs/` is organized into a browsable site: getting started, models and vision, per-platform build guides, serving, clients, performance, SSD streaming, distributed inference, speculative decoding, Qwen setup, testing, and contributing.

**Screenshots are in the comment below.**

## Why

The guides in `docs/` are good, but reading them on GitHub means no navigation, no search, and no way to move between related pages. A site makes the existing content easier to find and read, especially for people deciding whether their machine can run which model.

## Scope

- `site/` is a presentation layer only. The markdown in `docs/` remains the source of truth for reading on GitHub; no existing docs were moved or deleted.
- Static output only. No inference code, kernels, or build files are touched.

## Contents

- Grouped sidebar navigation and top nav
- Local full-text search
- Light and dark themes
- Platform cards using Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, and DeepSeek logos (inlined as `currentColor` SVG so they follow the theme)
- Inline SVG chart for model memory requirements
- Metric cards for platform throughput and latency percentiles
- Edit-on-GitHub links and last-updated timestamps

## Deployment

`.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml` builds the site on pushes to `main` that touch `site/` and publishes to GitHub Pages. It also supports manual dispatch.

**One-time setup:** repository Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source must be set to **GitHub Actions** for the first deploy.

## Verification

```sh
cd site
npm install
npm run build     # static build, ~1s
npm run preview   # serves the production build locally
```

Build completes cleanly; all 17 pages render, search index is generated.

## Notes

- The site duplicates prose from `README.md` and `docs/` rather than symlinking. This is deliberate: VitePress requires content under its own root, and it keeps the site buildable without restructuring existing files. The tradeoff is that content edits need to be mirrored. Happy to change this if you'd prefer a different arrangement, or to narrow the site to a smaller subset of pages.
- The Pages URL in the config assumes the upstream repo (`https://antirez.github.io/ds4/`). Forks need to adjust `base` in `site/.vitepress/config.mjs`.
- `site/screenshots/` holds the review screenshots. They are not part of the build output and can be dropped before merge.

title: Fix the GGUF block sizes of q8_1, iq1_s and iq4_nl
body:
`gguf_types[]` in `ds4.c` gives three quant types the wrong block geometry:

| type | table today | ggml layout |
|---|---|---|
| `q8_1` (9) | 32 weights, 40 bytes | 32 weights, 36 bytes: `d` + `s` + `qs[QK8_1]` |
| `iq1_s` (19) | 256 weights, 110 bytes | 256 weights, 50 bytes: `d` + `qs[QK_K/8]` + `qh[QK_K/32]` (uint16) |
| `iq4_nl` (20) | 256 weights, 50 bytes | 32 weights, 18 bytes: `d` + `qs[QK4_NL/2]` |

All three layouts are pinned by the `static_assert`s in `cuda/mmq/ggml-common.h` (lines 259, 420 and 442), and `cuda/mmq/ds4_ggml_stubs.h` and `gguf-tools/quants.c` already carry the right values. q8_1 came out of @emilianbold's review of the first two; the rest of the table was then checked entry by entry against those `static_assert`s, and nothing else disagrees.

`tensor_nbytes()` sizes every tensor from this table while the model loads, so an `iq1_s` tensor is measured at 2.2 times its real size and a `q8_1` tensor at 11 percent over, and the loader stops with `tensor points outside GGUF file` when the overshoot runs past the end, while an `iq4_nl` tensor is measured at about a third of its size. The released DeepSeek V4 Flash GGUFs use none of the three, so this only reaches third-party files.

The fix is the three table entries. `tests/test_session_state.c` gets a check, since it already includes `ds4.c` and runs in `make test` without a model: the three entries match the ggml layouts, and a 4096-weight row takes 4608, 800 and 2304 bytes.

Verified, Ubuntu 24.04 container on x86-64, CPU build (`-DDS4_NO_GPU`), no model:

- Before each fix the new check fails on the wrong value: ``Assertion `iq1_s->block_elems == 256 && iq1_s->block_bytes == 50' failed`` for the first two, ``Assertion `q8_1->block_elems == 32 && q8_1->block_bytes == 36' failed`` for q8_1.
- After it, `session state tests: ok`.
- Each of the eleven assertions was seen failing on its own line, breaking only the value it guards: each block size and count, the three names, and `tensor_nbytes()` itself (one extra byte; one block per 256 weights).
- `make cpu` builds with gcc 13.3 and clang 18.1, with no warnings in the touched files; `test_session_state`, `test-engram`, `test-ssd-cache`, `test-deepseek41-gguf`, `test-linux-memory`, `test_layer_pack`, `test_prompt_prefix` and `test_deepseek4_vision_image` pass.

Unrelated to this change and the same on `main`: `tests/test_tp_commands` fails here because it expects `SO_RCVTIMEO` to read back to the millisecond, and this kernel runs at `CONFIG_HZ=250`, so 50 ms comes back as 52. That one is #1096.

Not tested: no Metal, CUDA or ROCm machine and no GGUF here, so `make test` with the model and the logprob vectors are untested. The change is a table the loader reads and holds no backend code.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Compare the restored gate timeout with what the kernel keeps
body:
`check_bulk_exchange` in `tests/test_tp_commands.c` reads `SO_RCVTIMEO` back after the big gate exchange, to prove the socket went back to `gate_timeout_ms` instead of keeping the extra 2000 ms of grace. It expects the exact millisecond value, but Linux stores socket timeouts in jiffies and rounds up. With `CONFIG_HZ=250` (Debian's default kernel, WSL2) the 50 ms case reads back as 52:

```
set 50 ms -> read 52 ms
set 1234 ms -> read 1236 ms
set 3000 ms -> read 3000 ms
```

So `test_tp_commands`, and with it `make test-session-state` and `make test`, fails on those machines while `ds4_tp.c` does exactly what it should:

```
test_tp_commands: tests/test_tp_commands.c:54: check_bulk_exchange: Assertion `(uint64_t)timeout.tv_sec * 1000u + timeout.tv_usec / 1000u == peer[rank].tp.gate_timeout_ms' failed.
```

The test now compares with what a scratch socket reports for the same timeout, set with a plain `setsockopt` so the check does not go through the code under test. It still catches the bug it was written for: with the restore in `ds4_tp_big_gate_exchange` removed, the socket keeps 2052 ms against the expected 52 and the new assertion fails.

Verified in an Ubuntu 24.04 container on WSL2 (kernel 6.18, `CONFIG_HZ=250`), CPU build:

- before: the assertion above fails on `main`;
- after: `test_tp_commands` passes;
- with the timeout restore removed from `ds4_tp.c`, the new assertion fails;
