title: GLM 5.3 Flash on the DGX Spark: measured, and q4 on CUDA (#907)
body:
Two things, in four small commits:

- **Measured GLM 5.3 Flash Q2 decode speeds** on one DGX Spark, written into `docs/DGX_SPARK.md`.
- **A 26-line change to `ds4.c`** that lets the Q4 file reach the generic CUDA routed MoE
  launcher, behind an environment variable and **off by default**.

### What does not vary, stated once

One DGX Spark GB10, sm_121, driver **580.159.03**. **GLM 5.3 Flash Q2, 90 GiB**, one file for
every row below. **128 tokens generated** at each context. Base: main `8db1d1d1`. **Runs kept: 6
resident** after 2 discarded warm-ups, **4 streamed** after 3.

**The memory each number ran in is on the row itself**, because a decode t/s means nothing without
it.

### The numbers

| context | expert cache requested | experts delivered | decode t/s |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 2048 | **none**, the file fits, nothing streams | all of them | **14.68** |
| 4096 | **none**, the file fits, nothing streams | all of them | **14.64** |
| 6144 | **none**, the file fits, nothing streams | all of them | **14.60** |
| 2048 | `--ssd-streaming-cache-experts` **24GB** | **3,064** | **4.50** |
| 4096 | `--ssd-streaming-cache-experts` **24GB** | **3,064** | **4.32** |
| 6144 | `--ssd-streaming-cache-experts` **24GB** | **3,064** | **3.79** |

⚠ **A cache request is not a delivery, which is why there are two columns and not one.** Ask for
24GB and the engine gives you the slots that fit; it can also decline the cache outright while the
run still looks normal. **24GB is what was asked for, 3,064 is what was given**, and neither has
to be guessed from the other.

- **The resident rows are flat across context, and structurally so:** the KDA layers keep a
  constant-size state, the DSA layers read an indexed slice, and the engine logs a **0.37 GiB**
  compact DSA cache at 32K.
- ⚠ **Two warm-ups, not one**, on the resident rows. The second run still read low. Worth knowing
  if you reproduce it.
- **The streamed rows are not a recommendation.** The file fits; they exist so both shapes of
  **one file** sit side by side. Stream it only to study streaming.

Commands, verbatim:

    ./ds4-bench --cuda -m gguf/GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2.gguf \
      --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
      --ctx-start 2048 --ctx-max 6144 --step-incr 2048 --gen-tokens 128

    ./ds4-bench --cuda --ssd-streaming --ssd-streaming-cache-experts 24GB \
      -m gguf/GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2.gguf \
      --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
      --ctx-start 2048 --ctx-max 6144 --step-incr 2048 --gen-tokens 128

### Q4 on CUDA (#907, #682)

**The symptom.** `GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K.gguf` with `--cuda --ssd-streaming` dies at prefill with
`glm routed moe: unsupported types 12/12/12`.

**★ Four people have now reported it, on four different CUDA architectures, and both issues are
still open.** This is the reason the change is worth having rather than a Spark curiosity:

| who | where | GPU | arch | the file | dated |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `accdropdbd-ai` | **#907** (author) | H100 PCIe 80 GB | **sm_90** | `GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K`, 177.77 GiB | 2026-08-30 |
| `AlphaMo99` | **#682** (author) | Quadro RTX 5000 | **sm_75** | `glm-antirez-q4`, 404.35 GiB | 2026-08-04 |
| `ChicoPinto70` | #682 comment | 3x RTX 3090, dual Xeon, CUDA generic | **sm_86** | `GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K`, 177.77 GiB | 2026-09-12 |
| `chenwei0930` | #682 comment | not stated | not stated | not stated | **2026-09-19** |
| this branch | - | DGX Spark GB10 | **sm_121** | `GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K`, 177.77 GiB | 2026-09-20 |

- **It is not architecture-specific.** sm_75, sm_86, sm_90 and sm_121 all produce the identical
  `unsupported types 12/12/12`, and `ChicoPinto70` built **CUDA generic**, not for a specific arch.
- **It is not file-specific either.** `AlphaMo99`'s is a **404.35 GiB** `glm-antirez-q4`; the other
  three are the **177.77 GiB** `GLM-5.3-Flash-Q4_K`. **Two different Q4 files, one dispatch gap.**
- **The most recent report is 2026-09-19**, the day before this branch was prepared, so the queue
  is live rather than historical.
- ⚠ **`chenwei0930` gave no hardware and no file** ("I'm having the same problem too"), so that row
  corroborates the count and nothing else. It is listed for honesty, not as a fourth architecture.

**The cause is the dispatch, not the kernels.**
`glm_graph_layer_uses_generic_routed_moe()` sends a layer to the generic launcher **only when its
gate experts are IQ2_XXS**, so **every Q4_K layer lands in the GLM-specific launcher**, whose CUDA
side accepts Q2_K only and whose Q4 scalar entry is a stub. The **generic** launcher already has
what is needed: the Q4_K gate/up with Q4_K down path (#598 lists the pairs), `n_expert` and
`n_total_expert` as parameters, and the streaming selected-expert cache `ds4.c` already loads for
uniform Q4_K GLM layers.

- **#907's author reached the same diagnosis from the outside**, in his own words: *"This looks
  like a CUDA routed-MoE dispatch/type-support gap for the GLM-5.3 Q4_K layout rather than a
  loading or memory-planning issue."* The predicate-OFF row in the table below is that sentence
  turned into a measurement.
- **A different concern, but worth a glance while you are in there:** the next function down,
  `glm_tp_validate_ownership_kernels()`, already treats a **Q4_K** gate-expert type as legitimate
  alongside `Q2_K` and the generic-MoE layouts. So `ds4.c` already names Q4_K a supported GLM
  expert type elsewhere; `glm_graph_layer_uses_generic_routed_moe()` is the one that does not.

**The change.** Widen the predicate to the uniform Q4_K triple, behind `DS4_GLM_Q4_GENERIC=1`.
**Unset, every call site evaluates exactly as before** - Metal and ROCm keep their GLM Q4 paths
byte-identical. A **mixed**-quant file passes the widened predicate and is refused by the
launcher, as today.

**✅ Verified, and here is the whole of what was run** (same Spark, sm_121, driver 580.159.03;
the Q4 file is **177.77 GiB**, so every Q4 run below is **streamed**):

| check | result |
|---|---|
| build | rc=0, **1 min 29 s**, zero errors, zero warnings |
| predicate **OFF** | rc=1 **in one second**, `glm routed moe: unsupported types 12/12/12` |
| predicate **ON** | rc=0, coherent tokens. **The first CUDA decode of this file on record** |
| two mint runs | **byte-identical**, both prompts |
| **24GB** cache (**1,244** experts, 10.04 % of the routed set) vs **48GB** (**3,064**, 24.74 %) | **byte-identical**, across a **2.46x** change in resident expert population |
| `score_official` | `avg_nll` **0.300986170**, `first_match` **90**, `avg_lcp` **9.970**, 11,559 tokens |
| `make cuda-regression` | **GREEN** |

- **OFF confirms the issue author's diagnosis by measurement**: a dispatch gap, not loading and
  not memory. The streaming map, memory plan and KV cache all build first.
- **The 24-vs-48 row is the load-bearing one**: the output does not depend on which experts miss.
  That is why both cache requests and both delivered populations are named.
- ⚠ **`3,064` appears twice in this PR meaning two different runs, so do not read them as one.**
  In the decode table above it is **Q2 at a 24GB request**; here it is **Q4 at a 48GB request**.
  The collision is arithmetic rather than a copy error: a Q4 expert is **13.50 MiB** against Q2's
  **6.75**, exactly double, and the two prefill headrooms are **7.59 GiB** and **3.80 GiB**, so
  `(48 - 7.59)/13.50` and `(24 - 3.80)/6.75` both land on 3,064. **The requested column is what
  tells them apart**, which is the reason it is on every row.

⚠ **Two honest caveats.**

- **The reference is your Metal Q4 figure; no Spark or CUDA Q4 reference exists**
  (`QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md`: *"Q4 and Spark-to-Spark RDMA are not supported in this pass"*).
  Against it: `first_match` **90/100** exact on both, NLL **+0.0605 %** over the higher, `avg_lcp`
  above both.
- **177.77 GiB on a 121 GiB box is a streamed substitution, not your resident gate passing.**
  QA 908 forbids the artifact on one Spark; QA 909-910 asks for this when CUDA Q4 code changes.

★ **And there is an answer to that second caveat that is not ours to give.** #907's author closes
with *"Happy to test patches or provide more diagnostics on the H100."* An **H100 PCIe 80 GB** and
a **3x RTX 3090** box are both on that thread, so **the architectures this branch cannot reach have
volunteers already sitting on them.** If the predicate is worth widening, it can be confirmed on
sm_90 and sm_86 by the people who filed the issues, which is a stronger cross-check than anything
one Spark can produce.

### The sibling notes

Two prepared beside this one, same box, same session, and a third withdrawn:

| note | what it says |
|---|---|
| **`TripleSparkleAI/ds4:triple-glm53-hitsfirst-spark`** | the **hits-first lever** on this same Q2 file at the same 24GB cache: **+25.2 %** at 6144 against a **5.3 %** floor |
| **#1083 body additions** | recommend that PR's headline **down**, +7 to +12 % to **+5 to +8 %**, from +7.97 / +6.89 / +4.98 |

⚠ **A third note was prepared for #1073 and has been WITHDRAWN rather than sent.** It reported two
CUDA build breaks on that branch and a greedy-identity divergence, measured at `af7c02b59`. You
have since fixed both breaks yourself (`ed43e1a56`, `4fe6a7802`), and `ed43e1a56` also **removed
the fused CUDA entries our divergence was measured through**, so the code path is gone and the
finding is unknown at your new head. **It is not repeated here, because a finding against deleted
code is worse than silence.**

**Why they compare at all:** one DGX Spark GB10, sm_121, driver **580.159.03**, every figure
carrying its context **and its expert cache**, arms bracketed, and one rule with no exceptions -
**a delta inside its own measured floor is a tie, not a win.**

### Files

- `docs/DGX_SPARK.md` - the GLM 5.3 Flash section
- `docs/MODELS.md` - one pointer line and the Q4 note
- `ds4.c` - the predicate, **+26 / -5**
- `README.md` - a card appended **under** your text, unchanged above it

### Found and not fixed

- The full GLM 5.3 Q2 file has **IQ2_XXS routed down experts in 75 of 76 MoE layers**, and
  `ds4_cuda.cu` has no launcher for that pair. #598 had one; it closed unmerged.
- The GLM-specific CUDA launcher **hardcodes 256 experts in two places where GLM 5.3 Flash has
  288**. #466 is the router-side sibling.
- The fp8 target **packages weights nothing in `ds4.c` reads**.
- **Vision has a CUDA path I have not measured on GLM.**

title: GLM 5.3 Flash on the DGX Spark: hits-first generalises to a second model family (stacks on #1083)
body:
Stacks on **#1083** and on the **`TripleSparkleAI/ds4:triple-glm53-spark`** PR.

- **The engine code here is #1083's** **plus one 13-line env switch** in `ds4_cuda.cu`
  (`DS4_CUDA_HITS_FIRST_MIN_MISS`, default 1, measured below as the threshold arm).
- **The two new commits are docs.**
- What it adds: **the hits-first lever measured on a second model family**, beside the resident and
  streamed rows the **`TripleSparkleAI/ds4:triple-glm53-spark`** PR adds to `docs/DGX_SPARK.md`.

### Why the hits-first lever applies with no port

- The Q2 file's **gate/up experts are IQ2_XXS**, and `glm_graph_layer_uses_generic_routed_moe()`
  sends that layout through **`routed_moe_launch`**, the launcher #1083 changes.
- Your `c2c3ce324` prefill read-ahead is the CUDA-side neighbour: **it is prefill-side, hits-first
  is decode-side**, and both read the same selected-expert cache unchanged.

### What does not vary, stated once

One DGX Spark GB10, sm_121, driver **580.159.03**. **GLM 5.3 Flash Q2, 89.9 GiB**, the same file as
the **`TripleSparkleAI/ds4:triple-glm53-spark`** PR, **forced to stream** with `--ssd-streaming`. **128 tokens
generated** at each context. Method: **every hits-first ON run sits between two hits-first OFF
runs**, 3 cycles, 3 warm-ups discarded. Floor: **5.3 %**, from this round's own adjacent hits-first
OFF pairs.

**The memory is on the measurement rows rather than up here, because here it would look like
housekeeping and there it is the argument.**

### The measurement

| context | expert cache requested | experts delivered | hits-first **OFF** t/s | hits-first **ON** t/s | delta |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2048 | **24GB**, both arms | **3,064**, both arms | 4.50 | 5.28 | **+17.1 %** |
| 4096 | **24GB**, both arms | **3,064**, both arms | 4.32 | 5.20 | **+20.1 %** |
| 6144 | **24GB**, both arms | **3,064**, both arms | 3.79 | 4.74 | **+25.2 %** |

★ **The repeated cache columns are the point of the table, not clutter.** Both arms ran at the same
**24GB request** and the same **3,064 delivered** experts, so the delta is a measurement of
hits-first and **cannot be a measurement of a different cache size**. A reviewer who cannot see
that both arms shared a cache cannot rule the memory out, and it is the first thing worth ruling
out.

⚠ **A request is not a delivery, which is why there are two columns.** 24GB is what was asked for,
3,064 is what the engine gave; it can also decline the cache outright while the run still looks
normal. Stating both is also what lets this table be compared with the `glm53` PR's, which ran at
the same pair on the same file.

- **The headline is the slower context, as in #1083: +25.2 %.** 3 of 3 repeats above baseline,
  against the 5.3 % floor. The three cycle readings are **+25.2, +24.9, +25.3**.
- **The wall clock says the same thing with no statistic at all.** Every hits-first **OFF** run
  took **164 to 169 s**; every hits-first **ON** run **117 to 121 s**.
- **Prefill and time-to-first-token move too, and I report it rather than explain it.** Prefill
  went from about **90 to about 166 t/s** at 4096 and 6144; TTFT from about **560 to about
  315 ms**. On DeepSeek it was unchanged within noise. Here it moves.
- **The misses were real reads.** The page cache stayed at **2 to 3 GB** through all thirteen runs
  against the 89.9 GiB file, so there was wait available to hide.
- **The gain is bigger than the +7 to +12 % on DeepSeek V4.1 with these same two binaries, and
  only half the split is working.** At GLM's `n_expert_used = 8` the per-slot down split of #1083
  is off, because it needs six experts. ⇒ **this is the gate/up split alone, the same shape as
  your Metal GLM split.**

### The pool does most of the work, not the ordering

The commit has two parts. Turned on separately (round **GLM-A5**, its own total, not the table above):

| part | share |
|---|---:|
| threaded pread pool | **23.4** |
| hits-first ordering | **4.9** |
| both together | **29.4 %** |

- The ordering on its own sits near that round's floor. Said here because the branch is named
  after the smaller half.
- Both parts ship together and `DS4_CUDA_HITS_FIRST=0` keeps the pool, as in #1083. Read the
  headline as "this commit is worth +25.2 % here", not "the reordering is".

### Output is byte-identical

- Greedy `--temp 0 --dump-logprobs` on the streamed configuration above, **a short and a long
  prompt**, with hits-first **on**, **off**, and **with the miss threshold at three**.
- **Ten dumps** at the branch's engine commits, **one sha256 per prompt**: short
  `a84e448ec8e5458f`, long `89cffa1b02d565eb`.
- ★ **This exercises the `pair_mask` path at eight experts, which #1083's own gate only reached at
  six.**
- ⚠ **The GLM 5.3 Flash 100-case fixture in `QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md` was not re-run**, because the
  two commits on top of #1083 **change no kernel**.

### Your Metal threshold, tested again here

- Declining the split below three misses (`DS4_CUDA_HITS_FIRST_MIN_MISS=3`) measured **+22.1 %**
  against **+25.2 %** without it, same setup.
- ⇒ **the default stays at 1, as in #1083.**

### Streaming this file is a measurement, not a recommendation

- At 6144, resident decode is **3.9x** the hits-first **OFF** streamed speed and **3.1x** the
  hits-first **ON** streamed speed. The resident row is in the **`TripleSparkleAI/ds4:triple-glm53-spark`** PR.
- The point of the streamed table is **that the lever holds on a second family**, not that anyone
  should stream a file that fits.

### The two sibling notes

- **#1083 body additions** recommend that PR's own headline **down**, +7 to +12 % to **+5 to
  +8 %**, from three rounds (+7.97, +6.89, +4.98), and flag that its phrase *"two mechanisms"*
  already names a different pair than the decomposition does, so the two paragraphs must not be
  pasted side by side unedited.
- **A note prepared for #1073, now withdrawn, which contributed method rather than a number** -
  and this PR obeys that method: **bracket every arm, and carry an arm that cannot differ.** A
  first matrix there fired arms in fixed order with one bracket per cycle, which made
  distance-from-bracket a property of each arm - median **+0.61 / 0.00 / -1.58** at distance
  1 / 2 / 3, **`r` = -0.5018** - and **the two arms that looked like losers were simply the two
  furthest from a bracket.** What caught it was a bit-identical null arm measuring a **3.2258 %**
  spread of its own. **The method survives; the note's findings about #1073 itself do not, and it
  is not being sent.**

**And the contrast is the honest part.** Same Spark, same driver, same method, two levers:

- Your V4.1 fused-kernel branch measured **+1.74 %**, **inside** that round's own **3.10 %** floor.
  We called it a **TIE** and claimed no speed win.
  ⚠ **That reading is stamped at `af7c02b59`** plus two local build fixes, and **it is not a
  current statement about #1073.** That branch is 50 commits now, you have since fixed both of the
  CUDA build breaks we hit, and `ed43e1a56` removed the fused CUDA entries the run went through.
  **It is cited here only as the other end of one harness's range.**
- **Hits-first here measures +25.2 % against a 5.3 % floor.** The difference is the lever, not the
  harness: the same bracketing on the same box calls one reading a tie and the other a win.

### Files

- `ds4_cuda.cu` - #1083 plus the switch
- `docs/DGX_SPARK.md` - the hits-first column and the paragraph under it
- `README.md` - the card **under** your text, unchanged above it

title: server: cover Anthropic + verify Responses API for the tools-streaming guard fix (#1076)
body:
## Context

#1076 reported that a tool-enabled thinking answer buffers entirely until
generation ends. The merged fix (d31089d / 39bc628) only exempted Qwen
from `stream_needs_second_reasoning_guard()`; DeepSeek V4 Flash and GLM
5.3 Flash still hit the original unbounded wait, confirmed live on our
own production servers (OpenAI-compatible streaming, real checkpoints,
tools + thinking on):

| Model | Reasoning chunks | Content chunks |
|---|---:|---:|
| DeepSeek V4 Flash | 85 | 1 |
| GLM 5.3 Flash Q2 | 68 | 1 |

## What this PR does

Applies **@zonebond's fix from #1084** (full credit — the bounded
`SECOND_REASONING_GUARD_BYTES = 32` lookahead window in both
`openai_sse_stream_update` and `anthropic_sse_stream_update`, model-syntax-
agnostic rather than gated per protocol/syntax) and adds the coverage that
PR was still missing:

- `test_anthropic_tools_stream_content_is_incremental`: #1084's own
  regression test only covers the OpenAI-compatible path. The guard fires
  identically in `anthropic_sse_stream_update`, and our manual live testing
  needed the same fix there too — this codifies that as an automated test
  instead of a one-off manual check.

## Verification

- Full unit suite green, including the pre-existing
  `test_openai_stream_reroutes_second_reasoning_pass` (its synthetic
  "escaped draft" is 13 bytes, safely under the 32-byte window — the
  original #678 protection still fires).
- Live, real production models, OpenAI-compatible streaming:
  DeepSeek V4 Flash 1 → **101** content chunks (word-by-word), GLM 5.3
  Flash Q2 1 → **137**. Reasoning and tool-call payloads unaffected.
- Live, real Anthropic-format streaming (`/v1/messages`): DeepSeek, 130
  incremental `text_delta` chunks.
- Checked the third client-facing surface, `/v1/responses`: its
  `responses_stream` struct has no `guard_second_reasoning` field at all,
  and a live request against a real DeepSeek server streamed 128
  incremental `response.output_text.delta` events with no buffering — this
  API is unaffected, no fix needed there.
- Edge case: an immediate tool call with no preceding free text correctly
  yields zero content chunks (nothing to stream).

## Known, deliberate tradeoff (inherited from #1084, stating explicitly)

The 32-byte window protects a *short* stray second-reasoning draft right
after the first `</think>` (the original #678 scenario). A hypothetical
escaped draft longer than 32 bytes would stream as if it were the real
answer. This is a reasonable tradeoff given the historical case it guards
against, but worth stating rather than leaving implicit.

title: WIP: Qwen3-Next CUDA support and decode speedups (15%+ vs llama.cpp on dual RTX 5090s)
body:
**Draft PR** - I let Astra run for a while to see if I could run an 80B A3B coding model on dual GPU and it could beat llama.cpp in inference speed and it did, not sure if this PR is interesting for anyone or not as this is a relatively "old" model. I managed to get 15% speedup with DS4 vs llama.cpp.

---

AI generated PR description:

The measured model is **Qwen3-Coder-Next 80B-A3B Q5_K_M**, with 24 consecutive layers resident on each GPU. Five-run HTTP medians from the September 20 development build:

| Workload | DS4 | llama.cpp | Improvement |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Code | 246.59 tokens/s | 213.30 tokens/s | +15.61% |
| Fiction | 245.76 tokens/s | 213.23 tokens/s | +15.26% |

These are single-session, greedy decode measurements with a 32,768-token context allocation, a 4,096-token output cap, and no speculation. Throughput is `(completion_tokens - 1) / (last_content_time - first_content_time)`, excluding model loading and first-token latency. First-token latency remains worse than llama.cpp, and the engines produce different output lengths, so this is not an equal-length end-to-end latency comparison. The llama.cpp baseline was `b11042-ec9281505`, with flash attention and a 1:1 layer split. Ollama was not directly benchmarked.

The patch contains only the production source and build integration needed for Qwen3-Next support and these optimizations:

- GGUF loading, Qwen3-Coder tokenization/chat templates, session state, and CUDA layer placement across GPUs.
- Session-owned CUDA graph replay, grouped projections, optimized Q5_K/Q6_K operations and expert routing.
- Fused recurrent preparation and Q5 expert-down/residual kernels, plus GPU greedy selection with full logits copied to the host on demand.
- Required CLI, server, and agent integration and header dependencies.

**Benchmark code is not included in this PR. It is currently in a separate repository and can be provided separately.** Test additions, benchmark results, logs, generated artifacts, and unrelated changes are also excluded.

This remains an initial CUDA-only implementation: prefill processes one token at a time, session batches run serially, and CPU/Metal/ROCm inference for this model, SSD streaming, tensor parallelism, distributed slices, MTP, vision, and disk KV/snapshots are not supported. It still needs upstream review and broader validation before it is ready to merge.

The measured development build preserved exact tokens and sampled full logits against the previous DS4 build, and passed CUDA, session/API, Metal/SSD regression, frontend, and sampling checks. Those checks do not claim identical DS4/llama.cpp logits. This PR packages that implementation on current upstream; the CUDA/model implementation files are unchanged from the measured working tree. T


To build and run with a merged GGUF and CUDA 12.8 or newer:

```sh
make -j4 cuda CUDA_ARCH=sm_120
./ds4-server --cuda --gpu-devices 0,1 --gpu-vram auto \
  -m /path/to/Qwen3-Coder-Next-Q5_K_M-merged.gguf \
  --ctx 32768 --batched-session 1 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18084
```

API model ID: `qwen3-coder-next`.

title: CUDA: avoid Q8_K quantize grid.y overflow
body:
Fixes #625.

Laguna S 2.1 selects 10 routed experts per token. The Q8_K intermediate quantizer used `pair_count = n_tokens * n_expert` as `grid.y`; CUDA limits this dimension to 65,535 blocks.

The failure therefore starts at 6,554 tokens (`6554 * 10 = 65540`). The reported 9,366-token prefill creates 93,660 pairs and fails with `CUDA Laguna routed MoE intermediate quantize launch failed: invalid argument`.

Although #625 describes a simple user message (`Hallo`), its log records `chat ctx=0..25101:25101 ... TOOLS prompt start`: the effective prefill was 25,101 tokens. OpenClaw/Roo Code supplies system instructions, tool definitions, history, and the chat template, so the user-visible message length is not the relevant measure.

Map rows/pairs to `grid.x` and Q8_K blocks to `grid.y`, updating all matching launch sites to preserve indexing.

Add a CUDA regression that quantizes 65,536 rows and verifies the final row. It fails with the old axis mapping and passes on GB10 (`sm_121`, driver `580.173.02`).

Tested:

- `make cuda-spark`
- `make cuda-regression`

title: Add presence_penalty to server, CLI and agent sampling
body:
## Summary

Adds an OpenAI-style `presence_penalty` (float, `[-2, 2]`, default 0 = off) to `ds4-server` on all four API styles (chat/completions, completions, Anthropic messages, Responses), plus `--presence-penalty F` on `ds4` and `ds4-agent`.

Motivation: the Qwen3.8 Flash Next model card recommends `presence_penalty=1.5` for non-thinking mode alongside temperature 0.7 / top_p 0.8 / top_k 20, and the server had no way to honour it. Community reports of the model getting "loopy" match what the card warns about.

Semantics: for every token id that has already appeared in this request's generated output (thinking tokens included, prompt excluded), subtract the penalty from its logit before temperature/top-k/top-p/min-p. Flat subtraction, each id counted once.

## Design

- Session-level state (`ds4_presence` on `ds4_session`), derived from `s->checkpoint` rather than pushed at emit sites, so rejected drafts never enter the set and a rewind rebuilds it from the request boundary. Public API adds one function: `ds4_session_set_presence_penalty(s, penalty)`.
- Per-vocabulary tables are allocated only on first non-zero use; with penalty 0 the cost is one float compare per sampling site.
- The row is penalised in place and restored verbatim afterwards, so logprobs, MTP conditioning and KV payloads never see a penalised logit.
- Greedy picks go through the same penalised row, so temperature 0 and temperature > 0 agree about which tokens were suppressed.
- MTP: the Qwen4 cycle (single and batched multi-session) and the GLM cycle penalise verifier rows and draft-parent argmaxes, with accepted-but-uncommitted drafts included as the cycle advances. The two verifier families that take top-1 from the device (legacy DeepSeek MTP argmax verifier, DSpark sampled branch) fall back to one token per cycle while a penalty is active rather than accept on an unpenalised verdict.
- Request validation rejects out-of-range values with the parsers' existing error style. `-ffast-math` folds NaN checks in `ds4_server.c`, so `NaN` is rejected at the JSON text level.

## Testing

Machine: Apple M5 Pro 64 GB, macOS 27, Xcode 27.0, Metal backend. Model: Qwen3.8 Flash Next Q2 (`ds4flash.gguf` symlink). **CUDA, ROCm and distributed were not run**; those files do not reference the sampling API, and the shared `ds4.c` builds clean via `make cpu`.

Build: `make clean && make -j8` and `make cpu`, zero warnings.

Correctness track:
- `make test`: 23 failures in 5 groups (`logprob-vectors`, `local-golden-vectors`, `metal-short-prefill`, `metal-ssd-streaming-cache-pressure`, `long-context`). All are checkpoint mismatches between this Qwen Q2 GGUF and the DeepSeek V4 Flash fixtures; a normalized diff of every failure line against `main` at 8db1d1d built in a worktree is empty. Every other group is OK, and the remaining suite entries (`ds4-eval --validate-cases`, `ds4_agent_test`, all `tests/test_*` binaries) pass.
- `./ds4_test --server`, `--metal-kernels`, `--tool-call-quality`: OK. New `--server` cases cover parsing and range rejection on all four routes. `tests/test_sampling` gains penalty cases against a pre-subtracted reference row, including greedy and a duplicated seen id.
- Greedy MTP exactness: at temperature 0, `--mtp` and non-MTP output is byte-identical at penalty 0 and again at penalty 1.5, and the two penalties produce different text.
- MTP acceptance at temperature 0.7 / top_p 0.8 over 500 tokens: 64.5% at penalty 0, 61.4% at 1.5; decode 32.5 vs 32.2 t/s.
- Server: penalty 1.5 returns coherent 200s on chat, messages and Responses; out-of-range returns 400 on all four routes; `--trace` records the value; repeated greedy requests on one slot are identical, so history resets per request.

Speed track: the full `ds4-bench` sweep (2048 to 65536, step 2048, 128 gen tokens) completed on both branch and main. On this machine the sweep's run-to-run spread on an identical build is about ±25% prefill and ±8% decode, which swamps any real delta, and the sign of the branch/main difference flips with run order. Balanced ABBA paired runs on a fixed greedy prompt give `--mtp` decode 40.43 vs 40.45 t/s (main vs branch, +0.0%), with all 28 runs byte-identical in output. The local generation harness also reproduces the recorded output hashes of the base commit for all six cases.

title: Support server startup sampling defaults and multi-turn reasoning stripping
body:
## Summary

This PR introduces three related enhancements to `ds4-server`:

### 1. Server Startup Sampling & Thinking Defaults (with API Precedence)

Added CLI options for setting server-wide defaults:

| Flag | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| `--temp` | float | Sampling temperature |
| `--top-p` | float | Nucleus sampling probability |
| `--top-k` | int | Candidate limit |
| `--min-p` | float | Min-p threshold |
| `--reasoning-effort` | `none\|low\|medium\|high\|max` or `1..100` | Reasoning effort level |
| `--thinking` | `true\|false` | Enable/disable thinking |
| `--preserved-thinking` | `true\|false` | Enable/disable thinking preservation |

**Precedence rule:** If an incoming request payload provides any of these parameters, the request value takes precedence and overrides the startup default. If the client omits a parameter, the server startup default is honored (falling back to model-engine defaults if no startup default was set).

Strict option names are enforced (e.g. `--temp`, `--thinking`); unknown aliases are rejected.

### 2. Multi-Turn Reasoning Stripping (`preserve_thinking`)

In multi-turn chat completions (e.g. Qwen agentic workflows), previous assistant reasoning blocks (`.reasoning` and inline `
`) are stripped when `preserve_thinking` is `false`.

Configurable via:
- Per-request: `chat_template_kwargs.preserve_thinking` or top-level `preserve_thinking` in the request body
- Server-wide: `--preserved-thinking false`

### 3. Documentation & Help Text

Documented the new options under `ds4-server --help api` and `ds4-server --help thinking`.

---

## Verification & Testing

- **Server unit tests** – Added unit tests in `ds4_server.c` verifying startup option parsing, request-default application, and explicit API request overrides. `./ds4_test --server` passes (OK).
- **CLI smoke tests** – Added assertions in `tests/test_gpu_args_cli.sh` checking help text, valid option parsing, and negative tests rejecting invalid values/aliases. 107/107 passed.
- **Frontend tests** – `make test-frontends` passed.

title: Refuse the agent TUI without a terminal before loading the model
body:
`ds4-agent -p "..."` without `--non-interactive` starts the TUI and submits the prompt from inside it, which is what `--help` promises ("Submit an initial prompt after startup"). The TUI puts stdin in raw mode, so when stdin is not a terminal (a script, a pipe, a harness that runs the agent as a subprocess) `linenoiseEditStart()` fails in `enableRawMode()` and the agent stops with `failed to start line editor`, the message in #1046.

The check that fails lives in `run_agent()`, which runs after `ds4_engine_open()`. So a scripted run waits through the whole model load, minutes on the large GGUFs, before it learns that the UI cannot start.

This PR checks the same condition in `main()`, right after option parsing and before the engine opens. It uses the test `enableRawMode()` applies: `isatty()` on stdin, or `LINENOISE_ASSUME_TTY`, which the terminal tests set. On failure it exits with 2 and points to `--non-interactive`, the one-shot mode shown in the help examples:

```
ds4-agent: the interactive UI needs a terminal on stdin; use --non-interactive for scripted runs
```

Runs from a real terminal and runs with `--non-interactive` behave as before.

I don't know for sure that the reporter's stdin was not a terminal, since the issue does not include the command line. It is the most likely cause I found: the other ways `editor_start()` can fail (`tcgetattr`/`tcsetattr` erroring, or the prompt write to stdout failing) do not happen in an ordinary terminal session. If you would rather have `-p` switch to non-interactive mode by itself when stdin is not a terminal, which is what the reporter expected, it is a two-line change on top of this and I'm happy to do it. I kept the explicit error because it does not change what `-p` means.

## Verified

- `tests/ds4_agent_test.c` gains `test_tui_needs_terminal`: a pipe is refused, a pty (`posix_openpt`) is accepted, and `--non-interactive` and `LINENOISE_ASSUME_TTY` are each accepted on a pipe. `./ds4_agent_test` passes with stdin redirected from `/dev/null`.
- I broke each clause of `agent_tui_has_terminal()` one at a time (always true, no `non_interactive`, no `isatty`, no `LINENOISE_ASSUME_TTY`). Each break fails exactly its own assertion, and nothing else.
- End to end, with a CPU build of `ds4-agent` and a model path that does not exist:
  - `ds4-agent -m /nonexistent.gguf -p hello < /dev/null`: `main` prints `cannot open model` (it tries to load first). With this PR it prints the terminal message and exits with 2.
  - The same command under `script` (a real pty) and with `--non-interactive` still reaches the model load, as before.
- `make cpu` with gcc 13 and with clang builds with no new warnings. The model-free tests pass, except `tests/test_tp_commands`, which fails on 250 Hz kernels regardless of this change (#1096).

## Not tested

Everything above ran on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 24.04, gcc 13, clang) in a container. I have not built on macOS, so I have not confirmed that `posix_openpt`/`grantpt`/`ptsname` compile under `-std=c99` there without `_GNU_SOURCE`, although they are declared in `<stdlib.h>` on Darwin. I also have not run with a real model, Metal, or CUDA. On Linux the Makefile links `ds4_agent_test` with nvcc and the CUDA objects, so I linked it with `cc` and the CPU objects instead.

Refs #1046

title: Decode single-component JPEG scans in raster order
body:
A JPEG scan that carries a single component is non-interleaved. Its data units are single 8x8 blocks in raster order over that component (ITU T.81 A.2.2), whatever sampling factors the component declares. Iris groups the blocks into MCUs in two cases where it should not:

- **A progressive DC scan with one component.** `jpeg_decode_progressive_scan()` sends every DC scan through the interleaved MCU loop, including a scan that carries only Y (a script with one DC scan per component). With 2x2 luma the blocks are read in the wrong order.
- **A single-component frame that declares 2x2 sampling.** Its only scans are non-interleaved, but the decoder lays it out in 16x16 MCUs of four blocks, on both the baseline and the progressive path.

Either way the decoder gets wrong pixels, or rejects the file with `invalid or unsupported JPEG image` when the data runs out before the MCU count does. libjpeg-turbo decodes these files.

This PR sends one-component DC scans through the raster loop that AC scans already use, and treats a single-component frame as 1x1, since that is how its blocks are laid out. Files whose scans all interleave their components behave exactly as before.

## Verified

The files were made with `cjpeg` (libjpeg-turbo 2.1.5) from a synthetic 320x240 and 333x241 image. The numbers are the maximum per-channel difference from Pillow (the same libjpeg-turbo), using an ASan and UBSan build of `ds4_image.c`:

| File | `main` 320x240 | `main` 333x241 | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4:2:0 progressive, one DC scan per component | 165 | rejected | 0 |
| 4:2:2 progressive, one DC scan per component | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| grayscale baseline, `-sample 2x2` | 253 | rejected | 0 |
| grayscale progressive, `-sample 2x2` | 165 | rejected | 0 |
| 4:2:0 baseline / progressive, default scans (control) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| grayscale 1x1, 4:4:4 one DC scan per component (control) | 0 | 0 | 0 |

The 4:2:2 row is a check on the diagnosis. With `v_samp = 1` the MCU order and the raster order are the same, so `main` already decodes it.

- `tests/test_image_decode` gains two fixtures made by `generate.sh`. `prog_dc_per_component_420.jpg` is 48x32 4:2:0 with DC first and refinement scans per component; `main` decodes it with different pixels. `base_gray_2x2.jpg` is 40x24 grayscale with 2x2 factors; `main` returns NULL. With this PR both match `djpeg` bit-exactly, checked through the same fingerprint as the existing fixtures. `generate.sh` rebuilds the two existing ZRL fixtures byte for byte with 2.1.5.
- I undid each piece of the change on its own. Without the 1x1 rule `base_gray_2x2.jpg` fails to decode. Without the `num_scan_comps > 1` condition `prog_dc_per_component_420.jpg` gets the wrong fingerprint. Breaking the DC-first or the DC-refine call in the raster loop fails `prog_ac_refine_zrl_gray.jpg`, whose one-component DC scans now take that path.
- `make cpu` builds with gcc 13 and with clang, with no new warnings. The model-free tests pass, except `tests/test_tp_commands`, which fails on 250 Hz kernels regardless of this change (#1096).

## Not tested

I only compared against libjpeg-turbo 2.1.5, on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 24.04) in a container, with no macOS build and no model, Metal or CUDA. The decoder change is plain C and does not touch the GPU paths. I don't know how often encoders in the wild write these layouts: I made every test file with `cjpeg -sample` and `-scans`.

#1112 (luma sampled below chroma) edits the same test list, `generate.sh` and README. Whichever of the two lands second, I'll rebase it.

title: Upsample a subsampled JPEG luma plane instead of reading past it
body:
Iris sizes each component plane from that component's own sampling factors, but the RGB conversion reads luma as `y_data[y * y_stride + x]` for every pixel of the image. That is only right when Y has the largest factors, which is the usual layout but not a rule. JPEG allows any component to have the largest factors. In a frame sampled `1x1,2x2,1x1` (Y below Cb) the Y plane is about a quarter of the image, and the conversion reads past its end:

```
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
```

This happens on both the baseline and the progressive path. Where the read stays in bounds the pixels are still wrong, because a row of the plane is shorter than a row of the image. Without ASan I saw no crash, even at 4096x4096: the decoder just returns an image that contains bytes from after the plane. `ds4-server` decodes client images with this code.

This PR reads a subsampled Y through `jpeg_sample_chroma()`, like Cb and Cr, so it is upsampled the way the chroma planes already are: the centered triangle filter for 2x ratios, replication otherwise. When Y has the largest factors, which is the usual layout, the conversion keeps the direct read `plane[y * stride + x]`. The choice is made once per image, outside the pixel loop.

## Verified

The files were made with `cjpeg` (libjpeg-turbo 2.1.5) from a synthetic 320x240 and 333x241 image. The numbers are the maximum per-channel difference from Pillow (the same libjpeg-turbo), using an ASan and UBSan build of `ds4_image.c`:

| File | `main` 320x240 | `main` 333x241 | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| baseline `-sample 1x1,2x2,1x1` | heap-buffer-overflow | heap-buffer-overflow | 0 |
| progressive `-sample 1x1,2x2,1x1` | heap-buffer-overflow | heap-buffer-overflow | 0 |
| baseline `-sample 1x1,2x1,2x1` | heap-buffer-overflow | 250 | 0 |
| 4:2:0 baseline and progressive (control) | 0 | 0 | 0 |

- `tests/test_image_decode` gains two 40x24 fixtures made by `generate.sh`: `base_luma_subsampled.jpg` and `prog_luma_subsampled.jpg`, sampled `1x1,2x2,1x1`. On `main` the test fails on the fingerprint in the normal build and with `heap-buffer-overflow` under ASan. With this PR both fixtures match `djpeg` bit-exactly. They share one fingerprint, since progressive and baseline carry the same coefficients. `generate.sh` rebuilds the two existing ZRL fixtures byte for byte with 2.1.5.
- I forced the direct read at each call site on its own (`y_full = 1`). Each one fails its own fixture, and nothing else, with `heap-buffer-overflow` under ASan. Forcing the other way (`y_full = 0`, all luma through `jpeg_sample_chroma()`) keeps every fixture passing, so the direct read is only a fast path.
- Why the fast path: sending all luma through `jpeg_sample_chroma()` cost about 11% on a 2048x2048 4:4:4 baseline decode (157.6 ms to 174.8 ms), because of its per-pixel divisions. With the direct read kept, I measured no slowdown on 4:2:0 baseline, 4:4:4 baseline or 4:2:0 progressive. Those are minimums of 12 interleaved rounds on one core, built with the `make cpu` flags. The machine was shared with other jobs, so the noise is about ±7%.
- `make cpu` builds with gcc 13 and with clang, with no new warnings. The model-free tests pass, except `tests/test_tp_commands`, which fails on 250 Hz kernels regardless of this change (#1096).

## Not tested

I only compared against libjpeg-turbo 2.1.5, on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 24.04) in a container, with no macOS build and no model, Metal or CUDA. I don't know how common luma-below-chroma files are in the wild. I made mine with `cjpeg -sample`, and a hostile client can write one on purpose.

#1110 (non-interleaved scans) edits the same test list, `generate.sh` and README. Whichever of the two lands second, I'll rebase it.

title: Reject progressive JPEG scans whose band ends past coefficient 63
body:
A progressive scan header carries the spectral band `Ss..Se` of the coefficients it codes, and T.81 Table B.3 bounds `Se` to 63. Iris reads `Se` from the file without checking it. The AC decoders (`jpeg_prog_decode_ac_first()`, `jpeg_prog_decode_ac_refine()`) walk `k` from `Ss` to `Se` through `jpeg_zigzag[64]` and write `coef[jpeg_zigzag[k]]`. With `Se` above 63 and enough coefficients in the scan data, `k` runs past the table:

```
third_party/iris/jpeg.h:901:18: runtime error: index 64 out of bounds for type 'const uint8_t[64]'
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: global-buffer-overflow
```

The byte read past the table then selects which coefficient gets written. `ds4-server` decodes client images with this code.

This PR refuses a progressive scan with `Se > 63` right after its header is parsed. libjpeg-turbo refuses the same files: `djpeg` stops with `Invalid progressive parameters Ss=1 Se=64 Ah=0 Al=2`. Sequential scans do not use `Ss`/`Se` and are unchanged.

## Verified

- `tests/test_image_decode` loads the existing `prog_ac_refine_zrl_gray.jpg` into memory, sets `Se=64` on its first AC scan (`Ss=1 Se=63` in the file) and requires `ds4_image_decode_memory()` to refuse it. On `main` the test fails because the file is accepted; with this PR it passes, in a normal build and under ASan/UBSan. The unpatched file still decodes, and its fingerprint check is unchanged. No new fixture file.
- The file above ends its data before `k` reaches 64, so it shows the missing check but not the memory error. A 16x16 grayscale progressive file from `cjpeg` with `Se=255` on an AC scan gives the UBSan and ASan reports above on `main`, and `invalid or unsupported JPEG image` with this PR.
- Removing the check makes the new test fail.
- `make cpu` builds with gcc 13 and with clang, with no new warnings. The model-free tests pass, except `tests/test_tp_commands`, which fails on 250 Hz kernels regardless of this change (#1096).

I first also refused `Ss > Se`, which T.81 forbids too. No test could see that check: without it the file is refused later anyway, and with `Ss > Se` the decode loops do not run, so it is not a memory problem. I left it out to keep the change to what the table bound needs.

## Not tested

Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 24.04) in a container only, with no macOS build and no model, Metal or CUDA. The change is plain C in the JPEG parser and does not touch the GPU paths.

#1110 and #1112 also edit `tests/test_image_decode.c`. This PR adds its check at the top of `main()` and theirs go at the end, so the hunks should not overlap. If one does, I'll rebase whichever lands later.

title: Two fixes for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
body:
The first commit implements turboquant at all integer bit widths from 2 to 8.  This plus the yarn work allows you to run a 1m 8 bit kv cache quant context with comfortable amounts of memory overhead on a 128gb Mac M5.  The quant is implemented as a fused kernnel for prefill encode and decode, so there is minimal overhead for prompt prefill, and virtually none for tg/s.

The second is a series of tokenizer fixes based on the froggerific templates at huggingface.co/froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates and the fixes oMLX uses on the server side when handling conversations.

title: CUDA TP: lower the V4.1 layer-major prefill threshold to 32 rows
body:
## Summary

- On CUDA network tensor parallelism (`tp_world == 2`), send prompt suffixes of 32 or more tokens to the layer-major prefill instead of the 8-row short path. Metal TP already switches at 32.
- `DS4_CUDA_V41_TP_LAYER_PREFILL_MIN` (2..256) overrides the threshold for A/B checks. 256 restores the current behavior. Each rank chunks the prompt itself, so both ranks must see the same value.

## Why

With the threshold at 256, every suffix below 256 tokens goes through `ds41_graph_step_batch()` eight rows at a time. That includes the tail left after a 2048-row sweep. On two GB10 nodes each 8-row batch costs about one decode step, so the short path runs at ~50 ms per token (~20 t/s). A layer-major sweep costs ~1.8 s fixed plus ~4 ms per token, so it is faster from about 40 tokens up.

The jump is easy to see with the current thresholds. These are end-to-end times through `ds4-server` for new prompts with `max_tokens` 1 at ctx 32768. They were measured on 9139e2a; `ds41_prefill_count()` and `ds41_short_prefill_count()` are unchanged on main.

| prompt tokens | path | time |
|---|---|---|
| 114 | 8-row | 4.92 s |
| 206 | 8-row | 10.24 s |
| 277 | layer-major | 2.25 s |
| 457 | layer-major | 2.65 s |
| 2288 | 2048 layer-major + 240 8-row | 19.24 s |

Agent turns land in this range all the time. For example, a 233-token tool-call prompt took 14.9 s.

With this change (main + this commit, same prompts):

| prompt tokens | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 39 | 1.65 s | 1.01 s |
| 114 | 4.92 s | 1.01 s |
| 206 | 10.24 s | 1.31 s |
| 2288 | 19.24 s | 10.33 s |
| 233 (tool call) | 14.9 s | 3.4 s |

The "after" run came second, so the Engram rows of the same prompts were warmer in the page cache. On a suffix that was already layer-major, the cache alone gave 2.25 s → 1.52 s (277 tokens). That is much smaller than the effect of the path change.

## Correctness

Suffixes of 32-255 tokens now take the same path CUDA TP already uses for every longer suffix. There are no new kernels.

Test: a four-turn conversation at temperature 0, using the same binary with the threshold at 32 and at 256. It checks a code, a colour, a count and a city recalled across turns, the primes below 60, and the code reversed character by character. Both runs return the same facts and exact values. One sentence differs in wording, as expected from the different reduction order of the two prefill paths.

## Tests

Setup:
- two DGX Spark-class GB10 nodes (128 GB unified memory each) on a direct ConnectX-7 RoCEv2 link, CUDA 13.0;
- V4.1 Flash Q2 GGUF in the `ds41f-q2` layout;
- `ds4` worker and `ds4-server` coordinator with `--tensor-parallel --transport rdma`, 50/50 expert split.

Run:
- `make ds4 ds4-server CUDA_ARCH=sm_121`: no warnings. `make cpu`: builds with no warnings.
- API checks through `ds4-server`:
  - OpenAI chat with streaming, thinking, tool calls and tool results;
  - Anthropic messages;
  - a 23k-token prompt, then a follow-up that reuses the live KV.
- A 30-minute mixed soak with this change and #1117 applied, using `--batched-session 2 --ctx 131072`. The mix covered short, 5k and 23k-token prompts, tool calls, concurrent pairs and thinking. Result: 83/83 requests, stable memory.

Not run:
- the `ds4_test` suites and `ds4-bench`: the only GGUF on this setup is V4.1 Flash, not the default `ds4flash.gguf`;
- Metal and ROCm: this change does not touch them.

title: Linux: read decode Engram rows in parallel, probing the page cache first
body:
## Summary

- On Linux, decode read its 48 Engram rows (2 tables × 24) with serial `pread`s. The concurrent decode read from 6c00e2d is Apple-only (077a257), and `ds4_engram_read_batch()` only fans out above 256 rows.
- New `ds4_engram_read_sets()`:
  - it first probes every row with `preadv2(RWF_NOWAIT)`;
  - rows already in the page cache are decoded inline, without threads;
  - only the misses go to up to 16 reader threads, one per missing row.
- `ds41_graph_step()` now reads both tables in one call. `ds41_graph_step_batch()`, used for short prefills and multi-session decode, hashes all rows first, reads them in one call, then stages the GPU inputs in the same order.
- The row decode moves into a shared `decode_row()`, so values are unchanged. `DS4_ENGRAM_DECODE_PARALLEL=0` restores the serial reads for A/B checks. Apple builds are unchanged.
- `tests/test_engram.c` gains `test_sets()`. It compares sets over two tables with `ds4_engram_read()`, once with the file dropped from the page cache (reader path) and once cached (inline path). It also covers the EINVAL, EDOM and EIO cases.

## Why

When a token's n-gram rows are not in the page cache, each row is a random NVMe read. Test: buffered reads of 48 random 264-byte rows from the V4.1 GGUF, on one node with a local PCIe NVMe drive, pausing 40 ms between batches as decode does.

| | time per 48 rows |
|---|---|
| serial `pread` | 14.0-18.6 ms |
| 16 threads | 3.6-3.8 ms |

Decode showed the same gap. A 300-token text ran at ~16.5 t/s the first time and ~21 t/s when it was generated again. `/proc/<pid>/io` showed ~42 page reads per token on each rank in the first run and none in the second.

## Results

Two GB10 nodes, CUDA network TP, V4.1 Flash Q2, `--ctx 131072 --batched-session 2`. Each run generates three 300-token stories on topics not used before (temperature 0.7). Both variants use the same binary and are switched with the environment variable:

| run | serial (`=0`) | parallel |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 15.91 t/s | 19.51 t/s |
| 2, order reversed | 15.73 t/s | 19.77 t/s |

That is +23-26% on uncached text. On cached text the speed does not change: 20.3-21.4 t/s against 21.2-21.3 t/s.

These builds also carried #1116, which affects prefill only.

## Correctness

The same rows are read and decoded by the same code, so the output is bit-identical. Two checks at temperature 0:
- a four-turn conversation;
- a set of short prompts with short follow-ups, which exercises the row-batch path.

Both produce the same SHA-256 over all outputs with `DS4_ENGRAM_DECODE_PARALLEL=0` and with the parallel reads. The conversation's hash also matches a build without this change.

## Tests

Setup: same as #1116 and #1118. Two GB10 nodes on a direct ConnectX-7 RoCEv2 link, CUDA 13.0, V4.1 Flash Q2 in the `ds41f-q2` layout, 50/50 expert split.

Run:
- `make test-engram`: PASS, including the new `test_sets()`.
- `make ds4 ds4-server CUDA_ARCH=sm_121`: no warnings. `make cpu`: builds with no warnings.
- The A/B speed and hash checks above.
- A 30-minute mixed soak with #1116 also applied: 83/83 requests.

Not run:
- the `ds4_test` suites and `ds4-bench`: the only GGUF on this setup is V4.1 Flash;
- ROCm: it shares the Linux path in `ds41_graph_step()` but was not tested;
- Metal: unchanged.

title: server: make the idle prefill quantum configurable
body:
## Summary

- With `--batched-session`, `server_session_sync()` feeds prompts to the engine in 2048-token quanta while no slot is generating. `DS4_SERVER_PREFILL_QUANTUM` (512..1048576) overrides that value.
- The default stays 2048. The mixed quantum used while another slot is generating (`--mixed-prefill-quantum`) is unchanged.

## Why

Engines split long prefills themselves. V4.1 on CUDA network TP handles up to its carry capacity per call, tens of thousands of rows. Feeding it 2048 tokens at a time forces one 2048-row sweep per quantum. That roughly halves long-prompt prefill.

Setup: two GB10 nodes, `--batched-session 2 --ctx 131072`. Each prompt is a different 80 KB slice of `ds4.c`, so every run starts with a cold page cache.

| idle quantum | prompt | time | throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2048 (default) | 27,366 tokens | 155.1 s | 176 t/s |
| 16384 | 25,821 tokens | 76.4 s | 338 t/s |
| 16384 | 22,889 tokens | 81.3 s | 282 t/s |

Without `--batched-session`, a single resident session ran at ~320 t/s on a 23k-token prompt. With the larger quantum, two resident sessions keep that speed.

The cost is fairness. During a long prefill, a request that arrives on another slot waits up to one quantum before it starts: ~50 s at 16384 on this setup. Once a slot is generating, the mixed quantum applies as before.

Deriving the idle quantum from the engine, for example from its prefill chunk or carry capacity, might be better than a knob. I kept the default and the change minimal so the trade-off can be decided here.

## Tests

Setup: same as #1116 and #1117 (two GB10 nodes, CUDA network TP, V4.1 Flash Q2).

Run:
- `make ds4-server CUDA_ARCH=sm_121`: no warnings. `make cpu`: builds with no warnings.
- The measurements above.
- The 30-minute mixed soak ran on #1116 and #1117 with the quantum at 2048: 83/83 requests.
- After switching to 16384, the API checks passed: chat, streaming with thinking, tool calls, Anthropic messages and 23k-token prompts.
- With the variable unset the idle quantum stays 2048, which is what `test_mixed_prefill_quantum_option()` asserts.

Not run: `ds4_test`.

title: SSD streaming: LRU cache behaves pathologically during prefill
body:
During prefill, the activated weights per batch may be larger than the expert cache. When this happens I see a flat 0% hit rate, because the LRU replacement policy always evicts an expert between its allocation and its next use. Prefill is disk-bound as a result.

I did some experiments, and a simple trick that helps quite a bit is to temporarily freeze cache allocations after the first prefill batch. For remaining batches you still query the cache, still use cached experts, but anything not in the cache is filled from disk and immediately discarded after use. This avoids the pathological LRU cycling and ensures you get to hit the cached experts. Enabling cache allocations for the first batch is still useful for cache warming, especially when prefilling from 0 with a cold cache.

This trick increased my prefill from ~110 t/s to ~400 t/s running the Q2 quant of GLM-5.3 Flash on an RTX Pro 6000 using CUDA 13.1. I can provide a patch if it's interesting but I think there's enough info here to have an agent evaluate the idea.

Other issues: I looked at #503 which sounded related from the title, but on closer inspection it seems to be a problem with different cache arenas for different quantisation types, and not about this more general LRU problem.

title: Specialize resident M5 Metal decode shapes
body:
# Specialize Resident M5 Metal Decode Shapes

## Summary

- Specialize selected resident, one-token Metal projections for V4 Flash, V4.1 Flash, V4 PRO, and GLM 5.3 Flash. The MoE shape enum fixes only proven bounds and strides; expert IDs, route weights, clamp values, arithmetic order, and generic fallbacks remain intact. Selectors reject mismatched quantization/strides, SSD streaming, TP, quality mode, and non-M5 devices.
- Add a separately guarded dense Q8_0 specialization for GLM 5.3 KDA output (K8192, M4096, row stride 8704). It preserves the generic Q8 dot and reduction, has its own rollback, and is not part of the MoE enum.
- Expand bit-exact shape/fallback tests and balanced Metal benchmarks. The decode harness now supports multiple `--candidate-env` rollbacks in one paired run; the prefill harness can leave GLM chunk size to the model with `--prefill-chunk 0`.

## Individual Kernel Results

The model percentages below compare one specialized kernel against its generic rollback with the other specializations held as configured for that experiment. Parentheses are isolated synthetic GPU-span changes, **not** whole-model throughput. Do not add the rows.

| Kernel | V4 Flash | V4.1 Flash | V4 PRO | GLM 5.3 Flash |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q2_K six-route sum6 | +0.04-0.14% decode (2.3-5.8% faster isolated) | Model test needed (3.2-3.8% faster isolated) | Model test needed (2.8-4.1% faster isolated) | N/A |
| IQ2_XXS pack2 gate/up | +0.58-0.66% decode (0.5-1.5% **slower** isolated) | N/A | N/A | N/A |
| IQ2_XXS eight-route gate/up | N/A | N/A | N/A | +0.62-0.65% decode (1.4-1.8% faster isolated) |
| Q2_K eight-route per-expert down | N/A | N/A | N/A | +0.39-0.47% decode (1.1-7.9% faster isolated) |
| KDA-output dense Q8_0 | N/A | N/A | N/A | +0.04-0.08% decode, below some A/A offsets (2.01-2.56% faster hot, 1.16-1.28% faster rotating) |

The Q8 result is retained for its repeatable isolated improvement and narrow, bit-exact specialization, **not** as a statistically resolved standalone model-throughput claim. Flash IQ2's isolated regression illustrates why kernel-only measurements cannot replace real-model A/B. V4.1/PRO Q2 cases passed synthetic bit-exact tests but matching resident models were unavailable for throughput measurement.

## Combined Model A/B

On an AC-powered M5 Max with 128 GiB (macOS 26.6.2, high-power mode), one Metal engine alternated variant order and session assignment. Control used every listed specialization; candidate disabled them together. Both used a 4/0 graph split, 32 untimed decode steps, the same prompt, and identical full-vocabulary logits and selected tokens at every frontier. Prefill was identical and untimed.

| Resident model / simultaneous rollback | Normal shaped / generic | Reversed shaped / generic | Measured combined benefit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| V4 Flash Q2, IQ2 pack2 + Q2 sum6, 768 steps | 43.3406 / 42.9706 t/s | 41.0412 / 40.6088 t/s | **+0.86% / +1.06%** |
| GLM 5.3 Flash Q2, IQ2 pair + Q2 down + KDA Q8, 512 steps | 31.3639 / 30.9077 t/s | 31.2736 / 30.8494 t/s | **+1.48% / +1.38%** |

Contemporaneous identical-kernel A/A control/candidate offsets were +0.23%/-0.05% for Flash and +0.01%/-0.15% for GLM in the normal/reversed runs. Rates drift between processes; use paired ratios, not cross-run absolute rates. The combined results are measured directly, not sums of individual rows, and do not isolate Q8's contribution. All-on/all-off model decode is the scope here; it does not establish a prefill or application-wide speedup.

To reproduce the GLM combined comparison, run the following from the repo root with the resident GLM Q2 GGUF, then repeat with `--reverse-order`. Flash uses the same harness with a 2048-token prefix, 4096-token context, 768 steps, and the IQ2 pack2 and Q2 sum6 rollback names documented in `speed-bench/README.md`.

```sh
./speed-bench/metal_decode_schedule_bench -m "$GLM_Q2_GGUF" \
  --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
  --prefix-tokens 512 --ctx 2048 --warmup 32 --tokens 512 \
  --control-first 4 --control-second 0 \
  --candidate-env DS4_METAL_DISABLE_M5_IQ2_GLM53_SHAPE \
  --candidate-env DS4_METAL_DISABLE_M5_GLM53_Q2_DOWN_SHAPE \
  --candidate-env DS4_METAL_DISABLE_M5_GLM53_KDA_Q8_SHAPE \
  --include-selection
```

Note that the templates introduce new compilation. A cold run takes 40ms more, ie +1.8% but this is a one-time cost.

## Verification And Limits

- `make -j1 ds4-bench metal-decode-schedule-bench test-metal-q8-decode-shape test-metal-q2-decode test-metal-moe-prefill test-metal-ssd-experts` passed. Metal API validation, a generic-only Q8 checksum, and per-case dispatch tracing verify the KDA Q8 eligible shape and nearby width fallbacks. V4 Flash, V4.1 Flash, V4 PRO, and GLM MoE synthetic exactness profiles were also tested during the branch work.
- A GLM decode trace confirmed 68 shaped KDA-output calls in two tokens, and none on the Flash trace. Isolated 16-matrix comparisons used distinct PSOs, bit-identical outputs and guards, and reversed 64-sweep runs. Those GPU spans include encoder/barrier costs, not just instruction execution.
- No matching resident V4.1/PRO weights, Qwen weights, CUDA device, or physical multi-device TP were tested. Generic fallback is retained for those or other unmatched paths; do not extrapolate these M5 resident-model results to them.

Benchmark details and rollback flags are in `speed-bench/README.md`.

title: [Draft] Add resumable imatrix collection with isolated V4.1 prompt packing
body:
Need to generate imatrix for my own quantization. However, ds4's imatrix generation doesn't work on CUDA, and llama.cpp doesn't support DeepSeek 4.1 Flash yet. This change tries to improve speed of imatrix generation on limited computing devices (M5 Max 128GiB). By doing following:

1. Switch from token generation to prefill, and disable bounded replay for prefill to get closer to token generation states;
2. Batch prompts together but apply attention separately (seqlen) so there is no context leakage.

This helps to run at 8192 prefill length for the entire ~4000 prompts, getting closer to ~100 tok/s (still slow btw), than original ~10 tok/s.

The follow summary was generated by Codex:

SSD-streamed calibration pays a large layer-mapping/MoE cost for every independent prompt. Batch token-wise work across complete prompts while keeping their attention and Engram histories independent. Also make long calibration runs resumable without trying to reconstruct raw statistics from the normalized public imatrix file.

Packed prefill:
- Add opt-in --imatrix-batch-tokens 0..8192 (default 0/off).
- Greedily pack whole prompts in corpus order, bounded by context and prefill capacity. Oversized prompts run alone through the chunked path; a prompt that does not fit remains at the next pack's resume cursor.
- Share dense projections, HC, shared FFN and routed MoE across packed rows. Run the existing attention kernels on per-prompt row views, resetting positions and partitioning compressed KV/index storage by published keys. Odd prompt boundaries cannot share a compressor pair; reset Engram n-gram history per prompt. Reuse graph scratch and SSD mappings.
- Disable decoder-suffix replay for calibration so every token contributes routed activations at every layer. Leave normal inference behavior alone.
- No sequence-length-aware attention kernels or cross-prompt masks added.

Checkpointing and interface:
- Add --imatrix-checkpoint, --imatrix-resume and --imatrix-checkpoint-every. Save raw sums, per-expert counts, progress and next corpus byte offset in a checksummed private native-layout checkpoint using temporary-file flush/fsync/rename. Default interval is 16 prompts, rounded to a pack end.
- SIGINT/SIGTERM complete the current prompt/pack, save state and exit 128+signal without publishing a partial DAT. Failed partial forwards never advance the checkpoint. Restore the caller's signal handlers.
- Validate model device/inode/size/mtime, corpus hash, shape and context geometry; reject corrupt/truncated state and diagnose identity mismatches. Refuse accidental new-run checkpoint overwrite and input/output aliases. Disallow partial-prompt token limits with checkpoints.
- Preserve the original public collection API via an options-based API. Keep independent prompts and checkpointing-off as the defaults.
- Factor corpus parsing/packing into a model-free helper, preserve corpus contents, and accept explicit zero for the documented batch-off setting.
- Document that legacy DAT footer chunks count layer collection calls, not tokens. Unobserved experts remain zero; do not fabricate samples.

Validation on the cleaned, upstream-based tree:
- Clean Metal build of all executables and the new/existing regression tests.
- make test-imatrix: checkpoint round trips/replacement, identity rejection, checksum/truncation, EOF, corpus/packing limits, resume cursors and CLI PASS.
- test_deepseek41_prefill --dispatch PASS; DS4_NO_GPU syntax checks PASS.
- git diff --check PASS.

Earlier GPU validation of the packed implementation (2026-09-24, before this cleanup; M5 Max 128 GiB, V4.1 Flash Q4, SSD streaming/54 GiB cache):
- 112 bit-exact independent/packed/permuted attention comparisons and independently reset Engram hashes passed.
- Four prompts/3854 tokens took 134.753 s independently vs 33.733 s packed (3.995x collection-only speedup). Mean imatrix entry cosine was 0.9990124; the minimum was 0.9498554 from a 2-vs-1-sample expert. Restricting to experts with >=8 samples in both runs gave minimum cosine 0.9997653. Different batch sizes can change rounding and marginal routes; this is not a claim of bitwise imatrix equality or final quantization quality.
- A resumed full-corpus run completed 4690 prompts/2897897 tokens and 695495280 routes; 15335/15360 expert-layer pairs were observed.
- A fresh end-to-end GPU rerun after cleanup was not possible because the Q4 model was no longer present at its previous local path.

Keep this branch limited to imatrix code, tests and documentation; exclude model files, calibration artifacts, local benchmark reports and unrelated development history.

title: Cap the Metal GLM memory guard by memory wired at engine open
body:
Metal allocations made by other processes are wired and can't be reclaimed, so raising the GPU wired limit doesn't free them. With a model already loaded in LM Studio or llama-server, the GLM memory guard could approve a budget larger than the free memory. Wiring past physical RAM starves watchdogd and panics the host. This happened on a 128 GB M4 Max: an LM Studio model plus a ds4 load wired about 126 GB and the Mac rebooted.

The engine now records system-wide wired bytes (`host_statistics64` `wire_count`) at open and caps the budget at host RAM minus that baseline minus 8 GiB of headroom. An idle 128 GB host wires about 4–5 GiB, so resident GLM-5.3 Q2 still fits unless another runtime is holding memory. When the guard refuses, it now reports how much was already wired at startup. The change only applies to Apple builds with the GPU enabled.

A second ds4 process is already blocked by the instance lock. Also, ds4's own mmap-backed weights didn't raise `wire_count` in testing, so this cap is aimed at other runtimes.

## Testing

Apple M4 Max, 128 GB, macOS 27.0, Metal backend.

- `make`, `make cpu`: clean builds.
- `./tests/test_engine_mgpu_placement`: 118/118, including new live-cap cases (idle host, wired memory held by another runtime, saturation at zero, overflow).
- End to end, `./ds4 -m GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2.gguf -c 4096 -n 16 --temp 0 -p "Say hello in one short sentence."`:
  - **LM Studio idle** (5.9 GiB wired): runs normally, 53.15 t/s prefill, 27.78 t/s generation.

title: Metal: fix chunked-prefill SWA ring overflow and four latent kernel bugs
body:
Five small Metal fixes, in order of impact. Only the first one changes output on shipping models today; the others fix code that is wrong but that current shapes and default paths don't reach. They are separate commits so any of them can be dropped.

1. **Keep chunked prefill within the SWA ring capacity** (`ds4.c`). A nonzero chunk writes itself into the SWA ring before attention reads the previous window, so `chunk + window` has to fit in `raw_cap`. `raw_cap` is clamped to 8192, which is too small for 8192-token chunks (the PRO default, or `DS4_METAL_PREFILL_CHUNK` > 8064 on Flash). The fix caps later chunks at `raw_cap - raw_window`.
2. **Derive the HC expand barrier target from the arrival index** (`dsv4_hc.metal`, `ds4_metal.m`). The barrier target was `6 * dispatch_count`, computed on the host. One skipped dispatch left every later barrier waiting on arrivals that never came, and each one fell through the spin limit unordered. Each threadgroup now rounds its own arrival index up to the next group of 6. Output is unchanged on the normal path.
3. **Skip the pair-swiglu MoE matmul for any split TP world** (`ds4_metal.m`). That kernel has no expert ownership. The guard excluded `world == 2` but let 3- and 4-way splits through. It now requires `g_tp_split_world <= 1`.
4. **Fix IQ2_XXS pair-swiglu gate/up row indexing** (`moe.metal`). Every expert slot wrote gate/up to row `i11` (0 in decode). The activation output was always indexed correctly, so generated tokens were unaffected. Only `DS4_METAL_GRAPH_DUMP_PREFIX` dumps showed corrupt gate/up rows.
5. **Zero unused scratch lanes in the FP8 KV quantize amax reduction** (`dsv4_kv.metal`, `norm.metal`). When `n_nope % 64 != 0`, stale lanes could feed the amax, and the tail block read and wrote past `n_nope`. This is latent: DeepSeek V4 has `n_nope = 448 = 7 * 64`.

## Testing

Tested on an M4 Max with 128 GB, macOS 27.0, Metal backend, using `ds4flash.gguf` (DeepSeek V4 Flash, Q2).

- `make ds4 ds4_test ds4-bench` and `make cpu` both build without warnings.
- `make test` passes, except `metal-kernels`. That test fails on exactly the same assertions on unmodified `origin/main` (ds4_test.c:1675, 1751–1755, 3312, 3362–3363), so the failure predates this PR. `logprob-vectors`, `local-golden-vectors`, `long-context`, `metal-tensor-equivalence`, `streaming-decode-prefill-correctness` and the session/server tests all pass.
- **Fix 1, A/B test with `--dump-logits`.** The prompt was 19,020 tokens with `--ctx 32768`. I compared the final logits with `DS4_METAL_PREFILL_CHUNK=8192` against the default 4096-chunk run as the reference:

  | | KL vs 4096 | max \|Δlogit\| | top-20 overlap |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | origin/main, 8192 chunks | 0.338 | 4.52 | 15/20 |
  | this PR, 8192 chunks | 0.0025 | 2.29 | 17/20 |

  The 4096-chunk logits are bit-identical between origin/main and this PR. `--long-context` passes on origin/main even with 8192 chunks, so that test doesn't catch this bug.
- **Speed.** I ran `ds4-bench` at ctx 2048–16384 (step 4096, 64 generated tokens, 3 reps, the last in reversed order). Generation speed is within noise. Prefill at 2048 measured 338–351 t/s with the fixes and 339–351 t/s on origin/main.
- **Not tested.** I didn't run fix 3 on a 3- or 4-way TP setup, since I don't have that hardware. The change is a one-line tightening of the guard.

title: Metal: parallelize fused FP8 KV max reduction
body:
The decode-only fused q/kv norm, RoPE, and FP8 KV-store kernel currently reduces seven 64-value chunks serially for a 512-wide KV row with 64 rotary dimensions. This change assigns each chunk to a SIMD group, with two values per lane and `simd_max`, eliminating the max tree's threadgroup barriers. Two named template instantiations retain both schedules. FP8 scaling, quantization, the raw-cache half round-trip, and RoPE synchronization remain unchanged. The tree schedule remains the default; set `DS4_METAL_FP8_KV_SIMD_MAX=1` to select SIMD max. Standalone 64-thread finalizers and the compressor are unchanged.

The tree also zeroes inactive lanes in partial chunks before reduction, correcting a possible stale-scratch contribution to `amax`. The measured 448-value prefix consists entirely of full chunks. The new `test-fp8-kv-max` target compares both schedules on synthetic full and partial chunks.

## Performance

On an Apple M5 Max, the **full fused norm/RoPE/FP8-store dispatch is about 1.9x faster** with SIMD max: 12.77 us for the tree versus 6.82 us for SIMD max, averaged over 688 dispatches per variant. These are instrumented GPU timings; the end-to-end results below come from a separate benchmark without timeline instrumentation.

With a resident Flash 0731 GGUF, a 2,048-token prefix, 4,096-token context, 16 warmup steps, and 512 measured decode steps per variant, **overall generation throughput improves by about 1%**:

| Run | Tree | SIMD max |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 45.06 tok/s (11.36 s) | 45.53 tok/s (11.24 s) |
| 2 | 44.36 tok/s (11.54 s) | 44.80 tok/s (11.43 s) |

The same-engine benchmark alternates variants and checks full logits and selected tokens. The tree control includes the partial-tail zeroing fix; its cost was not measured separately. TP overlap was not measured on this single-device system.

## Validation

- `make test-fp8-kv-max`: 32/32 finite cases byte-identical for dequantized KV, raw-cache values, and Q output across full and partial chunks; 32/32 NaN/Inf probes also matched on M5 Max.
- Same-engine decode A/B: all 529 full-vocabulary logit rows and 528 selected tokens matched in each run.
- Checkpoint-matched Flash 0731 logprob smoke vectors passed. The 100-case official-continuation score TSVs for the tree and SIMD schedules were byte-identical (average NLL `0.409022334`, first-token match `54/100`).
- `make test-quality-api` and `python3 tests/test_glm_reference_render.py` passed.

title: Metal: fix SSD-streaming expert cache slot leaks, in-flight recycling and prune hang
body:
Four fixes to the SSD-streaming expert cache in `ds4_metal.m`, as separate commits. They are related, but each can be reviewed on its own.

1. **Return streamed-expert slab slots on every load error path.** A slab slot leaves the free list before its buffers are locked and filled. Several failure paths returned without giving it back: a failed lock, a nil `contents`, a failed pread or blit encoder, and `install_loaded` failing (in `get_protected`, `load_selected_missing`, the pending-load path and `prepare_selected_batch`). Each such failure lost the slot for the rest of the process. New `give_back_buffers`/`give_back_loads` helpers return the slot, or munlock a non-slab buffer, and nil the pointers. Loads that did install are nilled first, so the cache entry keeps ownership. The one exception: if install fails after GPU-copy blits were queued, those buffers are deliberately leaked, because the queued blits still write to them.
2. **Mark GPU-copy entries in flight until their blit runs.** `load_selected_missing` installs a GPU-copy entry as soon as its blit is encoded, but the bytes only land when `g_batch_cb` executes. Until then the entry looked idle, so pruning or `take_reusable` could recycle its slot for a CPU pread, and the queued blit and the pread then write the same slot. The entry is now marked in flight against the current batch sequence. This path runs by default: the DSV4 prefill hotlist seeds the cache through `seed_experts_gpu_copy` during SSD streaming.
3. **Keep per-layer counts in sync.** `clear_layer` forced `layer_count[layer] = 0` after `clear_entry`. But `clear_entry` already decrements the count, and it skips in-flight entries, so a layer that still had in-flight entries was left with a count of 0 and live entries. The forced reset is gone. With the count accurate, the victim scans also skip empty layers.
4. **Skip in-flight entries in `prune_global`.** The loop runs `while (entry_count > budget)` and clears the coldest unprotected entry. `clear_entry` does nothing to an in-flight entry, so if that entry was the coldest, `entry_count` never changed and the loop spun forever. In-flight entries are now excluded from the scan, as `prune_layer` already does.

## Testing

Tested on an M4 Max with 128 GB, macOS 27.0, Metal backend, with DeepSeek V4 Flash (`IQ2XXS-w2Q2K` Q2).

- `make ds4 ds4_test ds4-bench ds4-eval` and `make cpu` both build without warnings.
- `make test`: everything passes, including `metal-ssd-streaming-cache-pressure`, except `metal-kernels`. That one fails on exactly the same assertions on unmodified `origin/main` (ds4_test.c:1675, 1751–1755, 3312, 3362–3363), so it isn't caused by this PR.
- **SSD streaming A/B.** I compared `origin/main` against this branch with `ds4-eval --ssd-streaming --ctx 32768 --case-sequence 42`, 4527 generated tokens per run. Each configuration ran twice, in alternating order:

  | cache | origin/main | this PR |
  |---|---|---|
  | `--ssd-streaming-cache-experts 16GB` (80.8% hits, ~229k evictions, 1.5 TB re-read) | 20.67, 20.78 t/s | 21.13, 20.92 t/s |
  | auto (~65 GiB, 99.2% hits) | 24.98, 24.76 t/s | 24.96, 24.93 t/s |

  All 8 runs produced byte-identical output and passed the case (62/62), with no errors in stderr. Speed is within noise.
- **Not shown:** these runs never hit the bugs themselves. There were no load errors, and no in-flight entry was ever chosen for pruning. So the A/B shows the change is safe and doesn't cost speed; the fixes themselves are argued from the code above.
