title: GLM 5.3 Flash: long agentic thinking turn degenerates into one repeated token at temperature 1.0; no server-side repetition control
body:
## Summary

A long agentic thinking turn degenerated into one repeated token, even with the model card's sampling.

**Setup:**
- GLM-5.3-Flash Q2, resident: `--ctx 393216 --warm-weights`, disk KV.
- M5 Max 128 GB, ds4 at 5379c1c.
- Client: Hermes Agent through `/v1/chat/completions`, with `temperature 1.0`, `top_p 0.95`, `top_k 0`, `min_p 0` and `reasoning_effort: high`.

After 29 consecutive tool calls in one user turn, the 30th reasoning block degenerated:

| generated tokens | context position | content |
|---|---|---|
| 0 – 5,779 | 128,794 – 134,573 | ordinary (increasingly terse) reasoning |
| 5,780 – 7,559 | 134,574 – 136,353 | ` hmm —` repeated 890 times |
| 7,561 – ~20,600 | 136,355 – ~149,400 | token 68926 `aaaaaaaa`, repeated ~13,000 times |

Decode held ~21.9 tok/s throughout, and the client cut the stream after about 16 minutes. The token ids come from the `continued` checkpoint the server wrote at 143,360 tokens.

This is not greedy decoding, so it is a different case from #1196 and #1045 (DeepSeek at temperature 0 / 0.2).

## What led into it

This model keeps all previous reasoning by default (`clear_thinking` is false). So the turn's earlier reasoning blocks made up 51% of the 128,794-token prompt. Their style drifted, measured per 1K characters of reasoning:

| reasoning blocks | `hmm` | ` = ` |
|---|---|---|
| first 30 turns of the session | 0.8 | 0.2 |
| this turn, 1–10 | 2.0 | 8.7 |
| this turn, 11–20 | 3.4 | 12.4 |
| this turn, 21–29 | 10.4 | 18.2 |
| this turn, 30 | the loop above | |

## Engine side, as far as I can tell

- **Not the checkpoints.** Two `continued` checkpoints were written during this decode, at 133,120 and 143,360 tokens. The first came 1,454 tokens before the stutter began, and the GLM payload save only reads state.
- **No repetition control.** The request parsers silently skip `presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty` and `repetition_penalty` (`json_skip_value`); the sampler reads only `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `min_p` and `seed`. An OpenAI-compatible client has no way to push back on a loop, and nothing on the server stops a run of one repeated token before `max_tokens`.

## Possible fixes

1. Honour `presence_penalty` / `frequency_penalty` over the generated tokens, skipping speculative decoding while they are set.
2. Add a cheap guard in the decode loop: inside thinking, when the last few hundred generated tokens are an exact cycle with a short period, emit the think-close sequence so the model moves on to its answer. This is the trailing-block detection #1196 suggests, and it would also end the greedy loops there.

I can send a PR for either if you have a preference.

title: V4.1 Flash support and ~10 t/s Flash Q2 decode on a cheap dual-socket Xeon. Interested in a PR?
body:
I forked DS4 and used a coding agent to find out how far its CPU backend can go on Intel x86-64: a V4.1 Flash CPU path plus a performance series for V4 and V4.1, with correctness kept as the first constraint. The result, a working proof of feasibility, is public at https://github.com/10sephus/ds4/tree/cpu-perf-pr (the 184 commits on top of current main: https://github.com/10sephus/ds4/compare/main...cpu-perf-pr). Before polishing it into a PR, I would like to know whether this direction interests you.

**Why a CPU box.** A 128 GB DGX Spark costs more than €6,000 today, and a 128 GB M5 Max Mac costs more still (about €7,000 as a Mac Studio, €7,700 as a MacBook Pro); neither fits V4.1 Flash Q2 (152 GiB of main weights; its 189 GiB of Engram tables stay on disk) resident in memory on a single box. Refurbished multi-socket Cascade Lake servers with 192 GB of DDR4 hold all 152 GiB resident at a fraction of the price, scale to terabytes of RAM, and reach memory bandwidths from 85% to 2x a single Spark (decode is bandwidth-bound, while the extra AVX-512 cores on 4-socket boxes also scale prefill; I have only measured the 2-socket DDR4-2400 box so far, and the current NUMA pool handles two nodes and turns itself off on more, so a 4-socket R840 would first need it extended to four):

| Platform | Channels & RAM config | Max RAM (slots) | Peak bandwidth | Price, Italy, incl. VAT (Oct 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1× NVIDIA DGX Spark | Unified 128 GB LPDDR5x | 128 GB (fixed, SSD-streamed on V4.1) | 273 GB/s | > €6,000 |
| 2× NVIDIA DGX Spark (RoCE TP) | 2 × 128 GB LPDDR5x | 256 GB (fixed) | 2 × 273 GB/s | > €12,000 |
| Apple M5 Max (Mac Studio / MacBook Pro) | Unified 128 GB | 128 GB (fixed, SSD-streamed on V4.1) | 614 GB/s | ~€7,000 / ~€7,700 |
| **2S Xeon Cascade Lake (Dell R640, measured)** | **12 ch DDR4-2400 (12 × 16 GB = 192 GB)** | **up to 3 TB (24 slots)** | **230 GB/s** | **€1,000–1,500** |
| 2S Xeon Cascade Lake (Dell R640) | 12 ch DDR4-2933 (12 × 16 GB = 192 GB) | up to 3 TB (24 slots) | 282 GB/s | ~€1,300–1,800 |
| **4S Xeon Cascade Lake (Dell R840)** | **24 ch DDR4-2933 (24 × 8 GB = 192 GB)** | **up to 6 TB (48 slots)** | **563 GB/s** | **~€2,200** |

**Measured** (dual Xeon Gold 6230, 2x20 cores, DDR4-2400, 40 threads, the starting point at 32, its pool's maximum, `--warm-weights`, `speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt`, greedy; best of several runs on a shared host whose load average varied from 25 to 60 on 80 CPUs), against the numbers in `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, `docs/DGX_SPARK.md`, and `QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md`:

| Model, protocol | This CPU path | Start of the series | 1× DGX Spark (128 GB) | 2× DGX Spark (RoCE TP) | M5 Max (128 GB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| V4 Flash Q2, prefill 2048 tokens | 107 t/s | 1.1 t/s | 826 t/s | | 790 t/s |
| V4 Flash Q2, 128 generated tokens after 2048 | 9.6 t/s | 0.66 t/s | 18.05 t/s | | 39.35 t/s |
| V4 Flash Q2, decode at short context | 10.6 t/s | 1.9 t/s | 19.5–19.7 t/s | 26.0 t/s | |
| V4.1 Flash Q2, prefill 512 tokens (resident) | 50 t/s | 0.43 t/s | 88–100 t/s (SSD, 3.2K prompt) | 209 t/s (1K) / 411 t/s (32K) | |
| V4.1 Flash Q2, decode at short context (resident) | 9.0 t/s | 0.41 t/s | 9.3 t/s (SSD, after a 3.2K prompt) | 21.8 t/s (1K) / 18.0 t/s (32K) | |

"Start of the series" is the series' first commit on the same machine: upstream's CPU code plus the V4.1 CPU path, which upstream main does not have. Upstream main itself measured 1.5-1.7 t/s of V4 decode at short context there. Decode is about half of one Spark's at short context on V4 Flash Q2; at long contexts the gap widens, because long-context attention and the indexer are not tuned yet. On V4.1 Flash Q2 it is close to one SSD-streamed Spark's (whose 9.3 t/s comes after a 3.2K prompt), while the Xeon keeps all 152 GiB resident in RAM, at a fraction of the price. Prefill is where the GPU keeps its 8x. A V4 decode token reads 9.5 GB of weights, so the path sits near the box's memory bandwidth.

**Correctness.** The V4 logits are bitwise identical to the scalar CPU code this replaces, checked after every step with teacher-forced logit dumps (frontiers 16 to 3072). The build passes the correctness checks the Metal and CUDA backends are held to: `ds4_test --logprob-vectors` against the official DeepSeek continuations (all 5 vectors, zero mismatches) and the local golden vector captured on Metal (top-1 equal, top-20 overlap 20/20), so it produces the same model within floating-point rounding; like any two backends it is not bit-identical to Metal or CUDA, and a long greedy run can pick a different token at a near tie. On the 100 official V4 Flash continuations it scores 0.393 NLL per token with 86.2% greedy top-1 agreement; there is no recorded Metal or CUDA score on that fixture, and I would gladly run the comparison against one. V4.1 Q2 routed experts use the CUDA path's Q8_K activation arithmetic. On the 100 short official V4.1 continuations in gguf-tools/quality-testing they score 0.421 NLL per token with 90.0% API top-1 agreement: within 0.001 of the Metal scores shipped with that fixture (from a Q2 GGUF of the same size), and -0.0006 (CI includes 0) from this branch's exact F32-activation path. Every kernel has a scalar oracle in the unit tests (gcc and clang, AVX-512, AVX2-only and scalar builds).

**Shape.** 184 commits, +16.6k / -2.4k lines: +6.4k / -2.4k in ds4.c's CPU paths, five new `ds4_deepseek41_cpu*.inc` files (4.2k lines) and 5.8k lines of tests; 43 of the commits record their own before/after measurement. Vision, speculative decoding and SSD expert streaming are not implemented for `--cpu`.

**What still needs work before a PR.** This is a proof of feasibility: it works and it is verified, but it is not shaped for upstream yet, and I know it needs a polishing pass:

- leftover code from earlier iterations, and a few small fixes found in review;
- tests that can be shorter, and a history to squash or split into reviewable pieces;
- long contexts: long-context attention and the indexer are not tuned yet, so decode and prefill slow down with context much more than on the GPUs;
- it is tuned and measured on one Cascade Lake host only: the Metal and CUDA builds compile, but I have not run them on a Mac or a Spark.

Given the README's point that the project is a working template rather than a cover of every setup, I see three options and would follow your preference:

1. one PR with the whole series, squashed into a few logical commits if you prefer;
2. a sequence of PRs: the V4.1 CPU port with its tests first, then the x86 kernels, the scheduling and the NUMA placement as separately reviewable and separately measured pieces;
3. no upstream merge: I keep it as a public branch that other CPU users can take from.

If you are interested, I will fix the points above and polish the code to the bar AGENT.md sets (small, readable, no leftover code), in whichever shape you prefer.

title: fix(jpeg): validate SOS spectral parameters in progressive scans
body:
Closes #1292.

## Problem

`jpeg_load_mem` (`third_party/iris/jpeg.h`) copies Ss/Se/Ah/Al from the SOS segment without validation. The progressive AC decoders (`jpeg_prog_decode_ac_first`, `jpeg_prog_decode_ac_refine`) bound their loops only by `k <= dec->se` and index `jpeg_zigzag[k]`, so a scan with Se > 63 reads past the 64-entry table and uses that byte as a write index into the coefficient block. The decoder is reachable without authentication from `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/responses` image inputs when the server runs with `--vision`.

## Fix

Validate the scan header once at parse time, for progressive frames only (baseline ignores these fields, and some encoders write non-standard values there). Per ITU T.81 G.1.1.1.1, reject:

- Se > 63 or Ss > Se (this also bounds Ss);
- DC scans (Ss = 0) with Se != 0;
- AC scans (Ss > 0) with more than one component;
- Ah or Al > 13.

The per-iteration `k >= 64` guard suggested in the issue is not needed: every `jpeg_zigzag[k]` access is bounded by `k <= se`, so `se <= 63` at entry closes it.

## Tests

- New fixture `tests/vision-fixtures/jpeg/prog_sos_se_oob.jpg`: the exact bytes from the issue's reproducer (1x1 progressive grayscale, AC scan Ss=1 Se=200). `tests/test_image_decode` now asserts it is rejected.
- In-memory case for an invalid DC scan (Ss=0, Se=5).

Machine: Apple Silicon Mac, macOS (Darwin 25.6), 16 GB RAM, default Metal build.

- Before the fix, `tests/test_image_decode` built with `-fsanitize=address` reports `global-buffer-overflow` in `jpeg_prog_decode_ac_first` (jpeg.h:901) <- `jpeg_decode_progressive_scan` <- `jpeg_load_mem` <- `ds4_image_decode_memory`.
- After the fix it passes clean under `-fsanitize=address,undefined` and with the normal `make` build; the existing progressive ZRL fixtures still decode bit-exact.
- `uv run --with numpy --with pillow python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_jpeg_decode.py`: 3/3 pass (baseline + progressive JPEGs compared against Pillow/libjpeg).
- `make test`: everything builds; `ds4-eval --validate-cases`, `ds4-eval --self-test-extractors` and `ds4_agent_test` pass. `ds4_test` could not run (no `ds4flash.gguf` on this machine); I ran the remaining test binaries of the `test` recipe by hand and all passed. `ds4_test` does not reach the JPEG decoder.
- Not run (need models): `tests/test_glm53_vision_engine`, `tests/test_glm53_vision_prompt`, `tests/test_deepseek41_graph` vision-encoder check. They decode only valid JPEGs, the path `test_jpeg_decode.py` already covers.

title: server: accept OpenAI token-ID prompt arrays in /v1/completions
body:
The OpenAI completions API allows `"prompt"` as an array of integers (token IDs) for exact token-sequence control. `parse_prompt()` treated any array whose first element is not a string as an empty prompt, so token-ID requests silently prefilled almost nothing.

Reproduction against `ds4-server` (Jetson AGX Thor, sm_110, ds4f-q2):

```sh
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"deepseek-v4-flash","prompt":[100,101,102,...],"max_tokens":8}'
# usage.prompt_tokens: 9   (expected: the number of ids supplied)
```

This breaks OpenAI-compatible benchmark clients that rely on the token-ID form (evalscope with `--tokenize-prompt`, some vLLM test harnesses), and it fails silently: requests succeed with wrong lengths.

The patch:

- detects `[int, ...]` in the `prompt` field before the existing string parsing;
- parses the ids into `r->prompt` directly, marking the request with `prompt_from_ids`;
- skips the chat-template wrap and re-tokenization for those requests, so the ids are used exactly as supplied (the reason the API has this form at all);
- keeps `prompt_text` a non-NULL empty string so text-prefix KV-cache lookups and tracing take their ordinary path;
- relies on `json_int()`'s existing negative/NaN folding; out-of-range ids surface through the engine as before.

Behavior for string prompts and `["text", ...]` arrays is unchanged (`parse_prompt()` path).

## Verification (Linux/CUDA, Jetson AGX Thor, sm_110)

- `cc -fsyntax-only` clean; full `make cuda CUDA_ARCH=sm_110` build clean.
- `make test` suites: `ds4_test` ok, `ds4_agent_test` ok, `--validate-cases` ok (92 core + 50 hard), `--self-test-extractors` ok.
  Note: `tests/test_tp_commands` aborts `make test` early, but it fails **identically on pristine ee7e840** without this patch (`check_bulk_exchange` timeout assertion) — pre-existing, unrelated.
- Runtime equivalence: HF tokenizer encodes a prompt to 11 ids; sending `{"prompt":[...11 ids...]}` now reports `usage.prompt_tokens: 11` (previously ~9 garbage tokens for a 1000-id array), while the string form still reports 20 (11 + chat template) as before.

Motivation: this exact failure mode corrupted an evalscope `--tokenize-prompt` pressure-test run against ds4-server (1000-int prompts parsed as ~9 tokens), which is how it was found.

title: CUDA: server process dies during long prefill at ~512K tokens (ctx=1048576, managed KV cache) instead of returning an error
body:
## Environment

- Hardware: Jetson AGX Thor developer kit (sm_110, 128 GB unified memory, MAXN power mode)
- Build: current main @ ee7e840, `make cuda CUDA_ARCH=sm_110`, CUDA 13.0
- Model: Flash 0731 Q2 (`DeepSeek-V4-Flash-IQ2XXS-w2Q2K-AProjQ8-SExpQ8-OutQ8-chat-v2-imatrix-0731.gguf`, 80.8 GiB, resident)
- Server: `./ds4-server -m ds4flash.gguf --cuda --ctx 1048576 -t 8` (managed KV cache mode activates at this ctx)

## Reproduction

Send a single `/v1/chat/completions` streaming request whose user message tokenizes to **1,012,393 tokens** (real text, concatenated novel slices). The server accepts the request (it is below the configured context) and starts chunked prefill.

Startup memory lines:

```
ds4: memory detail: ctx=1048576 prefill_cap=4096 raw_kv_rows=4352 compressed_kv_rows=262146 backend=cuda
ds4: CUDA using managed KV cache for ctx=1048576 (kv cache 13.79 GiB, context buffers 21.79 GiB); this may degrade performance but is needed for very large contexts
1030 10:39:17 ds4-server: context buffers 22319.75 MiB (ctx=1048576, backend=cuda, prefill_chunk=4096, raw_kv_rows=4352, compressed_kv_rows=262146)
```

Prefill progresses normally (~211 t/s average, declining from ~260 to ~154 t/s as KV grows) for **40.5 minutes**, then the process dies at exactly chunk 512,000/1,012,393 (50.6%):

```
1030 12:10:38 ... prefill chunk 507904/1012393 (50.2%) chunk=155.07 t/s avg=212.06 t/s 2395.144s
1030 12:11:05 ... prefill chunk 512000/1012393 (50.6%) chunk=153.75 t/s avg=211.41 t/s 2421.784s
ds4: Metal synchronize after chunked prefill failure also failed
```

At the moment of death, physical memory was ~120/122 GiB per `free -g`. There is no further log line, no request completion record, no error response — the HTTP stream just ends (client sees EOF mid-prefill) and the process is gone.

## Two issues

1. **OOM should degrade gracefully.** With `--ctx 1048576` the server happily accepts a ~1M-token request, but the combination of resident 80.8 GiB weights + 21.79 GiB context buffers + growing managed KV + prefill transient buffers exhausts unified memory around 512K tokens of committed KV. Ideally the engine would return a 5xx/insufficient-memory error to the client and keep serving other sessions; today the whole server dies. A `--max-committed-kv` guard or an admission check (estimated KV commit vs. available physical memory) before accepting a request would make huge contexts fail safely.
2. **Wrong backend string on CUDA.** The last line says `Metal synchronize after chunked prefill failure also failed` on a CUDA-only build — the message appears to be shared with the Metal backend and not specialized per backend.

## Extra data points

- The same server served a 100,775-token prompt fine at ~353 t/s prefill (285.6 s) earlier the same day at the same ctx setting; the crash is depth-dependent, not prompt-dependent.
- After the crash, `--ctx 262144` runs the non-managed KV path with 5.86 GiB context buffers and is stable — we switched production to 256K.
- I have the full 126-line prefill progress log if useful.

Thanks for ds4 — the Thor numbers with PR #121 are great (decode 12.65 → 15.31 tok/s here).

title: [SECURITY] Control-Token Injection (Template Injection / CWE-1336) in chat prompt renderer (ds4_tokenize_rendered_chat)
body:
# Summary

A **control-token injection** vulnerability (template injection / prompt structure break) exists in the chat prompt rendering path of `ds4_server.c`. User-supplied message `content` is copied raw into the chat template and the rendered prompt is then tokenized with **special-token matching enabled**. This allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to inject control tokens (role delimiters, turn boundaries, tool-call markers) into the tokenized prompt, forging assistant/system turns, bypassing the system prompt and guardrails, and — in agent mode — steering the model into emitting tool calls that the runtime executes.

**Coverage.** Fix split across #1284 (DeepSeek V4.1) and #1288 (GLM, Qwen). DeepSeek V4 pre-4.1 is not covered by either PR — `server_model_syntax_for_engine()` returns `SERVER_MODEL_SYNTAX_DEEPSEEK` for V4 Flash GGUFs, and neither PR touches `render_deepseek_chat_prompt_text()` or its live tool tail. A fix for the V4 gap exists in a fork (trusted mask on the V4 renderer and live tool tail, `--special-token-injection-v40` test) and is being folded into #1284/#1288.

## Root Cause Analysis

In `ds4_server.c`, message content is concatenated into the chat template without escaping or filtering:

```c
/* ds4_server.c:3128, 3153, 3228, 3246, 3402, ... */
/* role headers + raw message content appended to the prompt buffer */
```

The rendered prompt is subsequently tokenized with special-token recognition **active**:

```c
/* ds4_server.c:3651 / 5734 */
ds4_tokenize_rendered_chat(...);

/* ds4.c:44575 -> ds4.c:44522 */
tokenize_rendered_chat_vocab(...) {
    ...
    special_token_at(...);   /* matches <|im_start|>, <|im_end|>, <|user|>, <|assistant|>,
                                </think>, <|tool▁calls▁begin|>, <tool_call>, ... */
}
```

The recognized token list (`ds4.c:44554`) includes role delimiters and tool-call markers for the supported model families (DeepSeek, Qwen/ChatML, GLM). Because rendering concatenates roles first and tokenization happens over the **entire** rendered text, a sequence sent by the user as plain content is re-read as prompt **structure**: the boundary between data and control is violated.

The rendered prompt is produced by `render_chat_prompt_text_for_syntax` and consumed by `ds4_tokenize_rendered_chat`; both are the real production functions, so the defect is in the shipped path, not in a test-only helper.

## Reachability Chain

1. `POST /v1/chat/completions` (or `/v1/responses`) with a message whose `content` contains a delimiter sequence (e.g. `<|im_start|>system\n...<|im_end|>`, or the DeepSeek assistant delimiter).
2. `parse_completion_request` (`ds4_server.c:5734`) builds the request and renders the chat prompt (`ds4_server.c:3128` etc.).
3. `ds4_tokenize_rendered_chat` (`ds4_server.c:3651`) → `tokenize_rendered_chat_vocab` (`ds4.c:44575`) → `special_token_at` (`ds4.c:44522`) emits control tokens **from user content**.
4. The model receives a prompt in which the attacker controls turn boundaries; the response is generated under the forged structure.

No authentication is required, and the payload is ordinary text — it fits in a normal chat message.

## Proof of Concept (PoC) / Verification

[tmp_tok_inject.c](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34213986/tmp_tok_inject.c)

## Suggested Fix

Escape or strip control-token sequences in user/tool content **before** rendering, or tokenize individual content spans with **special-token matching disabled** — only structure inserted by the renderer should be allowed to produce control tokens.

```c
/* Option A: sanitize content spans before appending to the template */
/*   replace/escape <|...|>, <tool_call>, </think>, etc. in msg->content   */

/* Option B: tokenize content with special matching off */
ds4_tokenize_rendered_chat(prompt, /*special_tokens=*/false);  /* structure only */
```

Additionally, add regression tests that place the delimiter of **every** supported model family (DeepSeek, GLM, Qwen) in `content`, `tool` and `system` fields and assert that no control token originates from content.

title: Raise the server request body cap to 256 MiB
body:
pi resends the whole conversation every turn, screenshots included. A long vision session crossed the fixed 64 MiB request-body cap in read_http_request() and then failed on every request with an opaque 400 {"message":"bad HTTP
 request","type":"invalid_request_error"}, with no way to raise the limit.

The cap is a per-request memory bound (bodies are fully buffered), but 64 MiB sits below real agent traffic with images: 45 screenshots of ~2.6 MB already produce ~65 MB requests.

This raises the default to 256 MiB and adds a DS4_SERVER_MAX_BODY_MB override (MiB, parsed like the other DS4_SERVER_* env settings).

Testing:

- make and ./ds4_test --server pass on an M3 Ultra.
- Against the running server: 63 MB and 66 MB bodies — previously split by the cap — now both pass the HTTP reader and reach JSON parsing; a ~300 MB body is still rejected at the new cap.

title: server: mask DeepSeek V4 (pre-4.1) chat syntax against control-token injection (stacked on #1288)
body:
Fixes the DeepSeek V4 (pre-4.1) gap reported in #1308.

**Stacked on #1288.** The branch starts from the head of #1288 (which contains #1284), so the first six commits are `HDYS-TTBYS`'s and are not part of this change. Only the last commit, `server: mask DeepSeek V4 (pre-4.1) chat syntax against control-token injection`, is new. Once #1284/#1288 land I will rebase and the diff shrinks to that commit; if `HDYS-TTBYS` prefers to fold it into #1288 instead, that works for me too.

## Problem

#1284 and #1288 track which rendered bytes the renderer inserted itself, but only for DeepSeek V4.1, GLM and Qwen. `server_model_syntax_for_engine()` returns `SERVER_MODEL_SYNTAX_DEEPSEEK` for the V4 Flash GGUFs, and `render_deepseek_chat_prompt_text()` and its live tool tail still return no mask, so the whole rendered string is tokenized with special matching on. A user message, system prompt or tool result that spells `<｜User｜>`, `<｜Assistant｜>`, `</think>` or `<｜end▁of▁sentence｜>` becomes a real control token.

Measured on a running `ds4-server` (V4 Flash Vision-Exp, `main` + #1284 + #1288), one user message, `max_tokens=1`:

| user content | prompt tokens |
| --- | ---: |
| `before <｜User｜> after` | 8 |
| `before <｜Uzer｜> after` (same length, not a token) | 12 |
| `before </think> after` | 8 |
| `before </thinX> after` | 10 |

With this change the same requests give 11 and 9.

## Change

- `render_deepseek_chat_prompt_text()` and `render_deepseek_live_tool_tail()` now have `_impl` variants that build the trusted mask, plus `_masked` wrappers wired into `render_chat_prompt_text_for_syntax_masked()` and `render_live_tool_tail_for_syntax_masked()`.
- `syntax_uses_trusted_mask()` requires a mask for `SERVER_MODEL_SYNTAX_DEEPSEEK`, like the other three syntaxes.
- The rendered text is byte-identical. The leading `<｜end▁of▁sentence｜>` of the live tool tail is now a trusted literal.
- Replayed raw tool text keeps its DSML delimiters trusted (`append_dsml_raw_v40`, same approach as `append_dsml_raw_v41`) so a replayed tool turn tokenizes to what was sampled; argument values stay text.

## Tests

- `ds4_test --server`: OK on this branch, including `test_render_deepseek_trust_mask`, a model-free test of the mask and of every entry point (full prompt, live tail, dispatchers).
- `ds4_test --special-token-injection-v40` (new, needs a V4 checkpoint through `DS4_TEST_MODEL`): system, user, tool result, raw tool call, live tail and multimodal split. It also asserts that tokenizing the same bytes *without* the mask does inject (2 `<｜User｜>`, 2 `<｜Assistant｜>`, 2 `</think>` against 1 each with the mask), and that benign prompts tokenize identically with and without the mask in all three think modes.

I ran `--special-token-injection-v40` on a real V4 Flash Vision-Exp checkpoint against the same change in my fork. I have since run it on this stacked branch, together with the V4.1/GLM/Qwen tests of #1284/#1288; results are in the comment below

## Not covered

- Raw `/v1/completions` prompts keep the scan-everything behavior, as stated in #1284.
- The `ds4_agent`, CLI and distributed paths tokenize without a mask; they are outside the chat server path this PR touches.
- A DSML delimiter spelled literally inside the text of a sampled raw tool call is trusted when replayed; this limit is inherited from #1284.

title: Proposal: a model-free CI gate for pull requests
body:
@antirez in #16 you mentioned wanting a CI that runs all the tests on your own
hardware after each commit. This is meant to complement that, not replace it:
a fast check on pull requests that needs no model or GPU, so contributors see
build and unit test failures before you do.

DS4 has a thorough manual release gate in `QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md`, but no
automated checks run on pull requests. Some of that gate could run on every PR.
I built this on my fork and would like to know whether it interests you before
opening a PR.

**What it runs**

- Warning-free builds, as QA already requires: any `warning:` line fails the job.
- `git diff --check` on the changes.
- Model-free tests, including `test_gpu_args_cli.sh`, `q4k-dot-test`,
  `mxfp4-dot-test`, `test-engram`, `test-web-recovery` and `test_image_decode`.
- `--help` for `ds4`, `ds4-server` and `ds4-agent`.
- `tests/test_jpeg_decode.py`, which compares the decoder with Pillow/libjpeg.
- On macOS only: the Metal build, `ds4_test --server`, `ds4_agent_test`,
  `test-session-state` and the `ds4-eval` self-checks. On Linux these link
  through `nvcc`, so the Ubuntu job builds `make cpu` and runs the portable
  tests only.

**What it adds**

Two files and no `Makefile` changes: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and
`tests/ci_gate.sh`. The script can also be run locally from a clean tree.

- Branch: https://github.com/giuliowaitforitdavide/ds4/tree/ci/pr-gate
- Green run: https://github.com/giuliowaitforitdavide/ds4/actions/runs/41303139651

The run took about 1.5 minutes on GitHub-hosted runners (`ubuntu-latest`,
`macos-latest`). I also confirmed locally that an added compiler warning makes
the gate fail.

**What it does not cover**

It does not replace `QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md`. It does not build CUDA or ROCm,
and it does not test inference, logits, speed, SSD streaming or distributed
execution: those need models and real hardware.

**Maintenance cost**

Failing checks can show up on PRs, and GitHub may ask you to approve workflow
runs for first-time contributors. Actions are pinned to commit SHAs and the
workflow has read-only repository permissions.

If you are not interested in CI for this repository, I will drop it. If you
are, I can also follow up separately with ASan/UBSan runs of the same tests.

title: ci: add a model-free pull request gate
body:
Closes #1311

Adds a fast pull request gate for the part of `QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md` that needs neither a model nor a GPU. It complements real-hardware testing and does not replace it.

## Changes

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: whitespace check plus the gate on `macos-26`, `ubuntu-26.04` and `ubuntu-26.04-arm`, with read-only permissions and actions pinned to commit SHAs.
- `tests/ci_gate.sh`: `build` compiles everything and fails on warnings, `test` runs the model-free tests, the CLI option smoke test and `--help` checks. The workflow runs them as separate `Build` and `Test` steps, so a red job shows which part failed. With no argument the script does both, for local runs after `make clean`.
- `Makefile`: new `ds4_test_cpu` and `ds4_agent_test_cpu` targets, which link the server and agent test runners with the CPU backend. `tests/test_q4k_dot` and `tests/test_mxfp4_dot` are now file targets, so the gate can build them without running them. `q4k-dot-test` and `mxfp4-dot-test` behave as before. `.gitignore` lists the two new binaries.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md`: describe the gate and what it does not cover.

The workflow also runs `tests/test_jpeg_decode.py` against Pillow/libjpeg.

All platforms run the same tests. Only the build step differs: Metal on macOS, `make cpu` plus the two CPU runners on Linux, where CI hosts have no `nvcc`.

## Changes after reviewing the first commits

A review of the first two commits led to these changes.

Reliability:

- Only build output is checked for warnings. Before, a test printing a runtime `warning:` would have failed the gate.
- Runner images are pinned, so a new compiler cannot fail every PR with new warnings.
- Python, `uv`, `numpy` and `pillow` versions are pinned, because the JPEG test compares against libjpeg output.
- Runs on `main` are never cancelled, so every commit keeps its result. Cancellation applies only to pull requests.
- `actions/checkout` and `astral-sh/setup-uv` use current releases on Node 24, and the `setup-uv` cache is off.

Smaller improvements:

- Removed the `ci/**` push trigger used to try the workflow on my fork.
- Tests run one at a time, not in parallel with the build, and warnings fail the gate before any test runs.
- `tests/ci_gate.sh` refuses a tree with existing objects, which would have passed the warning check unchecked.
- `persist-credentials: false` on checkout, since no step needs credentials.
- Added a Linux arm64 job, since DGX Spark is arm64.
- Documented the gate.
- Split the gate into separately named workflow steps, and named every step.
- `git diff --check` skips `*.txt` files. Across the last 200 non-merge commits on `main`, the check flagged 2 commits, and every hit was in a `.txt` file, with none in code. The repository keeps text fixtures and test data there, where whitespace can be part of the data, so those hits would be false alarms.

## Testing

- `tests/ci_gate.sh` on a clean copy, on a local Mac: passed with no warnings.
- GitHub-hosted runners on my fork, on a pull request: [green run](https://github.com/giuliowaitforitdavide/ds4/actions/runs/41324975594).
- Local checks of the gate itself: an added compiler warning fails it, a printed runtime warning does not, and a built tree is refused.

No model was used. CUDA, ROCm, inference, speed, SSD streaming and distributed execution are not covered, and this change touches no inference code.

title: CUDA: V4.1 routed experts on extra GPUs, parallel SSD expert reads, tested on 3090s with the 2bit quant
body:
V4.1 on CUDA was single-GPU. This lets 24 GB cards run it and spreads routed experts over extra GPUs.                      
  
  - Fit V4.1 SSD streaming on 24 GB GPUs: no q8→f16 cache under streaming; shrink the prefill reserve to one layer when the context doesn't fit.
  - `--gpu-devices A,B,...` with `--ssd-streaming`: the first GPU runs the graph, the others hold whole routed-expert layers, and only routed rows cross devices. Unplaced layers keep streaming. Knobs:
  `DS4_V41_EXPERT_ROWS`, `DS4_V41_EXPERT_RESERVE_MB`.                                                                        
  - Read streamed experts on parallel threads (`DS4_CUDA_SSD_READ_THREADS`, default min(8, CPUs)).                           
  - `score_official`: extra stderr `api_kl` line (truncated KL vs API top logprobs); TSV unchanged.                          
  
  Tested on 6× RTX 3090/3090 Ti with 1017 Q2 (29/40 layers on expert GPUs):
  - Decode: 1.18 → 14.8 t/s. 2.3K-token prefill: 15.6 → 100 t/s.
  - Greedy output identical to single-GPU.                                                                                   
  - Against fresh 1017 API references (router set): top-1 agreement 90.8%, vs upstream's Metal Q2 at 90.35%.                 
  - Known difference: ≥1024-row prefill batches on expert GPUs use a different MMQ variant, so long-prompt greedy output can differ at near-ties.

title: cuda: run the DeepSeek V4.1 vision encoder (tested with 1017)
body:
V4.1 vision was Metal-only. The CUDA encoder now follows the Metal V4.1 variant: 5120-wide aligner output and the three extra BF16 roundings (patch input, attention bias before the residual, SiLU before the multiply). DS4_DEEPSEEK4_VISION_DEBUG_PREFIX dumps the same encoder stages as Metal.

The V4.1 binder also accepts the encoder converted from the 1017 checkpoint (revision 1bae0e10) next to the original V4.1 revision. ROCm stays refused until it is tested.
