title: M5 Ultra: decode drift and repetition loops when M5_PARALLEL_FULL_FFN and M5_ROUTER_PROJECT_SELECT_FUSE are both enabled
body:
On an M5 Ultra, DeepSeek V4 Flash Q2 decode drifts badly from a fresh prefill and often degenerates into repetition loops. It only happens when `M5_PARALLEL_FULL_FFN` and `M5_ROUTER_PROJECT_SELECT_FUSE` are both enabled (the default). Disabling either one fixes it. Results vary run to run under greedy decoding, so it looks like a missing barrier between the fused router select and the parallel FFN.

## Repro

```sh
ds4 -p "Explain Redis streams in one paragraph." --nothink --decode-consistency 16
```

Sample degenerate output from a default run (thinking on, default sampling):

```
###. Redis streams are one paragraph explanation. Let's think about Redis streams. [...] They have "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" [...] "x" "y" "z" "z" "a" "b" "c" [...]
```

## Results

`--decode-consistency 16`, two runs per config:

| Config | max_abs | rms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default | 22.63 / 8.23 | 4.78 / 1.58 |
| `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_M5_PARALLEL_FULL_FFN=1` | 0.723 / 0.723 | 0.122 / 0.122 |
| `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_M5_ROUTER_PROJECT_SELECT_FUSE=1` | 0.723 / 0.723 | 0.122 / 0.122 |
| All 13 `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_M5_*` set | 0.723 | 0.122 |

<details>
<summary>Bisect details</summary>

1. All 13 M5 paths disabled except one, for each of the 13: every run gives 0.723 / 0.122, bit-identical. No single path breaks on its own.
2. Default with exactly one M5 path disabled: only `PARALLEL_FULL_FFN` and `ROUTER_PROJECT_SELECT_FUSE` bring drift down to 0.723 / 0.122. The other 11 stay in the 8-24 max_abs range.
3. Other toggles that did not help (single run each, max_abs): `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_METAL4=1` 13.2, `DS4_METAL_MATH_SAFE=1` 16.7, `DS4_METAL_KV_RAW_F32=1` 18.3, `DS4_METAL_HC_STABLE=0` 13.3.
4. `--metal-graph-prompt-test` agrees with CPU on the prompt (same top token, top logit 39.06 vs 39.03), so prefill looks fine.

</details>

Workaround: `export DS4_METAL_DISABLE_M5_ROUTER_PROJECT_SELECT_FUSE=1` (64.4 -> 63.9 t/s generation).

## Environment

- Apple M5 Ultra, 96 GB, macOS 27.2 (26B123), `iogpu.wired_limit_mb=90112`
- ds4 0.0.20261102.1026 (Homebrew, `temikus/tap/ds4`)
- `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-IQ2XXS-w2Q2K-AProjQ8-SExpQ8-OutQ8-chat-v2-imatrix-0731.gguf`, SHA-256 matches HF (`ca22ae2f...`)
- Default drift-patch flags: `hc_stable=on norm_unify=on kv_raw_f32=off rope_exp2_log2=off math_safe=off tensor_matmul=on`

title: server vision LRU cache thrash: the vision embedding cache holds ~12 images for qwen3.8-flash-next, so every turn re-encodes the whole image history if ≥12 images
body:
## Summary

On Qwen3.8 Flash Next with `--vision` specified, ds4-server's `request_tokenize_multimodal_prompt()` function encodes all image in the history in every request. Unfortunately, it's limited to a cache of 32 images or 128 MiB. In Qwen3.8's case, the cache effectively only contains 12 images, due to the size of the embeddings (2560 dimensions). Thus, if more than 12 images are in a conversation, the LRU cache thrashes, leading to 0 cache hits and full cost of vision re-encoding per-turn for all images in the conversation. There is no runtime method to increase the cache size, as the limits are hardcoded.

## Environment

- `ds-server` from main b3f5018
- Qwen3.8 Flash Next Q4 GGUF + Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-mmproj-F16.gguf
- Apple M5 Max with 128 GB unified memory, `--metal`, `--mtp` and `--ctx 262000`
- a single long-running computer/phone-use agent that keeps appending screenshots, so every request replays a long image history

## Observed

The `--trace` log shows repeated `vision embedding encoded; cache=126~127 MiB` lines ~3s apart, while the reported cache size is pinned at ~128 MiB. This sample had no "vision embedding cache hit" lines at all.

```
1104 15:02:19 ds4-server: vision embedding encoded; cache=126504183 bytes
1104 15:02:22 ds4-server: vision embedding encoded; cache=127227324 bytes
1104 15:02:26 ds4-server: vision embedding encoded; cache=126909203 bytes
1104 15:02:29 ds4-server: vision embedding encoded; cache=126928261 bytes
1104 15:02:32 ds4-server: vision embedding encoded; cache=127192949 bytes
...
```

Consecutive encodes complete ~3 s apart.

## Root cause

1. All images in history are encoded per-request, not just the new images. This is only efficient when `server_image_cache_get()` succeeds.

```c
for (int i = 0; msgs && i < msgs->len; i++) count += msgs->v[i].images.len;
...
server_inference_lock(s);
for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++)
    if (!server_encode_image(s, inputs[i], &embeddings[i], err, errlen)) { ... }
server_inference_unlock(s);
```

2. The size of image cache is hardcoded and too small for Qwen3.8's embedding size (2560).

```c
#define SERVER_IMAGE_CACHE_ENTRIES 32
#define SERVER_IMAGE_CACHE_BYTES (128u * 1024u * 1024u)
```

The LRU behavior of the cache is implemented properly, but is insufficient at these sizes. The size of each entry in the cache is computed as token_count * dim * sizeof(float). As `DS4_QWEN4_IMAGE_MAX_TOKENS` defaults to 1024 for Qwen3.8, this effectively means that the cache contains only 12 images (or 24 for `DS4_QWEN4_IMAGE_MAX_TOKENS=512`, or 32 if lowered to 256):

| `DS4_QWEN4_IMAGE_MAX_TOKENS` | bytes / image | fits in 128 MiB | binding limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 (default) | 10.49 MB | **12 images** | bytes |
| 512 | 5.24 MB | 24 images | bytes |
| 256 | 2.62 MB | 48 → **32 images** | entries |

126.9 MB / (1024 * 2560 * 4) = 12.1, matching the 126/127 MiB observed above.

3. Past the image limit, LRU thrashing means that you get 0 hits.

Each request will touch every entry in the history (effectively updating the cache clock, as `used = ++clock;`) then insert each miss, causing an evict. If N>12 images, then the end of the loop evicts the start of the loop, causing the next request to evict even more. There is no steady-state for this cache, and the effective cost is 100% cache miss rate.

4. `SERVER_MAX_IMAGES` = 256 but cache = 12

`SERVER_MAX_IMAGES` was raised from 16 to 256 by #1245, but the cache size is still effectively 12 (at the default 1024 tokens/image)

## Potential Fixes

1. Make the cache entry limit and byte limit configurable at runtime (`DS4_SERVER_IMAGE_CACHE_BYTES` and `DS4_SERVER_IMAGE_CACHE_ENTRIES`) and raise them.
2. Don’t re-encode image the live KV already covers. The docs note that live KV reuse keys on image fingerprints, and there is already a suffix-based path (`if (!live || !suffix || ...)` check). If an image span sits inside the reused prefix, can its embedding be skipped entirely rather than re-encoded and re-fed? That removes the O(history) cost instead of just raising a constant.
3. Halve the size of each image cache entry by storing in BF16 or F16 rather than 32-bit float (default image token budget of 1024 is 10.5 MB).
4. Persist image embedding cache to disk: #1278

## Workaround

If using Qwen3.8, setting env var `DS4_QWEN4_IMAGE_MAX_TOKENS=256` will increase the working set from 12 to 32 images. Or increase `SERVER_IMAGE_CACHE_BYTES` to ~400 MiB and rebuild.

title: ai-waf: a fail-closed reverse proxy in front of ds4-server — integration proposal
body:
`ds4-server`, by its own documentation, has no authentication of its own
([SERVER.md](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/blob/main/docs/SERVER.md)). The docs
say it in one sentence: *"Restrict access to trusted clients; for an
Internet-facing deployment, put authentication and TLS in front of the server."*
Nothing enforces it.
[CLIENTS.md](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/blob/main/docs/CLIENTS.md) has
clients export `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="dsv4-local"` -- a placeholder that
nothing on the server side reads.

`ai-waf` is a C11 reverse proxy that sits in front of `ds4-server`, without
touching ds4's source: it speaks HTTP/1.1 and SSE, and nothing else.
It is fail-closed on everything it knows how to judge: a request it cannot
parse, a body it cannot decode, a response or stream event it cannot inspect is
refused rather than forwarded. The one deliberate exception is the dialect relay
described below, which is listed rather than hidden.

Repository: https://github.com/Pierpaolo1223/ai-waf -- MIT License.

## What it does not do (read this first)

- **It is not an authorization boundary.** Prompt-injection detection is
  heuristic and bypassable by a determined attacker.
- **It has never seen a real inference run.** The end-to-end test against a
  real engine (`make ds4-e2e`) exists, skips without `DS4_MODEL`, and I have
  never seen it pass: I do not have the GPU. Everything below ran against a
  mock upstream and against ds4's own code paths
  (`ds4/tests/run_synth_wire.sh` -- the `/v1/models` serializer, the real
  `/tokenize` handler, the tokenizer over a synthetic vocabulary), **not
  against weights**.
- **It does not cover the whole of ds4's HTTP surface.**
  `POST /v1/chat/completions` gets the full policy, `POST /v1/messages` and
  `POST /v1/responses` are relayed with a reduced one, and
  `POST /v1/completions` is not proxied at all: the profile does not declare
  it, so a client that uses it gets a 404 from the gateway and has to talk to
  the engine directly.
- The rule vocabulary is English and Italian. Other languages are reached only
  by the language-independent signals (role markers, delimiters, encoded
  payloads).
- It sees only what crosses the HTTP boundary. An agent that reads a private
  key from disk in a shell and prints it itself never touches the proxy.
- **It is not an OS sandbox**, not a replacement for application-level
  authorization, and it does not make an LLM safe. A gateway that claimed to
  would be lying.

The full residual risk is in
[`SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/Pierpaolo1223/ai-waf/blob/main/SECURITY.md):
it is written so it can be checked without taking my word for it.

## What it does

Client-key authentication, per-client and per-tenant rate limiting, admission
by estimated token cost, a context-window shield with exact counts via
`POST /tokenize`, prompt-injection detection over the text fields, a RAG
sandbox, output secret scanning with an SSE holdback, strict JSON and HTTP
handling. The full control table is in the README.

The design point: **the parts that decide are pure C11 with no sockets and no
files**, and every policy is testable on its own; the mutexes guarding the
metrics and session tables are the only thread state inside the core. Inside
the request path, `app.c` is the only place that combines policy with I/O --
the limiter backends in `src/` do their own file and socket I/O. That is why
the code can be checked piece by piece -- and the reason it is worth reading
even if you do not adopt it.

## The trade-off I chose, and why

The full policy applies to `POST /v1/chat/completions`. On `/v1/messages` and
`/v1/responses` -- the two other dialects ds4 serves -- the gateway relays the
body and applies only the checks it can read without rewriting it: auth, rate,
admission, JSON validity, the injection scan over the declared text fields,
and the output secret scan with the event-level holdback.

The reason is structural, not a missing feature: those other checks need the
gateway to own the request schema, and it does not interpret that dialect's
message structure. Applying half of them to a relayed body would change it in
ways the client cannot see, so that path stays pass-through and keeps only the
checks that read without rewriting. The honest limit that follows: only the
profile's declared text fields are scanned, and a text-bearing member of the
dialect that is not in that list is forwarded without being inspected. The
table is verified against `src/core/engine.c:20-22` and is in the README under
*What the gateway checks in front of a local engine*.

## What I have verified

All of it on 2026-11-04, on the development machine (Intel Core i7-6700HQ,
16 GB DDR4, Linux Mint 21.3, kernel 5.15), **against a mock upstream** except
where noted:

- `make test` green: 93 cases (51 attacks, 42 benign, English and Italian),
  0 false positives, 0 false negatives, 3 benign cases flagged but not
  blocked. **I wrote the corpus myself**: the 3 flagged cases are the only
  signal that is not self-confirmation, and a set of real prompts from your
  usage would say different things. If you have a small set to add as a
  *test set*, that is the first thing I would ask for.
- `make integration`, `make controls`, `make security` (39 adversarial
  checks), `make mtls`, `make disconnect`, `make redis`, `make soak`,
  `make asan` green against the mock. `make asan` is the only target that runs
  the daemon itself -- `main`, the streaming loop and the TLS client -- under
  ASan/UBSan.
- `DS4_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18077 make ds4-e2e` against
  `ds4/tests/run_synth_wire.sh`: exercises ds4's own code paths without
  weights.
- `make fuzz`: six libFuzzer targets (HTTP, JSON, SSE, schema, injection,
  RESP), time-boxed. A smoke test, not a proof of correctness.
- `make ds4-e2e` **not run**: needs a GGUF, and this machine has no GPU and
  16 GB of RAM.

That list is a record of one run, not a claim about other machines. The row
that matters most is the last one: everything else ran against a mock
upstream, so the engine contract is tested but the engine is not.

## The request

One concrete ask, low-cost on your side:

> **An example under `ds4/docs/`** showing how to put an authenticating proxy
> in front of `ds4-server`, with the caveats from this proposal written next
> to it -- starting from the sentence already in `SERVER.md` ("for an
> Internet-facing deployment, put authentication and TLS in front of the
> server"). It does not have to be `ai-waf`: if you know something better,
> the example is still worth having, and I would be interested in what you
> would recommend instead.

Two natural anchors, if it convinces you. The first is that sentence in
`SERVER.md`. The second is the Claude Code wrapper in `CLIENTS.md`, where
`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="dsv4-local"` looks like a credential and is in fact a
string the server never looks at: a note there saying "this is a placeholder;
put a proxy in front if the server is reachable by anyone else" is the point
where a reader is actually misled today. The example is the request; the links
are a bonus.

If the MIT license is useful to reuse the profile table or the policies, take
them -- even without me. That is what it is for.

## If you already have a `ds4-server` running

The end-to-end test does not start or stop your server: it uses the same base
URL for the direct `/tokenize` check and as `upstream_url`, and starts only
`aiwaf` on a loopback port.

```bash
DS4_URL=http://your-host:8000 make ds4-e2e
```

It does send that server real requests: the catalog, `POST /tokenize`, one
non-streaming chat completion pinned to `max_tokens: 8` and `think: false`, and
one `/v1/messages` call -- so an idle engine does a little real work, and a
busy one is worth leaving alone until it is quiet.

What it checks, in order: the `/tokenize` contract, the `/v1/models` catalog
relay, a non-streaming chat completion, a `/v1/messages` relay, an injection
prompt on `/v1/messages` refused with 422 before the engine is contacted, and
no `engine.tokenizer_fallback` on stderr. What it does not cover is written
in the README: dialect streaming and therefore the event-level holdback, tenant
profiles, mTLS, and the full chat policy.

If you do not have an engine at hand, there is still a real socket to talk to:
`ds4/tests/run_synth_wire.sh` serves ds4's own code paths over a synthetic
vocabulary, with the same JSON shapes and the same 16 KiB cap.

```bash
(cd ds4 && tests/run_synth_wire.sh 18077) &        # from the repository root
cd ai-waf && DS4_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18077 make ds4-e2e
```

title: server: add --loop-guard to steer replies out of short-cycle repetition loops
body:
## Problem

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017, `IQ2_XXS-Q2_K-imatrix`) in thinking mode can fall into a short token cycle and stay there until the output budget is gone. The case that hit me was an agent turn at 591K context: while working out an IPMI/RMCP packet, the reasoning started writing the zero-filled header as hex (`06 00 ff 07 06 00 00 00 …`) and produced **83,500 tokens of `00` over 21 minutes** before the client cut the stream. Nothing in the server stops this; an uncapped request just keeps going.

It reproduces at short context. A ~110-token prompt asking for the RMCP presence ping and the IPMI 1.5 Get Channel Authentication Capabilities request as hex, thinking high, temperature 1.0 / top_p 0.95 / top_k 0 / min_p 0, 12,000-token cap, M5 Ultra 256 GB, resident Q2:

| Decode mode | Runs that ended in a `00` cycle | Longest run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DSpark (default opportunistic) | 4/4, all at the 12,000 cap | 5,682 |
| DSpark `--mtp-exact-sampling` | 4/4, all at the cap | 5,475 |
| no DSpark | 3/4 at the cap (4th: cap reached mid-reasoning) | 5,183 |

So it is not the draft acceptance rule. `--decode-consistency 16` is also clean and bit-identical across runs (max_abs 1.869, rms 0.315), with and without `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_V41_CONCURRENT_FFN=1`, so it does not look like the M5 Ultra race in #1316 either. Once such a run is long, the cycle token carries almost all of the probability mass and ordinary sampling does not leave it. Related: #1196, #1045.

## Change

An opt-in server option, `--loop-guard N` (default 0: off, no behaviour change). After each committed token the server checks whether the last N tokens are an exact cycle of period <= 8. It escalates instead of ending the reply:

1. First detection: mask the cycle's tokens that contain a letter or digit (`ds4_session_mask_token`) for the next 64 samples. Whitespace and punctuation are never masked.
2. A later detection inside the thinking: inject `I am repeating myself … I will stop thinking and respond.\n</think>\n\n` as forced tokens, so the model answers from what it has.
3. In answer text: mask again; after 4 detections stop with `finish_reason: "length"` and a `repetition loop` stop detail.

Speculation pauses while the guard masks or injects, because drafts that match the target's greedy token would bypass both. The check runs every 16 tokens over a 4,096-token ring; decode speed is unchanged. Only the non-batched decode path is touched.

## Results

Same prompt and settings, DSpark on, `--loop-guard 1024`:

| Run | finish | Tokens | Longest `00` run |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | length (answer text went back into the dump) | 12,000 | 517 |
| 2 | stop, complete answer | 5,377 | 518 |
| 3 | stop, complete answer | 9,167 | 516 |
| 4 | stop, complete answer | 7,445 | 522 |

Without the guard all four ran to the cap with runs of 5,000+. In each guarded run the first detection came in the reasoning (masking was not enough on its own: the model moved to `01 01 …` or back to `00`), the second closed the thinking, and three of four then answered normally.

Decode speed on three coding prompts (thinking, 2,000 tokens): 53.4–55.2 tok/s with the guard vs 52.9–55.0 without.

False positives: a requested 64-byte zero dump came back exact. "Write ha exactly 300 times" is the same failure in another form: without the guard the model never answers (5,155 and 5,818 consecutive `ha` inside the reasoning, then the 8,000 cap); with `--loop-guard 1024` it answers both times (`finish: stop`), though with ~1,040 `ha` rather than 300.

With N = 256 only 1 of the 4 runs ended in a complete answer: the guard stepped in early and often and two runs used up their detections. N = 1024 gave 3 of 4, so I would suggest values around 1024: a real loop is still cut after ~1-3K tokens instead of running to the budget, and requested repetition shorter than that is untouched.

## Tests

`./ds4_test --server` passes; `test_loop_guard_detects_short_cycles_only` covers ordinary text, a run shorter than the window, detection once it covers the window, ring wrap-around, periods above the limit and window bounds (checked that it fails when the expected period is wrong).

title: MiniMax M3.1 on M3 Ultra: expert scales, tool calls, and DFlash2
body:
This stacks on #1287 (`7001667`). The commits through that revision are that pull request. The new work is `0cb6d1c` and `0d908fd`.

Measured on a 256 GB M3 Ultra, resident 214.03 GiB abliterated GGUF, context 65536, greedy, thinking off.

- Decode with no drafter: 18.95 tok/s
- Decode with DFlash2, predictable integers: about 31 tok/s, 94.9% acceptance
- Prefill, 7472 tokens: 73.77 tok/s
- A sampled thinking turn stays near 20 tok/s, because it commits one token at a time

## What changed after #1287

- The loader recognizes llama.cpp's mixed Q3 layout: Q3_K gate and up, Q6_K down-experts on layers 16–42, NVFP4 down-experts elsewhere.
- Each routed expert's F32 scale is applied to gate and up before SwiGLU, and to down before the routed reduction. Skipping it prints token soup. The integer bench then prints `1, 2, 3` in order.
- `ds4-agent` prompts and parses MiniMax's own tool XML.
- DFlash2 drafts greedy turns, including tool-grammar bytes. Sampled thinking does not use it. An argmax draft on a temperature-1 turn was locking repetitions.
- Prefill chunks longer than 16 tokens use grouped Q3, Q6, and NVFP4 expert kernels. The 8-token draft verify stays on the one-token kernel. Expert overlap stays off.

The quant recipe, the gibberish notes, and the bench log are written up at https://github.com/jjakemaness/dwarfstar-minimax-m31. The GGUF is not in either repo.

title: DeepSeek V4.1: seed the SSD expert cache from a routing hotlist
body:
Short prompts leave the V4.1 prompt-driven prefill seed nearly empty, so a session's first decode turns pay a cache miss (disk read) for most routed experts, tens of GiB of preads mid-generation on a 64-token prompt. Long
prompts already seed well; short ones don't.

This seeds the SSD expert cache at V4.1 session create from a routing hotlist, mirroring the GLM seeder.

Also included `gguf-tools/hotlist_to_inc.py` plus a `docs/SSD_STREAMING.md` section: how to record a hotlist with `DS4_MOE_RECORD_SELECTED_HOTLIST` and reproduces the shipped table

Measured on M5 Max (64-token prompt, 96 greedy tokens):

|                          | before | after |
|--------------------------|--------|-------|
| steady decode            | 19.8 t/s | 26.2 t/s (+32%) |
| first token              | 55.6 ms | ~40 ms |
| short-prompt prefill     | 11.8 t/s | ~21.5 t/s |

Cost: a one-time seed read at session create (~6 s), clamped to the budget and skipped once warm. Greedy output is byte-identical.

Testing: `tests/test_deepseek41_graph --stream-decode-queue-parity` passes with seeding active (512-entry cache; the second session hits the warm skip; exact logits/history/cache spans).

title: server: let a request with an image use the disk KV cache
body:
A request with an image was kept off the disk KV cache in every direction. That is right for a
payload holding image KV, but two cases hold none: the text conversation an image request evicts,
and the text before the request's first image. Both now use the cache.

The workload: a photo indexer sending one image after another with the same instructions, while
a long chat continues on the same server. Before, every photo prefilled from zero and the chat
turn after one re-prefilled its last exchange.

Numbers, M5 Ultra, Metal, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash IQ2_XXS/Q2_K imatrix + V4.1 vision encoder, measured with
this change on 890898c (the commit it was written on) and rebased onto main here:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| second photo, same instructions | 5751 tokens, 5.66 s | 199 tokens, 0.64 s |
| chat turn after a photo | 2583 tokens, 4.06 s | 16 tokens, 0.22 s |

Checks run: `./ds4_test --server` (passes, one new test), `make cpu` builds. Not run: CUDA.

Written with Claude Code; reviewed and measured by me.

title: server: --kv-cache-cold-anchor last-user cuts the cold checkpoint before the prompt's final user turn
body:
The cold checkpoint is cut before the first task: the last user turn before the first assistant
turn. A client that repeats a long fixed history ahead of each question (a prompt test suite, a
few-shot preamble) gets only the part before that history. For a 40k-token test prompt the cut
landed at 11k and every test prefilled the other 29k, 19 s on an M5 Ultra with V4.1 Flash.

`--kv-cache-cold-anchor last-user` cuts before the prompt's last user turn instead. The default
(`first-task`) is unchanged. With `last-user` a request served by a shorter entry still writes
the longer cut when it lies beyond what was loaded, so the new entry appears on the first request
after the switch.

Same prompt after the change: the first request loads the old 17.5k entry and writes the new one
at 39.6k; every later request loads it and prefills the 20 tokens of its question, 0.28 s instead
of 16 to 19 s. A normal conversation still extends the live state.

I know AGENT.md discourages behaviour behind flags. If you would rather have this as the default,
or cut differently, I am happy to change it.

Checks run: `./ds4_test --server`, `make cpu` builds.

title: metal: select the shader language version explicitly
body:
## Problem

`MTLCompileOptions` takes its default `languageVersion` from the SDK the host executable was linked against, not from the SDK `ds4_metal.m` was built with. When ds4 runs inside a host linked against an older SDK, the kernels compile at an older language version. On macOS 15, a host linked against the macOS 14 SDK gets Metal 3.1, and `dsv4_hc.metal` and `dsv4_misc.metal` fail, so Metal init fails:

```
ds4: Metal shader compilation failed: ...
program_source:18509:48: error: use of undeclared identifier 'memory_order_seq_cst'
program_source:18509:70: error: use of undeclared identifier 'thread_scope_device'
```

We hit this while embedding libds4 in Python through ctypes (https://github.com/rochecompaan/ds4-py). The Nix Python we use is linked against the macOS 14.4 SDK.

## Change

`ds4_gpu_compile_options()` selects Metal 3.2 on macOS 15 and Metal 4.0 on macOS 26 when the SDK provides them. The tensor API probe and the main library both use it.

Binaries built the usual way are not affected. On macOS 15.7.1 with the Xcode 26.2 SDK, a normally linked executable already defaults to `languageVersion` 3.2, while one linked with `-platform_version macos 14.0 14.4` defaults to 3.1. So the kernels compile with the same version as before, with no change in speed or numerics.

## Testing

Mac Studio, Apple M4 Max 36 GB, macOS 15.7.1, Xcode SDK 26.2, Metal backend. No model is needed.

To reproduce an older-SDK host without Python, link `ds4_test` with an older recorded SDK:

```sh
make ds4_test LDLIBS="-lm -pthread -Wl,-platform_version,macos,14.0,14.4"
./ds4_test --metal-kernels
```

| `./ds4_test --metal-kernels` | main (b3f5018) | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| normal link (SDK 26.2) | 82 result lines, 29 assertion failures | identical result lines |
| linked as SDK 14.4 | Metal shader compilation fails (errors above) | identical result lines to the normal link |

The 29 assertion failures are the same on main and with this change on this machine (the fused pair compressor store at `tests/ds4_test.c:1678` and the f16 flash KV stage at `tests/ds4_test.c:3315`), so they are unrelated to this PR.

`make clean && make` and `make cpu` build cleanly.

I could not test on macOS 26.

title: server: evaluate Qwen's <|im_end|> after a thinking answer
body:
## Problem

After a Qwen chat turn with thinking and no tool calls, `build_thinking_visible_text()` remembers a reasoning-free key for the live KV, so a client that omits the reasoning on the next request can continue from the live KV. The key ends with `<|im_end|>\n`. But generation stops on that `<|im_end|>` without evaluating it, so it is not in the KV. The next request matches the key, evaluates only the text after it, and the model sees the answer followed directly by `<|im_start|>user`, with no end of turn.

The Qwen tool-call turn key already avoids this: `build_qwen_tool_turn_visible_text()` leaves `<|im_end|>` out "so the next suffix actually evaluates it".

## Change

Leave `<|im_end|>` out of the thinking-visible key in the same way, so the next suffix starts with `<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>user` and evaluates the end of turn. `test_qwen_thinking_visible_text_matches_render` encoded the old boundary; it now asserts that the text after the key starts with `<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>user\n`.

## Testing

Mac Studio, Apple M4 Max 36 GB, macOS 15.7.1, Metal.

`./ds4_test --server`:

| Tree | Result |
|---|---|
| main (b3f5018) | ok |
| updated test, old key | fails at `test_qwen_thinking_visible_text_matches_render` |
| this PR | ok |

End to end with `ds4-server`, temperature 0, thinking on, no tools: turn 1 "What is 2+3? Answer in one short sentence.", then turn 2 sent with the assistant answer but without its reasoning, plus "And 4+5?". Both runs took the `thinking-visible` cache path with 107 cached tokens. A local debug print of the tokens around the junction between the live KV and the new suffix:

```
before: 106 live "."  | 107 sfx <|im_start|> | 108 sfx "user"
after:  106 live "."  | 107 sfx <|im_end|>   | 108 sfx "\n" | 109 sfx <|im_start|>
```

I ran this with a dense Qwen3.8 27B (Q4_K_M), which needs a tree with dense qwen35 support on top of 5379c1c. That tree does not touch `ds4_server.c`, and every function involved here is identical between 5379c1c and main.

`make clean && make` and `make cpu` build cleanly.

## Note

The DeepSeek branch of `build_thinking_visible_text()` has the same shape: its key ends with `<｜end▁of▁sentence｜>`, which also stops generation without being evaluated. I could not run a DeepSeek model here, so I left it unchanged.

title: prompt prefix: close imported Qwen assistant turns once
body:
## Problem

`ds4_prompt_prefix_append()` pushes the EOS token after every imported assistant turn unless the model is GLM. For Qwen, `ds4_chat_append_message()` already closes the turn with `<|im_end|>\n`, and `<|im_end|>` is also Qwen's EOS token. So with `--prefix-file` (in `ds4-agent` and `ds4`), every imported assistant turn ends with an extra `<|im_end|>`:

```
... 5 . <|im_end|> \n <|im_end|> <|im_start|> system ...
```

## Change

Skip the extra EOS for Qwen (`ds4_engine_is_qwen4()`), so the turn is closed once, as the chat renderer does for live turns.

Tests:

- `ds4_test --prompt-prefix-qwen` imports a USER and an ASSISTANT turn and checks that the tokens contain exactly one `<|im_end|>` per turn and do not end with one. Like the other Qwen3.8 cases, it skips when `DS4_TEST_MODEL` is not a Qwen3.8 model.
- `ds4_test.o` now lists `ds4_prompt_prefix.h` as a dependency, since the test includes it. Without that, a change to the header alone did not rebuild `ds4_test`.

## Testing

Mac Studio, Apple M4 Max 36 GB, macOS 15.7.1, Metal.

With a dense Qwen3.8 27B (Q4_K_M). Running it needs a tree with dense qwen35 support on top of 5379c1c; that tree does not change `ds4_prompt_prefix.h`, which is identical in 5379c1c and main.

| Check | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `DS4_TEST_MODEL=<27B> ./ds4_test --prompt-prefix-qwen` | 2 failures | ok |
| `ds4-agent --prefix-file` with `USER: What is 2+3?` / `ASSISTANT: 2 + 3 equals 5.`, tokens from `--trace` after the answer | `<|im_end|> \n <|im_end|> <|im_start|>` | `<|im_end|> \n <|im_start|>` |

On main without a Qwen3.8 model, the new case behaves like the existing `--session-rewind` case.

`make clean && make`, `make cpu`, `./tests/test_prompt_prefix` and `./ds4_test --server` pass.

title: server: keep literal Qwen ChatML markers as message data
body:
## Problem

Qwen chat rendering places message text into a ChatML prompt. Literal spellings such as `<|im_end|>` in a user message, tool result, or tool argument can therefore become control tokens instead of quoted data. For example, asking the model to explain `"<|im_end|>"` should not insert a turn boundary into the message body.

## Implementation

- Encode `<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`, and `<|endoftext|>` in Qwen message data and tool schemas, while leaving the template's own boundaries intact.
- Use reversible, narrowly scoped escaping: `<|im_end|>` becomes `<|im_end|>`, while a literal `<|im_end|>` gains an `amp;` layer. Distinct inputs remain distinct in rendered cache keys.
- Decode this protocol in generated content, reasoning, and tool arguments, including Chat Completions, Responses, Messages, and text-completion output paths. Ordinary HTML entities are not generally decoded.
- Apply the same encoding to reconstructed assistant suffixes and sampled tool-call replay. Withhold incomplete escape sequences across streaming chunks.

The change is confined to `ds4_server.c`, including synthetic regressions in the existing server test suite. Tokenizer, sampling, MTP, and inference backend code are unchanged.

## Regression coverage

- Literal markers in system/user/assistant/tool messages, reasoning, tool schemas, arguments, and continuation rendering.
- Distinct literal and already-escaped inputs, assistant replay-prefix agreement, and exact tool-argument round trips.
- Tool-argument streaming at every byte split for Chat Completions and Messages.
- Content/reasoning streaming at every byte split for Chat Completions, Messages, and Responses, including ordinary entities and UTF-8 text.
- Streaming and non-streaming text-completion serialization.

The message-data regression produces eight assertion failures on unmodified `main` at `b3f5018`; the complete server suite passes with this patch.

## Validation

Machine: Apple M5 Max, macOS arm64. Metal/default and CPU builds; model-free tests, so no model or quantization applies.

```sh
make clean
make -j8
make -j8 ds4_test ds4_agent_test test-session-state
./ds4_test --server
./ds4_agent_test
make -j8 cpu
git diff --check
```

## Limits / remaining validation

- This branch has not had model-backed inference or throughput validation. The deterministic tests establish codec, renderer, parser, and streaming behavior, not that a model always reproduces the encoded text correctly. Keeping this PR in draft pending model-backed validation.
- Streaming currently decodes the accumulated output on each update. This keeps parser offsets consistent but can be quadratic over a long stream of small chunks; an incremental decoded buffer is the alternative if profiling warrants it.
- CUDA, SSD-streaming inference, and physical distributed inference were not run. The session/protocol tests are not hardware-backend coverage.

title: Overlap streamed Qwen decode layers with their expert loads on Metal
body:
## What

With `--ssd-streaming`, every Qwen decode layer drains the GPU so the CPU can read the router's expert ids, load the missing experts and bind them. This PR removes most of the idle time that costs, in two pieces that each live in their own include file with a few lines of hooks in `ds4_metal.m`:

- **Early commit** (`ds4_metal_stream_overlap.inc`, 21 lines). The layer's expert work used to sit in the open command buffer until the next layer's drain committed it, so the GPU idled while the CPU encoded the reduce and the next layer's attention and router. The buffer is now committed as soon as the experts are encoded. With the handshake on, this is what the ordinary path (MTP verification steps, Q4_K gate/up layers) still gets.
- **Handshake** (`ds4_metal_stream_handshake.inc`, 310 lines). A single-token layer is encoded before its experts are known: the router's ids are copied to a shared buffer and the command buffer signals an event; the next command buffer starts with a wait on a second event and runs the experts through the layer's expert address table. The CPU blocks on the first event (`waitUntilSignaledValue`, no spinning), loads the missing experts, writes their addresses and signals the second. The GPU idles only for that service. On by default; `DS4_QWEN4_STREAM_HANDSHAKE=0` keeps the ordinary path, `DS4_QWEN4_STREAM_HANDSHAKE_PROFILE=1` prints per-layer wait and service times. MTP verification steps (2-3 tokens) and Q4_K gate/up rows keep the ordinary path.

**Failure semantics match the ordinary path.** A failed read makes the call return 0 with the batch still open; the cached and shared slots are computed, the missing slots stay untouched (their address-table entries are zero and the decode kernels now skip a zero or out-of-range entry, `qwen4_expert_rows` in `qwen4.metal`), the layer's entries are dropped and a retry is exact. Every exit, including a failed flush, returns with the caller's batch open. The experts' command buffer is committed without opening its successor (`ds4_gpu_commit_batch_commands`, split out of `ds4_gpu_flush_commands`), so a failure to open the next buffer cannot wait on a buffer parked at the release. A failed load now returns its slab reservations to the free list on every path (`ds4_gpu_stream_expert_return_load_reservations`, shared by the batch loader, the selected loader's failure exits and the handshake); before, the selected loader's failure exits and the non-matrix batch path leaked them for the process. The released experts' slots are marked in flight; when the next layer's ids arrive, the service checks that the buffer which published them and every buffer committed before it have completed (none of them can be parked at a release), then retires the marks up to that buffer before the load, so no load ever waits on in-flight GPU work. A cache budget below the slot count keeps the ordinary path, which falls back to mapped reads there. If the budget's slabs cannot be allocated, if the cache has lost slab slots, or if the loader places an expert in an explicit buffer the encoded kernels cannot see, the handshake switches itself off for the process with one message and the ordinary path serves every layer; the first two are checked before anything is encoded.

**Memory.** The kernels must see every expert slab when they are encoded, so the handshake allocates the whole expert-cache budget's slabs on its first layer (13 GiB at the default 256K allocation on a 48 GB M4 Pro); slots stay unlocked until used and the cache policy is otherwise unchanged.

**Other backends.** The only graph-side change is in `ds4_metal.m` and the Metal shaders inside `DS4_HAS_QWEN4_METAL`; `ds4.c`, `ds4_gpu.h` and CUDA are untouched. `make cpu` builds with zero warnings; the two Metal build warnings are pre-existing on main.

## Measurements

M4 Pro 48 GB, AC power, High Power Mode, Q2 model (`Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf`, 147,207,127,040 bytes), `ds4-bench --ssd-streaming --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt --ctx-alloc 262144 --gen-tokens 128` against `main` at b3f5018, all runs interleaved in the same session:

4K frontier (`--ctx-start 4096 --ctx-max 4096 --prefill-chunk 4096`), three rounds, tok/s min-max:

| | Prefill | Decode | Steady decode |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main | 217-223 | 17.4-18.2 | 18.7-19.5 |
| this PR | 223-224 | 19.5-19.7 | 20.6-20.9 |

Sweep (`--ctx-start 2048 --ctx-max 16384 --step-incr 2048`), two rounds, averaged over the eight frontiers: decode 15.8 → 16.0 tok/s, steady 16.8 → 17.2. Each decode phase there follows a 2048-token prefill chunk that churned the expert cache, so expert reads rather than drains dominate. CSVs attached below.

`--mtp` (5942-token prompt, 256 tokens, three rounds): 22.5-22.9 tok/s on main, 22.3-23.2 with this PR.

Spinning on the arrival words instead of blocking on the event measured about 3% more steady decode (21.3-21.6) but pegs a CPU core; this PR blocks.

## Fidelity and tests

- Frontier logits at 4096 tokens bit-identical to main (full vocabulary); 64-token greedy continuations on two prompts (29 and 575 tokens) identical with identical top-20 logprobs at every step.
- `tests/test_qwen4_generation MODEL --ssd-streaming`: passes bit-exact with the handshake on.
- `make test-qwen4-ssd-experts`: all 103 checks pass, and every single-token streamed case now runs through the handshake, including warm hits without a readable fd, failed reads with exact retry, and the resident/missing split cases. A test-only hook counts handshake layers and failures, and the test asserts the path was taken (the predicate honours the diagnostics that route to the ordinary path, so the suite also passes under `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_STREAMING_EXPERT_EARLY_LOAD=1`). The invalid-id contract stays on the ordinary path, which can reject ids before encoding anything.
- `tests/test_qwen4_ngram_state MODEL --ssd-streaming`: passes (failed n-gram reads during prefill, decode and MTP, exact recovery).
- `./ds4_test --metal-kernels` with the Qwen GGUF reports the same 29 DeepSeek compressor/flash-KV failures on main and on this branch; unrelated.

## Commands

```
make test-qwen4-ssd-experts
./tests/test_qwen4_generation gguf/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf --ssd-streaming
./tests/test_qwen4_ngram_state gguf/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf --ssd-streaming
./ds4-bench -m gguf/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf --ssd-streaming --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
  --ctx-start 4096 --ctx-max 4096 --ctx-alloc 262144 --prefill-chunk 4096 --gen-tokens 128 --csv /tmp/4k.csv
./ds4-bench -m gguf/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf --ssd-streaming --prompt-file speed-bench/promessi_sposi.txt \
  --ctx-start 2048 --ctx-max 16384 --step-incr 2048 --ctx-alloc 262144 --gen-tokens 128 --csv /tmp/sweep.csv
./ds4 -m gguf/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q2.gguf --ssd-streaming --mtp --ctx 32768 --nothink --temp 0 -n 256 --prompt-file PROMPT
```

title: Feature Request: Huawei Ascend / CANN backend for personal multi-NPU MoE workstations
body:
Hi Salvatore and contributors,

First of all, congratulations on DwarfStar!

I really appreciate the philosophy behind the project: building a focused, highly optimized inference engine for a selection of excellent open-weight models, rather than trying to support every possible architecture.

I'm particularly interested in the work on large MoE models, specialized quantization, multi-GPU inference, and SSD streaming.

I'm evaluating building a dedicated personal AI workstation based on Huawei Atlas 300I Duo accelerators, and I'd like to ask whether adding Huawei Ascend support could be technically feasible.

My use case: personal AI workstation

I want to clarify something important about my intended usage.

This is a personal homelab/workstation, primarily for a single user, not a production inference server serving hundreds of concurrent requests.

My main activities include:

- Local AI-assisted coding and software development.
- Agentic workflows and experimentation with coding agents.
- Running large, capable open-weight models locally.
- Testing newer MoE architectures as they become available.
- Using long contexts when necessary.

My priorities are the ability to run large models, good single-user interactive performance, reasonable latency, and efficient use of available memory.

I don't need the architecture to maximize aggregate throughput across hundreds of concurrent users.

In fact, I'd happily trade some total throughput for the ability to run a significantly larger or higher-quality model locally.

Hardware: Huawei Atlas 300I Duo

The Atlas 300I Duo is a PCIe inference accelerator based on two Huawei Ascend 310P processors.

Specifications:

- 96 GB aggregate memory per card (2 × 48 GB)
- PCIe 4.0 x16
- Approximately 150 W maximum board power
- Relatively affordable pricing compared with high-memory professional GPUs

A four-card workstation would provide:

- 384 GB aggregate accelerator memory
- 8 Ascend NPUs
- Approximately 600 W maximum accelerator power

Of course, the memory is distributed across independent processors rather than being a unified memory pool.

Proposed support

I'd like to explore whether a CANN/AscendCL backend could enable DwarfStar to run large MoE models on this hardware.

The models I'm interested in include:

- Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and future Qwen MoE architectures
- GLM 5.x, including Flash and larger variants
- DeepSeek V4 / V4.1 Flash and future versions
- Other large sparse MoE models that DwarfStar may support in the future

I'm not particularly attached to one specific model family. My goal is to build a flexible local inference platform capable of running increasingly powerful open-weight models.

Technical questions

1. Backend architecture: Would DwarfStar's current architecture allow a CANN/AscendCL backend, or would this require major restructuring?

2. Multi-NPU inference: Could the existing tensor/pipeline parallelism mechanisms potentially be adapted to multiple Ascend 310P processors?

3. Memory utilization: Would it be realistic to distribute a single large model across multiple Atlas 300I Duo cards and their independent memory pools?

4. Expert offloading: Could DwarfStar's existing quantization and SSD streaming strategies be adapted to Ascend hardware?

5. Quantization: Would the specialized low-bit formats require entirely new Ascend kernels, or could some components be reused?

6. Single-user performance: Given that my workload is almost entirely single-user, could the hardware provide reasonable interactive generation speed even if its overall compute throughput is lower than modern NVIDIA accelerators?

7. Hardware limitations: Are there fundamental limitations in the Ascend 310P architecture that would make inference with modern Qwen, GLM, or DeepSeek MoE models impractical, regardless of memory capacity?

8. Community development: Would you consider accepting an experimental, community-maintained Ascend backend?

Why I think this could be interesting

One of DwarfStar's most appealing characteristics is its focus on making very capable models practical on hardware that individuals can actually own.

The possibility of building a workstation with 192–384 GB of aggregate accelerator memory, at a fraction of the price of equivalent professional NVIDIA hardware, seems worth exploring.

I understand that the Ascend software ecosystem is significantly different from CUDA, Metal, and ROCm, and that the Ascend 310P is not Huawei's latest architecture.

I'm not asking for an immediate implementation.

Before investing in the hardware, I'd primarily like to understand whether the architecture is technically viable, what the major obstacles would be, and whether it could be an interesting direction for DwarfStar.

Thanks for your work and for making this project open source!

title: Metal: g_transient_buffers not reaped on shared-event drain success paths (bounded on main, unbounded under owner-scoped reaping)
body:
## Summary

Both shared-event drain helpers in `ds4_metal.m` clear `g_transient_buffers` on their drained-error branches but return success **without clearing**:

- `ds4_gpu_commit_and_wait_selected_readback()` (ds4_metal.m:10417) — reached when IQ2/MXFP4 selected-shared-overlap decode runs without the default async selected-load worker (`DS4_METAL_DISABLE_STREAMING_SELECTED_ASYNC_LOAD`, or worker start failure: the `else if` drain at ds4.c:27091), and on the Q4 overlap lane (`DS4_METAL_Q4_SELECTED_OVERLAP_SHARED`).
- `ds4_gpu_signal_batch_and_wait_event()` (ds4_metal.m:11816) — opt-in via `DS4_METAL_Q4_SELECTED_SHARED_EVENT`.

Every non-event drain clears wholesale via `ds4_gpu_finish_command_buffer()` (`removeAllObjects`), so the intended invariant is "the list only holds buffers of not-yet-drained batches". The success returns break it: entries for an already-signaled batch linger until the next non-event drain (at latest the next `end_commands` at layer or token close). On `main` the window is therefore **bounded** - late release of finished buffer refs, and a slightly larger one-time reap - but any reaper that filters by owner or generation instead of clearing wholesale turns the same lingering refs into **unbounded retention with an O(list) scan at every reap**. Metal-only; CUDA/ROCm do not compile `ds4_metal.m`.

## Reproduce (bounded but visible on main)

`DS4_METAL_CB_TIMES=1` already prints the transient list count + bytes at drains. With a V4.1-family Q2 (IQ2_XXS gate/up + Q2_K down, e.g. `ds41f-q2`) and `--ssd-streaming DS4_METAL_DISABLE_STREAMING_SELECTED_ASYNC_LOAD=1`, the count observed at each non-event reap includes buffers from batches the event path finished long before; with the success-path clear they do not.

## Why we care: our fork makes the same defect unbounded

Our fork reworks this pool to owner-scoped reaping (`release_transient` scans and filters by retaining thread). Under that contract the never-reaped success path is catastrophic - same two missing clears, no wholesale backstop:

- list grew ~90 entries per decoded token (3 -> 129,440 in ~2 minutes); surviving conversation switches, reset only by process restart
- decode decayed 19 -> 2.5 t/s within one agentic session; flat 19 t/s after restoring reap symmetry
- `ds4-bench` (same machine, 2048..65536, gen 128, back-to-back): 64k `gen_tps` **6.58 -> 23.76**; first-token 326 -> 201 ms; the pre-fix curve decays inside a single bench run (late/early 0.34)

## Proposed fix

A two-line PR (clear on both success returns, mirroring the functions' own error branches) - posted shortly; author: nazerim.

## Asks (beyond the fix)

1. Reap symmetry on all drain paths.
2. Design suggestion, not a patch commitment: a helper (or assert) so inserts and reaps cannot drift apart if the pool's element contract changes - the class of bug that bit our fork at exactly that seam.
3. Optional: per-thread entry lists instead of one global array scanned at every reap.

title: Clear transient buffers on shared-event drain success paths
body:
Fixes #1330

Adds the missing `[g_transient_buffers removeAllObjects];` on the success return of both shared-event drain helpers, mirroring what their own drained-error branches and `ds4_gpu_finish_command_buffer()` already do. Restores the invariant that the list only references buffers of not-yet-drained batches.

**Scope of behavior change:** only where these helpers are the drain - IQ2/MXFP4 overlap with the async selected-load path disabled (or after a worker start failure), the Q4 overlap lane env, and the `DS4_METAL_Q4_SELECTED_SHARED_EVENT` readback path. Default Metal configs keep byte-identical results; on the default lanes this just releases already-signaled refs at the same point the error branches do. CUDA/ROCm binaries are unaffected (they do not compile `ds4_metal.m`). The motivation is a reaper variant (our fork's owner-scoped pool) where the missing success-path reap turns bounded lingering into unbounded accumulation and a measured 19 -> 2.5 t/s decode decay; full data and reproduction in #1330.

## Testing (per CONTRIBUTING.md)

- Machine/backend/quant: M5 Max 128 GB, Metal, `ds41f-q2` (V4.1 Flash IQ2_XXS/Q2_K imatrix), `--ssd-streaming`.
- `make clean && make && DS4_TEST_SSD_STREAMING=1 make test`: green except `--long-context` and `--tool-call-quality`, which fail **identically on the pre-patch build** at `ds4_session_create(engine, 100000)` (harness opens the 341 GiB Q2 without streaming cache budget; model-family scope, not patch scope). `--metal-kernels`, `--server`, agent/TP/unit suites pass.
- `ds4-bench` before/after, identical sweep 2048..65536, gen 128, greedy, back-to-back, same thermal state: 64k `gen_tps` 6.58 -> 23.76, first-token 326 -> 201 ms, mean gen 12.70 -> 22.24 (absolute magnitudes are the fork-pool substrate; delta direction and invariant are what upstream gets).

title: Metal resident mode: queue residency set floods the kernel log with `required > max` (2× model size)
body:
## Summary

On an M4 Max with 128 GB, running `ds4-server` built from current `main` (b3f5018) with a resident (non-streaming) load of a 96.4 GB DeepSeek V4 Flash GGUF, the kernel rejects GPU command preparation about **75,000 times a minute**. Each rejection reports that the command needs **twice the size of the Metal model views**: 195 GB against `maxWired` 115.4 GB. With `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_QUEUE_RESIDENCY_SET=1` the count is **zero**, and decode speed is the same. We have tested the env switch only; we have not tested a code fix.

## Repro on main (b3f5018)

```
make ds4-server
./ds4-server -m <model>.gguf --ctx 32768 --port 8011                                         # A
DS4_METAL_DISABLE_QUEUE_RESIDENCY_SET=1 ./ds4-server -m <model>.gguf --ctx 32768 --port 8011  # B
```

Each phase served ~3 minutes of `/v1/completions` decoding (15 requests × 400 tokens). Afterwards we counted the kernel's lines for `ds4-server` in each phase's window with `log show --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS "required > max"'`.

| | A: default | B: `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_QUEUE_RESIDENCY_SET=1` |
|---|---|---|
| window | 22:13:04 – 22:16:24 | 22:16:34 – 22:19:47 |
| `required > max` lines | **246,023** (58,062 · 79,671 · 77,047 · 31,243 per clock minute) | **0** |
| `FAILED To Free` lines | 1 | 0 |
| decode speed (mean per request) | 33.1 tok/s | 33.5 tok/s |
| completions | 15/15 | 15/15 |

A typical line from phase A:

```
kernel (IOGPUFamily) virtual IOReturn IOGPUCommandDescriptor::prepare(uint32_t) <ds4-server> (<private>) :
  required > max : requiredBytes = <195042312192> preparedBytes : <195041263616>
  maxWired = <115448725504> maxWiredInternal = <14431092736> currentWired = <99449323520>
```

90% of the lines (222,004) carry exactly `requiredBytes = 195042312192`. The rest range from 195.04 to 199.81 GB. During the phase, `currentWired` stayed between 98.3 and 105.0 GB, **under** `maxWired`.

## The number is exactly twice the model views

`ds4-server` logs that it mapped the model as 2 overlapping shared buffers:

```
ds4: Metal model views created in 1.984 ms, residency requested in 2462.423 ms, warmup 14.684 ms (mapped 91913.67 MiB from offset 5.09 MiB)
ds4: Metal mapped mmaped model as 2 overlapping shared buffers
```

`ds4_gpu_add_model_view_range` overlaps adjacent views by the largest tensor plus a page. In this model the largest tensor is `blk.37.ffn_gate_exps.weight`, 1,140,850,688 B (MXFP4). So the two views add up to the mapped size plus about one tensor:

- requiredBytes / 2 = 97,521,156,096
- mapped size = file 96,383,787,904 − data offset 5,333,824 = 96,378,454,080
- difference = 1,142,702,016 = the largest tensor + 1,851,328 B (1.77 MiB)

So `requiredBytes` ≈ **2 × the summed length of the model views**. Those views are exactly the allocations in `g_model_residency_set` (`ds4_metal.m` ≈2213–2229). The flag only stops that set from being added to the command queue (`addResidencySet:`), and with it the count drops to zero. Our reading, not proven: the kernel's per-command budget counts these allocations once through the queue's residency set and again through the command's own use of the same buffers. If that is right, attaching the set to the queue buys nothing in resident mode that `requestResidency` doesn't already do, and it pushes every command over the wired limit.

## Same symptom on a longer run

We first saw this on our own build: upstream `fc80bd6` (2026-10-07) plus local patches to server request handling, steering and a lens readout. None of those patches touch residency, the model views or command-buffer setup. That build runs at ctx 393216 and serves for hours. Without the flag it logged about 48,000 lines a minute (48,346 · 49,653 · 39,900 in three consecutive minutes), with the identical `requiredBytes = 195042312192`. After a relaunch with the flag it logged **0 in the following 61 minutes**, with decode unchanged at about 25.5 tok/s at ctx ≈ 94k. That the value is identical at ctx 32k and ctx 393k is why we think it's the model views and not KV.

Without the flag, that server process exited twice in one afternoon while the log was flooding. **We have not shown that the flood caused those exits.**

## Environment

- macOS 27.0.1, Apple M4 Max, 128 GB, Metal backend
- `ds4-server` built from b3f5018 with the stock Makefile
- Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash, a custom imatrix requant (IQ2_XXS routed experts, Q2_K/Q8_0 elsewhere, some routed-expert layers in MXFP4), 96,383,787,904 bytes
- No other `DS4_METAL_*` variables set. In particular `DS4_METAL_NO_RESIDENCY` and `DS4_METAL_UNRETAINED_COMMAND_BUFFERS` were not set.

## Related, as far as we can tell

- **#931:** a commenter found that `DS4_METAL_DISABLE_QUEUE_RESIDENCY_SET=1` alone cured 120 s hangs on non-streaming requests, and asked what the flag risks. That is still unanswered. This may be the same cause, seen from the kernel log's side.
- **#845:** a commenter got one GPU hang with this flag *combined* with `UNRETAINED_COMMAND_BUFFERS`. We have not seen a hang with the flag alone (about an hour on our build, 3 minutes on main).
- **#638:** whole mmap-backed views are *actually* wired on first GPU use, in streaming mode. Ours is different: resident mode, an inflated *declared* `requiredBytes`, and actual wired memory stayed under the limit.
- Since our base, main has added a second queue-attached set for built weights (`g_weight_residency_set`), behind the same env gate. We haven't looked at whether it contributes.

## Not done (happy to do any of these)

- `make test` / `./ds4_test --metal-kernels` and a `ds4-bench` before/after with the flag
- a patch, e.g. not attaching the model set to the queue in resident mode, with a bench CSV
- a longer soak on main with the flag
