title: Barrier checkpoint writes before the rename that exposes them
body:
## Problem

`ds4_kvstore` publishes a checkpoint by writing `<path>.tmp.<pid>`, `fflush`ing,
`fclose`ing and `rename`ing it into place. Nothing between the last `fflush` and the
`rename` ensures the bytes have left the page cache — `ds4_kvstore.c` contains no `fsync`
at all (count 0 at `b3f5018`).

Entries are found by the sha1 of their prompt text and, on load, accepted on the strength
of the envelope: magic and header version, the payload-ABI byte, file size not below the
header's expectation, the header token count against the restored token count, and the
payload's own magic/version/layout tags. The stored text is re-hashed and compared against
the file name. **The KV rows behind it are not checked** — there is no checksum over the
payload anywhere in the file.

So a checkpoint whose *directory entry* survived while its *data* did not is accepted as a
valid cache hit carrying stale or zeroed rows. That is the difference between a slow
session and a wrong one: the load succeeds, the session resumes, and the next miss looks
like model behaviour.

A plain process crash is already safe — the kernel keeps the bytes and finishes writing
them. The exposure is a kernel panic (dirty pages die with the RAM while the rename can
still land through the journal), power loss, or a device that drops a volatile write
cache. This project documents targets where external NVMe is the norm — `docs/DGX_SPARK.md`
and `docs/STRIX_HALO.md` — which is the configuration this hazard needs.

## Change

`fsync(fileno(fp))` after the final `fflush`, before `fclose` and `rename`; on Apple
platforms additionally `fcntl(fileno(fp), F_FULLFSYNC)`, which asks the device to commit
what it holds in its own write cache. Both run while the file is still the hidden `.tmp`
name, so no observer can ever see a partially durable entry.

- **A barrier failure is a failed store.** `ok = false` ⇒ the existing cleanup skips the
  rename and unlinks the temp file. No visible-but-broken entry, no leaked temp file.
- **An unsupported ioctl degrades instead of failing.** `EINVAL`/`ENOTSUP`/`EOPNOTSUPP`
  leaves the checkpoint standing on `fsync` alone. Tolerating it also clears `errno`, so a
  rejected ioctl cannot later be reported as the reason an `fclose` appeared to fail.
- **`fsync` runs first** because `F_FULLFSYNC` on its own does not flush the buffer cache.
- **A compile-time `#error` on Apple builds if `F_FULLFSYNC` is not visible.** Not
  decoration: without `<fcntl.h>` the macro is undefined, the `#if` below it is skipped
  silently, and this becomes an `fsync`-only barrier with a clean warning-free build. I hit
  exactly that while writing the patch.

## Cost

Measured in a build of this path with temporary instrumentation around real stores (the
instrumentation is not in the diff; `grep -c BARRIER-PROBE` is 0 on the pushed commit):

| configuration | first barrier | second barrier, same file, nothing pending |
|---|---|---|
| this tree, internal NVMe, `--ssd-streaming`, 167–218 MiB checkpoints, Qwen3.8, 12 stores | **16.7 – 51.6 ms** | **3.7 – 4.1 ms** |
| our fork's build of the same path, external NVMe (journaled APFS), ~647 MiB checkpoints whose unbarriered `save=` was already ~166 ms | 4.05 ms mean over 6 stores | — |

The two runs bracket the real cost rather than agreeing, and the gap is not noise: the
calls themselves cost ~4 ms, and everything above that is writeback the kernel had not yet
performed. That write is not new work — without the barrier it happens asynchronously
later, or not at all before a power loss — but it now lands inside the store's synchronous
window. A store long enough for background writeback to finish sees only the floor.

Both syscalls returned 0 with `errno` 0 on all twelve stores, and the barrier's cost tracks
the amount of dirty data, which is consistent with real commits reaching media on the
internal volume. A success code alone cannot prove that for an external bridge, and I have
not tested one here.

Speed, since this is inference software: same machine, model and sweep, alternating order
(A/B/B/A, 2 reps per arm) because one run is not a speed result.

| | baseline `b3f5018` | this patch | delta | largest same-arm spread |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `prefill_tps` (mean over 32 context points) | 115.81 | 116.42 | **+0.52 %** | 0.92 % |
| `gen_tps` | 23.08 | 23.01 | **−0.27 %** | 1.47 % |

Each delta is smaller than the largest same-arm spread, so: no measurable regression. And
to be precise about what that evidence does and does not cover — `ds4_bench` has no
references to `ds4_kvstore`, so the sweep cannot exercise this patch at all. It is a
control on the inference path; the store numbers above measure what actually changed.

## Testing, and what is missing

- `make clean && make` on the upstream base: 0 errors, 0 warnings.
- `./ds4_test --server` → `server: OK`, `ds4 tests: ok`. That subset is model-independent
  (it does not open an engine), which is why it passes where the model-backed groups below
  cannot.
- **Full `make test` did not complete here, and I would rather say it than bury it.** The
  unmodified base commit fails the identical 17 cases (control run, same command), so
  nothing below is introduced by this patch — but I cannot claim a green suite. The
  reasons are environmental and mixed: most are `ds4_engine_open` refusals because the
  V4.1 test file needs ~156 GiB against a ~112 GiB safe budget; the DeepSeek V4-era files
  I also have are refused outright by this build (`required metadata key is missing:
  deepseek4.block_count`); and at least one is a model-free server unit assertion that
  fails on this base regardless. Tell me which fixture you run CI against and I will
  re-file with a full pass.
- **No new test, deliberately.** The store path needs a live engine and session
  (`ds4_session_write_staged_payload`), so it is not reachable from a model-free test, and
  the durability effect itself needs fault injection. I did not want to fake coverage for a
  change whose entire value is that the old code looked like it worked.
- Machine: Apple M5 Max, 128 GiB, macOS, Metal backend. Checkpoints went to an external
  NVMe/APFS volume in production and to the internal volume in the upstream-tree run; both
  are named because the cost differs between them.

**Platform scope: built and tested on macOS/Metal only. I am making no claim about Linux
or CUDA** — neither was built on nor run on such a host. The `fcntl` call sits under
`#if defined(F_FULLFSYNC)` and the `#error` fires only under `__APPLE__`, so a platform
without that macro compiles to `fsync` alone; that is a reading of the preprocessor, not a
measurement.

## Interaction with open work

#1343 edits `ds4_kvstore_store_live_prefix_text`, the same function this inserts into, in
the `fwrite` chain whose final `fflush` is the barrier's anchor. I expect at most a trivial
conflict and will rebase onto whichever lands first rather than leave that to you.

## Deliberately not included

- **No `fsync` of the directory after `rename`.** Losing a rename loses a checkpoint, which
  for a content-addressed cache is a safe miss. The hazard closed here is the reverse one:
  an entry that survives while its data does not.
- **No payload checksum.** The better fix — it detects corruption from any cause instead of
  closing one window for it — but it changes the on-disk format and adds a pass over
  hundreds of MiB. Happy to open a discussion.
- **Two sibling call sites in `ds4_agent.c`** write the same envelope through tmp→rename
  with no barrier either. Left alone deliberately: this fixes the disk-cache path the
  server reloads, and widening the blast radius makes a small correctness fix harder to
  review for no extra safety.
- The trailer update path opens an existing checkpoint with `fopen(path, "r+b")` and
  rewrites the trailer in place — a related atomicity gap, separate change.

title: Greedy completions change when --kv-disk-dir is enabled, because storing the cold checkpoint inserts an extra prefill boundary
body:
## Summary

For the same prompt, same binary, same build, `temperature 0`: requests to a server started with
`--kv-disk-dir` produce a different completion than requests to the same server started without it. Nothing is
being loaded from disk in the comparison — one side never touches the cache. The cause is that the cold
checkpoint write path syncs the session to `cold_store_len` *mid-prefill* so the checkpoint can be written,
which inserts an extra prefill chunk boundary; chunk boundaries change floating-point reduction order
(documented in `ds4.c`), and greedy decoding then compounds the flip.

The same mechanism makes completions depend on **which checkpoint survived eviction**: resuming from a
checkpoint that sits on the cold schedule's own boundary reproduces the cold answer exactly, while resuming
from a shallower mid-prefill (`reason=continued`) checkpoint merges the last two chunks and changes the answer.

## Reproduction

Verified on a clean `b3f5018` checkout built with `make`, `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q4.gguf`, macOS/Metal, shell with
`DS4_API_KEY` unset. Two servers, **one flag apart**, driven by `curl`. Nothing is read from disk on the second
server: its log contains zero `kv cache hit` and zero `kv cache stored` lines, while the first logs 2 hits and 4
stores.

Prompt, deterministic and corpus-free (76,011 chars, sha256 prefix `9dc9f22c81921e73`, `prompt_tokens = 13858`):

```sh
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
SENT = ("The catchment's baseflow is sustained by fractured bedrock rather than soil moisture, "
        "which decouples stream response from rainfall intensity. ")
doc = "Archive 0. " + (SENT * (76000 // len(SENT) + 1))[:76000]
open("prompt.json", "w").write(json.dumps({
    "model": "default",
    "messages": [
        {"role": "system", "content": doc},
        {"role": "user", "content": "In one paragraph, what single factor governs the effect described above, and why?"}],
    "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 256, "stream": False,
    "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}}))
PY

# A: disk KV on
mkdir -p /tmp/kva
./ds4-server --model MODEL.gguf --ctx 65536 --port 8079 --kv-disk-dir /tmp/kva &

# B: identical, minus --kv-disk-dir
./ds4-server --model MODEL.gguf --ctx 65536 --port 8079 &
```

Then POST `prompt.json` to each. The difference is visible in the logs without comparing any prose:

```
A:  chat ctx=0..13858:13858 prompt start
    prefill chunk 8192/13858 (59.1%)
    prefill chunk 12288/13858 (88.7%)        <-- cold-checkpoint sync; exists only with the cache
    prefill chunk 13858/13858 (100.0%)
    kv cache stored tokens=12288 trimmed=1570 reason=cold key=token-text size=482.82 MiB

B:  chat ctx=0..13858:13858 prompt start
    prefill chunk 8192/13858 (59.1%)
    prefill chunk 13858/13858 (100.0%)
```

The completions:

```
A  609 chars  sha256 9ecec8d5303ae277d66e1707231ae51e813748c8bfba3d3b70fac3bf9c8397a4
   "The single governing factor is the **geological structure of the bedrock**, specifically its fractured
    nature. This is because the fractured bedrock acts as the primary reservoir and conduit ..."

B  754 chars  sha256 417a4130d5e43f1536abcc9a1201e4452ae637c7e4881450f4986b7d430e8faa
   "The single governing factor is the **geological structure of the catchment**, specifically the presence
    of **fractured bedrock**. This factor dictates the hydrological pathway because it shifts ..."
```

A second prompt (`"Archive 1. "`) behaves the same way: **A** 707 chars `1be64c1daffd...`, **B** 615 chars `225c29c7f71b...`.

**Determinism is asserted, not assumed.** Each config was requested twice and the two replies within a config
were byte-identical. That is what rules out run order and noise, so it is worth repeating if you try this.

One extra observation from those repeats: in server A the second request did not re-run the prefill - it logged
`kv cache hit text tokens=12288` then `chat ctx=12288..13858:1570 prompt start`, a real disk resume - and produced
a completion **identical to the cold one**. The checkpoint is therefore fine; resuming at the cold boundary is
faithful. What changes the answer is the chunk schedule, however you arrive at it.

Any prompt where the cold boundary lands strictly inside the prompt reproduces this; the defaults
(`cold_max_tokens` 30000, `min_tokens` 512) already bracket 13,858 tokens, so no cache tuning is involved.

## Measured

| comparison | my fork (same base commit) | upstream `b3f5018` |
|---|---|---|
| cold **disk ON** vs cold **disk OFF**, real prose ~12k tokens | **6 / 6 differ** | **4 / 6 differ** |
| cold disk ON vs resume at the cold boundary (`ctx=10240`) | 0 / 28 differ | 0 / 8 differ |
| cold disk ON vs resume at a mid-prefill checkpoint (`ctx=8192`) | 8 / 8 differ | 7 / 8 differ |
| resume@8192 vs cold disk OFF (same merged tail chunk) | 6 / 6 **identical** | not run |

The top row is the headline and needs no checkpoint read at all: same prompt, same binary, one flag different.
Across the ten divergent pairs, median character-level similarity is **0.30** (range 0.059-0.757) and the
first difference appears ~100-230 characters in: substantively different answers, not different wording.

The 6-vs-4 difference between the two builds on the top row is **not** a claim that the fork is
worse. At n=6 the
Fisher exact two-sided p is 0.455; what is claimed is only that both builds change answers when the boundary
moves (pooled 10/12).

Upstream ran the *same* prompts (identical token counts, identical chunk schedules, calibration reproduced to
six decimals) and two of the six came back byte-identical. A moved reduction order is a chance of flipping the
argmax, not a guarantee of it - which is what makes this an amplification effect rather than corruption, and is
why the `resume@8192 == cold-disk-off` cell is the load-bearing one for "the checkpoint is faithful".

## Not claimed

* **Not a state-corruption bug.** The mid-prefill `continued` checkpoint restores engine state faithfully —
  the `resume@8192 == cold-disk-off` result is what establishes that, and I checked the checkpoint inventory
  (per-layer GDN recurrent and conv state, attention K/V and index keys, PLE history, mRoPE delta, position
  rows) before concluding it.
* **macOS/Metal only.** Every number here was measured on that backend; no claim is made about CUDA, ROCm
  or Linux, and no measurement was attempted there.
* **No claim that either completion is worse.** Both are fluent; the complaint is that output is a function of
  cache configuration and cache history, not quality.
* **Sample size is small and the prompt range narrow.** Twelve realistic prompts in total across both builds,
  all ~12k tokens of English technical prose. The repetitive synthetic corpus was tested first and showed the
  same effect (6/6), so this is not a corpus artifact; but short prompts are unmeasured, where the tail chunk
  is large relative to the 8192 prefix and the rate may well be lower.

## Why it matters

`--kv-disk-dir` is meant to be a transparent latency optimisation, so any deployment that enables it is
serving the split-schedule answers, for every prompt where the cold boundary lands inside the prompt
(with the defaults, 512-30000 tokens). A/B measurements over the disk cache are
also not comparable across cache states, which is how I found this: two runs with identical binaries and
identical schedules agreed on only 247 of 440 replies, because eviction left them different checkpoints and
therefore different resume depths. The eviction score is dominated by a per-checkpoint fixed payload cost
rather than by usefulness (for zero-hit entries it reduces to "evict the fewest-token file"), so which
checkpoints survive, and therefore which chunk schedule a later request runs, is decided by size rather
than by reuse value.

## Possible directions to discuss

1. Write the cold checkpoint from an already-computed boundary instead of forcing a new one (avoid the extra
   sync), if the state at an existing chunk edge is sufficient.
2. Fix a canonical chunk schedule per absolute prompt position so that boundary insertion/removal does not
   change reduction order for the tokens after it.
3. Prefer checkpoints that lie on the cold schedule when several are valid, making resume shape-stable.
4. Or document that enabling the disk cache can change greedy outputs, so nobody is surprised by it.

I would not attempt (2) without your view on the cost.

title: Keep Metal queues warm for distributed Kimi inference
body:
This patch uses the existing `ds4_gpu_warm_command_queue()` to keep Metal queues from going idle. When serving across two nodes (m3 ultra 512gb + m5 ultra 512gb in my testing) this prevents 4+ second stalls, taking prefill from 3.88 tok/s to 69.93 tok/s on short contexts and decode from 0.09 tok/s to 5 tok/s.

I used the existing converter to build the K3.1 gguf used for testing:

https://huggingface.co/fairfieldt/Kimi-K3.1-Pro-IQ2_XXS-Q2_K-GGUF

title: Render DeepSeek V4.1 effort for low and medium reasoning
body:
## Problem

`ds4_deepseek41_reasoning_effort_text()` writes V4.1's numeric "Reasoning Effort" line only for `high`/`xhigh` (75) and `max` (100). `DS4_THINK_LOW` and `DS4_THINK_MEDIUM` are named modes, not numeric levels, so `ds4_think_mode_level()` returns -1 for them and the function returns NULL. A client that sends `reasoning_effort` `"low"`, `"minimal"` or `"medium"` gets thinking turned on with no effort line in the prompt at all.

Traced on `b3f5018` through `ds4-server --trace`, with Hermes Agent sending each level (`--reasoning <level>`):

| client sends | think_mode | rendered |
|---|---|---|
| none | none | no thinking |
| minimal | low | **no effort line** |
| low | low | **no effort line** |
| medium | medium | **no effort line** |
| high / xhigh | high | Reasoning Effort: 75 |
| max | max | Reasoning Effort: 100 |

## Change

Map low to 50, which is what DeepSeek's V4.1 encoder does (`REASONING_EFFORT_MAPPINGS`: `"low": 50, "high": 75, "max": 100` in `encoding/encoding.py`). The encoder has no medium; this uses 62, between low and high. That value is a choice, not something DeepSeek specifies, and I'm happy to change it. Numeric levels (`"30"`) are unchanged. GLM and Qwen rendering is untouched.

A test in `test_reasoning_effort_mapping` checks the effort prefix for low, medium, high, max, none and a numeric level.

## Testing

M5 Max 128 GB, Metal, `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-IQ2_XXS-Q2_K-imatrix.gguf` (the `ds41f-q2` download) with `--ssd-streaming`.

- `make clean && make`, no warnings; `./ds4_test --server` passes.
- With the parent's `ds4.c`, the new test fails twice (low and medium); with the fix it passes.
- The same trace with the patch: minimal/low → 50, medium → 62, high/xhigh → 75, max → 100, none → no thinking.
- This changes prompt text only, not kernels or the inference graph, so I did not run speed or logprob vectors.

title: Render GLM low reasoning as Low
body:
## Problem

GLM 5.3's chat template (`zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash`, `chat_template.jinja`) has three effort levels:

```jinja
{%- set effective_reasoning_effort = reasoning_effort if reasoning_effort is defined and reasoning_effort in ['low', 'high'] else 'max' -%}
```

`ds4_glm_reasoning_effort_text()` collapses `DS4_THINK_LOW` to `Reasoning Effort: High`, so a client asking for low effort gets high. `test_reasoning_effort_mapping` asserts that mapping, so it may be deliberate; if it is, I'd like to know the reason.

## Change

Render `Reasoning Effort: Low` for `DS4_THINK_LOW` and update the assertion. `DS4_THINK_MEDIUM` stays High. The template would send medium (and anything else, including xhigh) to Max, but changing that would raise effort for clients that send medium today, so I left it alone and am raising it here as a question instead.

## Testing

M5 Max 128 GB, Metal, `GLM-5.3-Flash-Q2.gguf`, resident.

- `make clean && make`, no warnings; `./ds4_test --server` passes. With the parent's `ds4.c` the updated assertion fails; with the fix it passes.
- Live trace: Hermes Agent sends `reasoning_effort: "low"`, `think_mode: low`, and the rendered prompt carries `Reasoning Effort: Low`.
- The level has a real effect. On seven CPython 3.14 bug fixes run as agent tasks (two runs each, same harness, the fix's own tests hidden), GLM at Low generated 84–130K tokens across the seven tasks against 261–370K at High, finished in 1.3–1.9 h against 4.0–6.7 h, and hit the one-hour task limit 0 times against 7. It resolved 4–5 of 7 tasks either way.
- Prompt text only; no kernel or graph change, so no speed or logprob runs.

title: Lower Python-style Qwen booleans when the tool schema says boolean
body:
Qwen3.8 writes boolean tool arguments Python-style:

```
<tool_call>
<function=set_light>
<parameter=on>
True
</parameter>
...
```

`True` is not valid JSON, so `parse_qwen_generated_message_ex` emitted `"on": "True"` (a string). Clients that validate arguments against the tool schema (opencode, openHAB-style function calling) reject or mishandle the call.

Fix: when the tool schema declares the parameter as `boolean`, lower `True`/`False` to `true`/`false`. `qwen_param_declared_string` is generalised to `qwen_param_declared_type(..., want)`; parameters declared as `string` still keep the literal text (covered by the new test).

**Tests**
- `make ds4_test && ./ds4_test --server` → `server: OK` (new `test_qwen_python_bool_with_boolean_schema`)
- Mac Studio M5 Max 128 GB, Metal, Qwen3.8 Flash Next Q4: a set_light probe (`{"room": enum, "on": boolean}`) went from 0/3 to 3/3 correct `{"on":true,...}`; opencode `edit` with `replaceAll=true` now receives a JSON boolean.
- No backend or kernel code touched, so no speed impact.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: ROCm SSD streaming on a 32 GB discrete gfx1201: device-resident non-routed weights cap the expert cache, long prompts thrash
body:
### Setup

- GPU: AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, discrete, 32 GB VRAM), ROCm 7.2.2, Linux 7.0
- Host: 32 cores, 121 GiB RAM. The GGUF is on NVMe behind dm-crypt + LVM (`max_sectors_kb` 128 on every layer); `dd bs=16M` reads the GGUF at 1.3 GB/s
- Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash Q2 (`ds4f-q2`, 80.8 GiB)
- ds4 at b3f5018 plus a local build patch for gfx1201 (`DS4_ROCM_NO_WMMA`, same idea as #558 / #599 / #744), built with `make strix-halo ROCM_ARCH=gfx1201 ROCM_EXTRA_CFLAGS=-DDS4_ROCM_NO_WMMA`
- Server: `ds4-server --rocm --ctx 100000 --ssd-streaming --ssd-streaming-cache-experts <N> --kv-disk-dir <dir> --kv-disk-space-mb 16384`, with `DS4_ROCM_STREAM_FREE_RESERVE_GB=2`

### Baseline: June build

80ebbc3 (2026-06-17) with the same gfx1201 patch and `--ssd-streaming-cache-experts 22GB`: about 2.4 tok/s decode (median of our runs), and a 6.2K-token prompt answered in about 87 s end to end (median).

### b3f5018 on the same machine

| `--ssd-streaming-cache-experts` | Short prompt (13 tokens) | ~4K-token prompt |
|---|---|---|
| 22GB | first request fails (log below) | — |
| 16GB | 3.6 tok/s decode | 3,854 tokens: prefill not finished after 16 min |
| 10GB | 1.3 tok/s decode | prefill 17.5 tok/s (1,806 new tokens; the first 2,048 came from the KV disk cache), decode 1.0 tok/s |
| 16GB + `DS4_ROCM_STREAM_NO_DIRECT=1` | 2.1 tok/s decode | 4,215 tokens: prefill 202 s, decode 1.3 tok/s |

So short prompts are faster than the June build at 16GB, but prompts of a few thousand tokens become unusable, and smaller caches slow decode to about 1 tok/s.

22GB, first request:

```
ds4: ROCm model arena alloc failed for stream_span (144.79 MiB request): out of memory
ds4: ROCm streaming model cache allocation failed for stream_span range 144.79 MiB; refusing host-pointer fallback
ds4: ROCm streaming model range stream_span at offset 74.94 GiB is not device-cached; refusing host-pointer fallback
... finish=error error="rocm decode failed"
```

16GB, during the 3,854-token prompt (repeated many times):

```
ds4: ROCm q8 fp16 cache budget exhausted; using q8 kernels (request=16.00 MiB cached=0.00 GiB limit=3.98 GiB free=1.86 GiB reserve=2.00 GiB total=31.86 GiB)
ds4: ROCm releasing 0.06 GiB q8 fp16 cache for streaming model spans (request=1.86 GiB free=3.48 GiB reserve=2.00 GiB)
ds4: ROCm loading model tensors 0.06 GiB cached
```

The "loading model tensors" progress went from 0 to 8.69 GiB several times within that one prompt, and the process read 295 GiB from storage (`read_bytes` in `/proc/<pid>/io`).

Read profile (`DS4_ROCM_STREAM_READ_PROFILE=1`):

```
16GB: jobs=57180 bytes=125.64 GiB read=1596611.897 ms upload=8973.606 ms wait=64320.049 ms avg_job=28.079 ms avg_wait=10.430 ms
10GB: jobs=89643 bytes=196.97 GiB read=1846913.778 ms upload=14895.318 ms wait=199385.918 ms avg_job=20.769 ms avg_wait=20.670 ms
```

About 2.25 MiB per job at 20–28 ms each, roughly 0.5 GB/s overall, on a disk that streams the same file at 1.3 GB/s.

### What I think is happening

Since the September builds the non-routed weights (8.2 GiB for this GGUF: attention 5.37, shared experts 1.07, `token_embd` 0.99, output 0.52, other 0.25) must be device-resident: `cuda_model_range_ptr_from_fd()` refuses the host-pointer fallback. They sit on top of the expert cache, so on 32 GB the cache tops out near 16 GB. During a long prefill the q8→fp16 cache, the prefill expert reserve and the spans compete for the last GiBs; spans get evicted and reloaded from disk at the ~0.5 GB/s above. The June build kept those weights in host memory and ran with 22 GB of experts.

### Page cache experiment (no gain)

Local patch: no O_DIRECT fd and no `POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED`, so spans and experts go through the page cache, pre-warmed with `dd`. Not better: a 4,094-token prompt took 98 s of prefill, the next 4,215-token one 165 s, then decode stalled; 358 GiB were still read from disk, and afterwards only 34.5 GiB of the GGUF was resident. Prefill scans ~72 GiB of experts per prompt and the page cache left by other processes is smaller than the 80.8 GiB model, so LRU evicts each page before it is reused. This matches the reasoning in #629.

### Questions

1. Would an opt-in to keep the non-routed weights in host memory on discrete GPUs (what the June build did) be acceptable for ROCm?
2. During prefill, could eviction prefer the q8→fp16 cache or experts over non-routed spans?
3. Is a routing-aware host-RAM tier for experts like #629 planned for ROCm as well? With 121 GiB of RAM it would cover most of this model.
4. Are `DS4_ROCM_STREAM_MODEL_CACHE_GB` or `DS4_ROCM_STREAM_Q8_F16_CACHE_GB` worth trying here? I have not tuned them.

Happy to run more measurements or test a branch. Related: #16, #629, #858.

title: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next decode on M5 Max: in-situ per-kernel breakdown, MTP depth, n-gram speculation estimate, and some negative results
body:
**Not a bug report.** I measured where the decode time goes for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on an M5 Max, and I would like to share the data and hear what others see (other chips, the official quants). Everything below was measured with `DS4_METAL_ENCODER_TIMELINE`, which gives per-kernel GPU timestamps in situ.

*Disclosure: the measurements and this write-up were done with Claude Code on my machine.*

## Setup

- M5 Max (40-core GPU), 128 GB. Source: `main` at `ce4ac36`, plus local diagnostics gated by env vars that were inactive in these runs.
- Model: a third-party Qwen3.8-Flash-Next quant: dense tensors Q8_0, routed `down` Q8_0, routed `gate`/`up` Q4_K (45 layers) and Q8_0 (4 layers), hyper-connection tensors F16, router F32. So the `moe_mid_q4k_nr1` numbers below are Q4_K gate/up.
- Decode only. `ds4-bench`, ctx 1024, greedy, 62 tokens after warm-up (51.5 t/s in the bench; the server gives 55.6 t/s at temp 0).

## Roofline

- Bytes read per decoded token (excluding KV and the n-gram table, routed experts counted as 10/512): **7.34 GB**.
- Metal read microbenchmark: best 598 / 584 / 509 GB/s for 1 / 4 / 16 GiB buffers (Apple quotes 614 GB/s).
- 55.6 t/s means about 408 GB/s, roughly 70% of the best measured. So the theoretical headroom is about 1.3-1.4x, not 2x.

## Where the time goes

GPU busy time is 18.58 ms out of a 19.50 ms token period in normal mode (95%), and 18.62 ms with the timeline enabled, so the per-kernel durations are representative. Wall time is attributed without double counting (the two GDN projections `qkv` and `z` run concurrently, so they are counted as one pair). Weight bytes for the MoE kernels include the shared expert (grid y = 11).

| kernel | calls/token | us/call | ms/token | MB/call | GB/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GDN `qkv` + `z` (q8_0 mul_mv, concurrent pair) | 36 | 84 | 3.11 | 44.6 | 530 |
| `ssm_out` / `attn_output` (q8_0 mul_mv) | 49 | 34.5 | 1.69 | 16.7 | 484 |
| `attn_q` (q8_0 mul_mv) | 12 | 64.4 | 0.77 | 33.4 | 519 |
| output head (q8_0 mul_mv) | 1 | 1150 | 1.13 | 675 | 587 |
| `moe_mid_q4k_nr1` | 44 | 51.7 | 2.28 | 21.9 | 424 |
| `moe_mid` (Q8 layers) | 4 | 88.4 | 0.35 | 38.3 | 433 |
| `moe_down` | 48 | 44.5 | 2.14 | 19.2 | 430 |
| `hc_gate_mix_f16_pf` | 97 | 15.5 | 1.50 | 6.55 | 424 |
| `hc` F16 GEMV (`mul_mv_f16_f32_4`) | 97 | 10.1 | 0.98 | 6.55 | 650 (*) |
| `hc_norm_f16` | 96 | 10.3 | 0.99 | | |
| router blend + top-k, `moe_reduce` | 48 each | 7.5 / 8.0 / 8.8 | 0.74 + 0.42 | | |
| `gdn_front` / `gdn_scan` / `gdn_out` | 36 each | 9.5 / 9.3 / 3.2 | 0.79 | | |
| `attn_prep` / `attn_decode` / `attn_merge` / idx / k,v `multi_gemv` | 12 (idx: 3) | 31 / 47 / 14 / 14 / 17 | 1.15 + 0.21 | | |
| `hc_combine` | 48 | 6.0 | 0.29 | | |

(*) above the 614 GB/s rating, so presumably partly SLC hits; do not read it as DRAM bandwidth.

Families: routed experts + router 5.9 ms (32%), mixer (GDN + attention) 7.7 ms (41%), hyper-connections 3.8 ms (20%), head 1.1 ms (6%). Attention cost grows with context; this is at ctx 1024.

What I take from it:

1. The dense Q8_0 GEMVs and the head are already at 484-587 GB/s. There is little left there.
2. The routed-expert kernels sit at 424-433 GB/s for both Q4_K and Q8_0, so they do not look dequantization-bound. They are short (45-52 us) and sit in a dependent chain. The three expert kernels read about 2.0 GB/token: 3.64 ms at 560 GB/s versus 4.77 ms measured, so roughly 1 ms is on the table if they reached ~530 GB/s (what a scattered-read microbenchmark reaches).
3. About 470 dispatches of 10 us or less (`hc_norm`, `hc_combine`, `router_topk`, `moe_reduce`, `gdn_*`, `attn_prep`...) add up to about 4 ms (23%), out of about 800 dispatches per token. An empty dependent dispatch plus barrier costs about 1.1 us in a microbenchmark, so fusing saves roughly 1-3 us per removed boundary (my estimate: 0.3-0.5 ms for 100-200 fusions), not much.
4. The GPU is idle 0.92 ms/token (5%): 0.47 ms between tokens (sampling/readback) and 0.42 ms before the large command buffer (the first three command buffers, layers 0-3, last only 0.4 / 0.5 / 0.8 ms, then the CPU has not finished encoding the 16.9 ms one). This may be cheap to shave by splitting the early command buffers differently.

## MTP depth (maybe worth a docs note)

Reading `qwen4_spec_depth`, `DS4_QWEN4_MTP_DEPTH=2` or `3` force a depth and any other value (0, 1, unset) selects the auto policy. At production sampling (temp 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, thinking), 4 synthetic prompts, pooled n=14: no MTP 55.2 t/s, auto 57.9 t/s (+5%), forced 3 53.8 t/s (-2.5%); forced 2 gave about 50.8 t/s but with only n=6, so it is noisy. Forward wall time per verify pass: 1 row 17.7 ms, 2 rows 23.5 ms, 3 rows 29.4 ms, i.e. each extra verified row costs about 0.33 of a decode step, close to the whole MoE family's time, which is consistent with the experts being re-read for each row. Small samples and synthetic prompts, so treat this as indicative. It suggests that forcing depth 3 can lose at temp > 0.

## n-gram / prompt-lookup drafter for Qwen? (estimate only, nothing implemented)

#396 and #1167 do prompt lookup for V4 (greedy). For Qwen at temp > 0 the building blocks seem to exist already in `ds4_session_qwen4_spec_cycle` (3-row verify with GDN state snapshots and point-mass exact acceptance), so the missing parts would be the lookup and decoupling from the MTP head state.

Simulation: 56 real agentic (OpenCode) sessions, 2.14 M generated tokens, tokenized with the real tokenizer; a draft counts as accepted when the recorded sampled token equals it; cost model from the measured row cost above. Result: about +9% overall (n-gram of 5-6 tokens, 2 drafts); per session median +7%, min +3%, max +24%. By token type: tool calls +20%, text +2%, reasoning +1%. Longer drafts are worse (4+ drafts: +5% or less). Caveats: the history does not include the system prompt or tool schemas, the MTP + n-gram hybrid is not simulated, and the snapshot cost with exact sampling is not measured. It is about the size of the auto-MTP gain and probably not additive with it.

## Negative results (so nobody has to redo them)

- Skipping a kernel (ablation) over-attributes: `gdn_front` "costs" 2.3 ms when skipped but about 0.2 ms when the kernel is repeated, because the downstream data changes. The timeline is much more reliable.
- Prefetching the next kernel's weights into the SLC: the SLC keeps about 32-48 MiB hot at about 980 GB/s versus about 530 GB/s from DRAM (microbenchmark with a checksum check). A separate prefetch dispatch running concurrently with a chain of dependent kernels does not hide: it adds roughly its own duration (+25 us with 128 threadgroups, +41 us with 32), whether the barriers are resource-scoped or global. Piggybacking read-only threadgroups on the small kernels gives 0% (20 MiB) to -2.6% (45 MiB) of the iteration at best. The routed experts cannot be prefetched anyway: the router result is known about 8 us before `moe_mid`.

## Questions

1. Does anyone see better than about 430 GB/s on the routed-expert kernels (M3 Ultra / M4 Max, official Q4_K quant)? Any idea for `moe_mid_q4k_nr1`?
2. Is there interest in a Qwen n-gram drafter with exact sampling, given an estimate of +5-10%?
3. Is the 0.4 ms stall before the main command buffer known or intentional?
4. Should the MTP depth semantics (2/3 force, anything else is auto) be documented?

I can share the analysis scripts. I am happy to turn any of this into PRs that follow AGENT.md, but I would not do it without feedback first.

title: Restart the Qwen draft depth policy on new prompt tokens
body:
The adaptive draft depth of the Qwen3.8 MTP cycle (`qwen4_spec_depth`) keeps four fields in the session: the first-draft acceptance window, the cycle count, the second-draft rejection streak and the engaged flag. Nothing clears them, so a request opens with the state left by the previous answer. On `ds4-server` the same temperature-zero request is then drafted on a different schedule of 2-row and 3-row cycles depending on what the process served before.

This PR clears the four fields in the Qwen branch of session sync when there are new prompt tokens to evaluate. It is 10 lines in `ds4.c`.

## What I could test

I have no Metal or CUDA machine, and main does not run Qwen on ROCm, so **on main this is only build-checked**:

- `make ds4.o` (Linux default flags, which compile the Qwen GPU code in `ds4.c`; the new lines are in the preprocessed source): no warnings;
- `make cpu`: no warnings;
- `make test-qwen4-mtp-policy`: PASS.

The behaviour was tested with the same hunk on the ROCm port of #1070 (Q2 model, Radeon 8060S gfx1151, ROCm 10.1). That branch predates `92f57fc`, so the tree also carried a stopgap that initializes the predictor cache rows; details are in [this comment](https://github.com/antirez/ds4/pull/1070#issuecomment-7082310629).

The check sends three prompts (prose, code, a 6.9K-token prompt) to one server process at temperature 0, 384 tokens each, ordered so that each prompt follows itself and each of the others. Every request is compared with the first send of the same prompt, on the answer text and on the `DS4_QWEN4_SPEC_TRACE` cycle trace.

| | Different trace | Different text |
|---|---|---|
| Without the hunk | 5 of 10 requests | 2 of 10 (both prose) |
| With the hunk | 0 of 10 | 0 of 10 |

With the hunk, three processes that each start with a different prompt (18 requests) also give the same text and trace per prompt.

## What I do not know

- On ROCm the text changes because verify passes of 2 and 3 rows are not bit-identical. I could not check whether that is also the case on Metal or CUDA. If it is not, the effect there is limited to the draft schedule, so to the speed and acceptance numbers of a request.
- Requests that extend a kept transcript, temperature above 0 and image turns were not tested.

## Cost

After each new prompt the policy needs 8 cycles again before it can engage the second draft. On the ROCm port the server decode speed did not change with this hunk and the cache stopgap together (prose 31.2–31.3, code 38.6 tok/s, against 31.1–31.2 and 38.5–38.7 before).

If carrying the acceptance window from one request to the next is intended, feel free to close this.
